title: Initial considerations
text:
This section covers some initial considerations that NSOs are recommended to review before setting out to use alternative data sources in the production of consumer price statistics. 
Section contents:

Overview of alternative data sources — This page contains a general introduction to each of the alternative data sources used to compile consumer price indices. 
Why use alternative data sources? Strategic motivations — Common reasons shared by NSOs as a driver for using these new data sources.
Key challenges and trade-offs — Alternative data sources introduce a number of challenges and trade-offs that National Statistical Offices (NSOs) must actively manage.
Key decision points — The adoption of alternative data sources involves a sequence of related decisions that shape both the technical and organisational direction of implementation.
Resource implications and organisational readiness — The adoption of alternative data sources typically requires a different mix of resources and capabilities compared with traditional survey-based price collection.



Overview
In this Handbook we define alternative data sources as data sources that differ from traditional price collection in how price information is generated, observed and accessed.
The use of alternative data sources has the potential to fundamentally change how consumer price statistics are produced. These include transaction data such as scanner data, e-invoice data and administrative transaction data where prices are associated with actual purchases and typically include information on quantities or expenditures, and non-transaction data such as web-scraped data and online advertisements data, where prices reflect posted or offered prices but typically do not include quantities, expenditures or confirmation that a transaction has occurred. Both types of data sources offer potential improvements in coverage, accuracy and efficiency. 
However, before moving to implementation, national statistical offices (NSOs) are encouraged to take a structured and deliberate approach to assessing why alternative data sources are being introduced, what role they are intended to play within the index framework, and how they can be integrated into existing statistical processes. Early decisions in these areas can have lasting implications for index design, operational practices and resource requirements.
This section sets out key considerations relevant during the early stages of exploration and planning. It is intended to support informed decision-making and to help NSOs identify the areas that require more detailed investigation, many of which are addressed in subsequent chapters of the Handbook.
While this Handbook focuses on the use of alternative data sources in the production of consumer price statistics, many of the data sources and processes described are also relevant to other areas of official statistics, including purchasing power parities, national accounts, business price indices, and business statistics. Where appropriate, the handbook highlights considerations that may support broader reuse of data across statistical domains, while recognising that conceptual requirements and methodological choices may differ.

title: Monitoring, validation and plausibility checks for scanner data
text:
Recommended checks to carry out on the incoming flows of scanner data



Monitoring, validation and plausibility checks for scanner data
Processing scanner data sets is a challenging task. The development of an automatic routine control for data on arrival is essential to identify, avoid and minimize errors on the processing of scanner data by National Statistical Offices (NSOs).
Eurostat's HICP - Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data suggests that monitoring data on arrival should be part of a quality framework for scanner data and describes several data quality indicators that should be adopted in this process, see Table 2 in the practical guide for more details. It also points that when dealing with such large data sets “errors are bound to occur and should be seen as acceptable within certain limits”. Hence, the monitoring and validation procedures will rely on the manual and automated control checks performed and the degree of severity that is attributed to inconsistencies found to produce the Consumer Price Index (CPI) or other statistics of interest.
Important checks to perform include:

check if the data was received
check if the data in the files received are in the right format and contain all the variables of interest (in the correct data type) as agreed with the supplier

If the data received by the retailer is disaggregated per store:

check if the data for all the stores is contained in the files and also check for important changes such as closure and opening of stores or whether a store has changed its category along time (for instance, a supermarket turning into a discount store) - see Ref. (1) for more details.

For the data received by each retailer/store:

check if the total revenue by retailer/store are within certain range limits which can be determined by the historical series
check if the number of article codes agree with previous rounds and if collecting a specific sample the target article codes are contained in the files
check if unit value prices per article code, between consecutive periods, lie within an acceptable range of variation (3)
check time series of monthly quantities and prices to evaluate data consistency and the appearance of outliers (2)

One point to note is that data received on a more frequent basis provides the opportunity to identify inconsistencies at an early stage and increases the possibility to fix the problems faster. 
A nice example of the implementation of a system to test scanner data files at arrival can be found in Ref. (1). Authors also discuss the use of a fall-back plan in case scanner data sets cease to be delivered for some reason. Another interesting example can be found in section 5.2 of Ref. (2).

title: Other uses of alternative data beyond CPI
text:
Beyond CPI production, many of the data sources and processes described in this handbook may also support a range of other official statistical domains.
In many cases, early consideration of cross-domain needs can help reduce duplication of data acquisition and processing efforts.


Price statistics beyond CPI
Alternative data sources can support several price-related statistical outputs beyond the CPI, including:

Purchasing Power Parities (PPPs), where detailed price information for comparable products and services is required across countries
Producer Price Indices (PPIs) and other business price indices, particularly for retail, wholesale, and selected service activities
Export and Import Price Indices, where transaction-level or invoice-based data may be available
residential property and rental price statistics, where web-scraped listings and administrative records are increasingly used



National accounts and macroeconomic statistics
Transaction and administrative data can contribute to national accounts compilation, particularly where they provide detailed information on prices, quantities, or turnover. Relevant areas include:

household final consumption expenditure, including detailed product-level breakdowns
deflators used to derive volume measures in national accounts
supply-use tables, where consistent price and quantity information supports balancing
short-term indicators, such as monthly or quarterly estimates of consumption or turnover



Business and structural statistics
Alternative data sources may also support business-focused statistical domains, including:

retail and wholesale trade statistics, using turnover and quantity data
structural business statistics, where administrative or transaction data can supplement or replace surveys
business demography and firm dynamics, through transaction records and administrative datasets
service sector statistics, particularly for digitally delivered services and platforms



Household and distributional statistics
Where access and legal frameworks permit, alternative data sources may support more granular analysis of household behaviour, including:

consumption patterns and expenditure distributions, when combined with other sources
experimental distributional measures, subject to confidentiality constraints
analysis of substitution behaviour and market dynamics, particularly during periods of rapid change



Emerging and cross-cutting statistical domains
In some cases, alternative data sources may support newer or cross-cutting statistical needs, such as:

digital economy and platform statistics, including e-commerce and digital services
environmental and sustainability statistics, where transaction data can support consumption-based analyses
experimental statistics and research outputs, particularly where timeliness or granularity is prioritised
nowcasting for Central Banks / other forecasting organisations

While conceptual and methodological requirements can differ across statistical domains, many processing steps such as data cleaning, product identification, and temporal aggregation are common. Early consideration of potential reuse can therefore support more efficient and coherent use of alternative data across statistical systems.

title: Classification
text:
The goal of this section is to provide guidance on the critical step of classifying new data sources and make them ready for price index compilation. Similar to other applications within official statistics (section 5.2. and 5.3 of the GSBPM define this task), classification must be done to calculate low level aggregates by strata. Specifically, once data preparation steps are complete, all prices in each retailer dataset need to be categorised to a classification system (or taxonomy) utilised by the NSO as part of index stratification. In other words, the output of the classification step is to assign all prices in the dataset to a category that will support the stratification process in the aggregation step (1, 2, 3). Categorising prices to each geographic strata also used for aggregation, and the assigning of data to structured variables used for quality adjustment methods, can both also be considered classification. Furthermore, the activity of classification is done both initially when preparing to integrate a new data source into the CPI or to support the research process, and on a recurrent basis once the dataset is in production.
While classification activities can be outsourced (or already classified data could be acquired), typically NSOs have chosen to do classification in-house. The below guidance provides an overview of the common classification methods and demonstrates notable aspects using code notebooks and public data. Each method is outlined
The below guidance also provides key considerations necessary to consider before beginning classification and how to choose an appropriate classification method, as well as best practices of combining classification methods to achieve better performance.

title: Initial steps in the acquisition of scanner data
text:
Recommendations on how an NSO can approach retailers to acquire scanner data



Initial steps in the acquisition of scanner data
Once the retailers that fit the sample purposes of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) are identified, the National Statistical Office (NSO) needs to approach data owners to negotiate data acquisition. As stated in the reference guides Eurostat's HICP - Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data and the CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods, 2020, the most recommended practice is to negotiate and get the data directly from the retailers. This approach encompasses advantages such as the possibility to negotiate a data supply at reduced costs (or even free), and to discuss with the retailers the data requirements desired in terms of data content that should be provided, and timetables that agree with CPI production routines.
As scanner data contains valuable sensitive information of the retailers and the ongoing data supply involves extra costs as the implementation and maintenance of an IT structure, retailers might be reluctant to provide the information to the NSOs and can require funds for their extra costs (Ref. (1)). The existence of legislation that allows the NSO the right to get access to the data can support any access requests but discussions are still required to ensure the data provided meet the requirements of the NSO.
Previous experiences show that negotiations with retailers to get scanner data can take several months. This can include the following steps:

Identifying suitable contacts within the retailer to take forward the request. Generally, you will need to work with the retailer's data team on the specific requirements and data access, but it is likely you will also need to gain approval from higher level decision makers within the retailer to progress the project, and the retailer's legal team may also need to sign off any data sharing agreements or contracts that are put in place.
Agreeing a data transfer method. There are many methods available, from using secure encryption email services to cloud sharing technologies such as Amazon S3 buckets.
Agreeing a data specification. This is likely to require a few iterations from receiving an initial test data set, resolving any outstanding queries or requirements and finalising the format and shape of the desired output.
Agreeing a frequency of delivery. This is likely to include the regular feeds but also any historic data that the retailer can provide.
Finalising these agreements in a data sharing agreement or contract.

Some NSOs have a separate commercial data acquisition team that work on behalf of the whole office to acquire administrative data. It is helpful to have a clear point of contact within the NSO and maintain a high level of engagement to ensure negotiations remain on track. To identify suitable contacts within the retailer it is sometimes easier to target high-level company managers to ensure a suitable priority is given to this work. The discussions on data content are then generally delegated to a specific data team within the retailer. The retailers are also likely to have separate legal teams that will need to be involved when agreeing the terms of the data sharing agreements.  
A key point for the success of the approach relies on the NSO building and maintaining a good relationship with the retailers (Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data). A clear argument for the statistical purpose of accessing the data and the relevance of the results produced for the society are important points to present. The benefits for the retailers should also be emphasized. The response burden is lowered by the adoption of scanner data since the staff of the retailers will no longer need to reply to the collectors' questions nor be bothered by the collectors walking around in the stores every month. Some NSOs also provide opportunities for collaboration with the retailer (ensuring this does not lead to a specific competitive advantage), for example providing specific retailer prices indices back to the retailer. 
In the training course 2 about data acquisition, in module 2.1 a general description of the process to arrive at obtaining scanner data is traced in the form of a decision three.
Readers can also find a list of recommendations for obtaining scanner data in section 5 of Eurostat's Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data.

title: Pre-conditions and deciding on appropriate classification methods
text:
There are several factors that NSO typically consider when approaching or implementing classification, such as the scale and complexity of the task, whether this is just the initial phase of classification or recurrent classification in production, or the structure and quality of the data. Evaluating these factors is useful to select the method(s) most appropriate for each use case.
Also see another article in this section:

title: Pre-conditions and deciding on appropriate classification methods
text:
Scale of the task
In most datasets, there is a many-to-one relationship between rows in the dataset and unique products. For example, if a supermarket provides daily data for 400 stores, then a single year of data may contain up to (365 days x 400 stores = ) 146,000 entries for a single barcode (GTIN). Typically, classification should be performed at the product-level (using SKUs or GTINs) so that each product is classified once, then propagated across its many entries within the transactional dataset. Since we classify at the product-level, the scale of the classification task can often be significantly less than it first seems. (1)
The NSO has some flexibility on what it chooses as the unique product when classifying. Ideally, the same granularity is used for clasification as for price index compilation (for instance SKU is used to classify to avoid the overly detailed nature of GTIN). However this is not always desirable if the unique products for price index methods are aggregates of lower level products (as unique products for price indices are often described as outputs after 'aggregate across products') and require classification category as the input for that aggregataion. In this case, a granularity that is stable should be chosen. For instance NSOs may classify to GTIN knowing that all GTINs with the same product name falling under the same SKU within that category are aggregated up to get one unique product and its unit price for input to the price index methods step.  
When an NSO first acquires a large dataset, the NSO faces a challenging initial task of classifying the dataset for the first time, particularly if the retailer stocks a lot of products. After the initial classification task, the ongoing monthly task of maintaining a fully-classified dataset depends on the overall scale of the unique products and the product churn rate within the data.
Table 1 shows synthetic examples of stores of varying complexity when it comes to the scale of the classification task:

The electronics store stocks few products and the resulting classification task is small both initially and on an ongoing basis. The NSO may avoid complex automation techniques that may take more time to maintain than they save.
The supermarket requires significant classification work to classify it initially, but due to a small product churn rate, the ongoing work to sustain a classified dataset is relatively small. The NSO may choose to invest into automation to improve efficiency (and likely favour simpler automation methods) but this may be optional depending on NSO resources. 
The clothing store not only stocks a lot of products, but also has a very high churn rate and as a result automation is likely a necessity for maintaining a fully-classified dataset.

title: Pre-conditions and deciding on appropriate classification methods
text:
Homogeneity of the desired classifications
At a minimum, all NSOs classify data into groups of similar products or services according to the COICOP classification hierarchy (or similar taxonomy used within the NSO). However, NSOs may choose to further stratify into additional hierarchical levels. Stratifying further in this way improves homogeneity, which is desirable for index compilation, but can also increase the complexity of the classification task. 
An example is shown in Figure 2. As (this) NSO uses COICOP, they are required to classify to COICOP-5 and, therefore, at a minimum must split men’s, women’s, and children’s clothing. NSOs then decide to what extent they further stratify the data:

Classifying to COICOP-5/NSO-1 and no further produces very heterogeneous elementary aggregates which may not be desirable.
Classifying to NSO-3 may increase the chance of misclassification when the labeler or algorithm lacks sufficient information to accurately choose between classes. This lack of information can introduce large class imbalances, which can complicate machine learning processes, especially if there there are few examples available for training.
Classifying to NSO-2 may offer a suitable balance between homogeneity and classification complexity requirements.

Figure 2: NSOs will need to consider the trade-off between homogeneity and classification complexity when deciding how granular to make their strata.

NSOs may also choose to classify at a lower level than the level that elementary aggregates are calculated (for instance if the classification performance is easier to do at the lower level but there is insufficient weight data to integrate at this lower level). In this case, the price index step may need to have a mapping to join the lower level classes into the class at which the elementary aggregate method needs to be calculated (i.e. a concordance, such as to go from NSO-3 to NSO-2 if NSO-2 is the level at which elementary aggregate is calcuated as per Figure 2 above). See Aggregation for more detail about integration approaches.

title: Pre-conditions and deciding on appropriate classification methods
text:
Data quality or stability considerations
Data quality and stability consideration are often key decision points for NSOs to select appropriate methods. Sometimes structured variables are very stable and simpler methods may sufficice (more on this in the below scenario). Sometimes however, data may be either of bad quality thereby making classification challenging, or the variables are not very stable and more sophisticated methods are needed:

Low data quality issues - could occur if specific variables are sometimes missing for specific products in the dataset. Sometimes so much information is missing that it may be impossible to classify the product at all. While it is not desirable to drop (or filter out) such records, if the NSO does not know what category the product applies to, it may be appropriate to remove them from all in-scope categories as false positives may contribute to bias due to misclassification (4).
Low stability of data in variables used for classification - data may be present but be very different across time. For instance product descriptions or breadcrumbs from a website may vary quite a lot over time, hence it may be difficult to apply to simpler rule-based approaches. In this case, NSOs can approach the situation with an eye to the scale of the task. Small scale classification tasks could be handled with manual classification (see Method 0 for more details), whereas high volume cases can be handled with Machine Learning approaches with Natural Language methods to find patterns in the data (see method 4 and in part method 3 for more details on Machine Learning methods).

title: Pre-conditions and deciding on appropriate classification methods
section: Similarity of retailer hierarchy to NSOs chosen classes
text:
Similarity of retailer hierarchy to NSOs chosen classes
Sometimes the way that the retailer organizes its products is very similar to the class design chosen by the NSO. If the NSO has a laptops class, and the retailer’s hierarchy contains a laptops section, then the classification approach could be as simple as automatically mapping from hierarchy to class. You can read more about rules-based classification in the chapter on Method 1.
Note that care must be given when performing automatic mappings in this way. Retailers often cross-sell products. For instance when someone looks to buy a laptop, they may also want to buy a laptop bag at the same time, so retailers may stock and list the two adjacently. This can make laptop bags (and other cross-sold products) appear in the laptops hierarchy. A keyword classifier for filtering out unwanted products could be considered for removing products like these. See Method 2 for more information on this case.

title: Other uses of alternative data within CPI
text:
While much of this handbook focuses on the use of alternative data sources for the calculation of price indices, these data may also support other aspects of CPI production.
In some cases, alternative data can complement or enhance existing processes even where they are not used directly in index compilation.
Recognising these additional uses may help NSOs extract greater value from data acquisition efforts and support more coherent CPI systems. 


Supporting sub-national and regional CPI statistics
Alternative data sources often provide broader geographic coverage and higher observation density than traditional price surveys. Where conceptually appropriate, these data may support:

the production of regional or sub-national CPI indices
improved analysis of geographic price variation

Even where national indices remain the primary output, alternative data can help assess regional representativeness and inform stratification decisions.


Supporting variants of CPI indices
Alternative data sources may support the production of different CPI variants, for example:

constant tax CPI indices, where price movements are analysed net of changes in indirect taxes
analytical CPI series that distinguish between market-driven price changes and policy-driven effects (such as tax or fee changes)
enhanced analysis of discounts, promotions, and fees, where these are treated differently across CPI variants

Where such variants are envisaged, this may have implications for data acquisition, as access to VAT-exclusive prices or explicit tax or discount breakdowns may be required from data providers.


Informing expenditure weights and aggregation structures
Transaction data and other data sources containing quantity or expenditure information may also be used to:

inform elementary or higher-level expenditure weights
support more frequent updating of weights
validate weights derived from household or retail surveys

These uses may be particularly valuable where survey-based expenditure data are infrequent, lagged, or subject to high sampling variability. 


Supporting product selection, classification, and sample design
Alternative data sources can also be used upstream of index calculation to:

identify emerging products and services
assess product turnover and life cycles
support sample maintenance and rotation strategies
improve classification to CPI structures

In some cases, these data may be used as a sampling frame, even where index compilation continues to rely on traditional survey-based prices. 


Enhancing data validation and quality assurance
High-frequency or high-volume data can provide additional signals for:

detecting unusual price movements
monitoring product availability and relaunches
validating survey-based prices or indices
conducting sensitivity analysis of methodological choices

These uses may improve confidence in CPI outputs even where alternative data are not the primary source for index calculation. 


Supporting analysis and communication
Alternative data sources may also be used for analytical purposes, such as:

understanding drivers of inflation
analysing substitution behaviour
producing experimental or analytical outputs alongside official CPI releases

Such uses can enhance transparency and help explain CPI movements to users.

title: Seasonal products
text:
This page contains information on the treatment of seasonal products in the CPI and implications of using the new data sources



Traditional treatment of seasonal products in the CPI
Seasonal products are products that are either not continuously available on the market (strongly seasonal) or show regular fluctuations in quantities and prices linked to a season or time of the year (weakly seasonal). For example, fresh fruits and vegetables often have particular seasonal production and consumption patterns.
Weakly seasonal products do not require direct intervention by the index compiler. However, large price fluctuations (for example, when the product is out of season) can increase the volatility of the price index. Measures of core inflation address such issues (see, for example, Chapters 12 and 14 of the CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods, 2020). Strongly seasonal products pose a bigger problem as it is not possible to calculate price relatives when a price is available only in one of the two periods being compared.
The CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods (2020) discusses two main approaches to overcome the difficulties for CPI compilation raised by strongly seasonal products: (i) the fixed-weight approach, and (ii) the seasonal-weight approach. For both methods, the in-season and out-of-season periods need to be determined. Also, a conservative approach is recommended for the start of the in-season period to avoid the use of influential abnormal (high) prices of items of low quantities and high demand (for example, for a fresh crop of summer fruits).
In the fixed-weight approach, weights remain constant over all periods of the year, and prices are imputed when the item is out-of-season and thus not available for price collection. The main drawback is that annual fixed weights are not representative of monthly or quarterly consumption patterns and that artificial prices are introduced which do not exist in the market. However, the method is easy to implement and theoretically consistent with the concept of a fixed basket.
In the seasonal-weight approach, a zero weight is given to an item out-of-season and the annual fixed weight when the product is in-season. This method is usually applied within a COICOP subclass for which the weight is considered to be constant and total expenditure is assumed to not vary between different times of the year but to switch between similar items only.  The advantage of this method is that price imputations are minimized. However, they cannot be completely avoided as, for example, unusual weather conditions could delay the start of the season such that no prices are observed even though a nonzero weight has been allocated to that period. Also, this method is inconsistent with a fixed-basket index and price changes do not only reflect changes in price relatives but also in weights.
There are several other important issues related to seasonal products:

The geographical dimension, as seasonal availability may vary between different regions of a country, between rural and urban areas, or between market stalls and luxury outlet stores.
The lack of well-defined seasons, as seasonal products do not always appear and disappear in the same month every year. Also, the seasonal pattern can change over time.
The equivalence or comparability of imported products that replace/substitute domestic ones when the item is out-of-season.
The dependence on supply conditions (fruits and vegetables).
The changes of specifications or discounted end-of-season prices (clothing).



Treatment of seasonal products using new data sources
In the traditional treatment of seasonality, one has to define the in-season periods a priori and derive relevant weights from past periods. Weights are usually provided for a given year and not by month which makes it difficult to define the in-season periods. With alternative data sources, it is possible to select seasonal products and their seasons directly from the data. This information could be used, for example, to better design the traditional index. Note further that scanner data is very good in overcoming the problems 1 to 2 mentioned above as actual weights of each period can be used. To address issues 3 to 5 with scanner or web scraped data, usually, a lot of effort is needed for the definition of the individual product. For example, the individual product Apple consists of several GTINs referring to different varieties of apples. Or for clothing, homogeneous products are created which are composed of different article codes.
New data sources also open up the potential to use new price index methods, for example multilateral methods.
Rolling window methods estimate multilateral indices on a rolling window with a fixed length which is shifted forward each period. However, the choice of the window length is a point of concern as well as the extension method used. Ivancic et al. (2011) propose a 13-month (or five-quarter) window as this is the shortest window that can deal with strongly seasonal goods. Calendar constellations (e.g. the dating of Easter), administrative measures (e.g. the dating of school holidays), or weather conditions (e.g. fluctuations in harvest periods) can cause seasonality such that the in-season periods may change from year to year and a larger window than the absolute minimum of 13-months is necessary. Chessa (2021) Extension of multilateral index series over time: Analysis and comparison of methods shows that indices can be significantly improved with a 25-month (or nine-quarter) window. Note further that not all splicing methods work equally well.
Multilateral methods implicitly account for seasonality (as the chosen window includes several in-season periods) and a broader definition of the product class is recommended (e.g. a price index for fruit including strong seasonal goods like cherries). 
It is also possible to construct weighted GEKS indices which consider the reliability of the bilateral price indices (Rao, 2001). Melser (2018) proposes a weighted GEKS method where the weights depend on the degree of matching of the items, for example, concerning expenditure shares. Here, the choice of window length is less important since bilateral indices with a lower degree of matching will be down-weighted.





References
Ivancic, L., Diewert, E.W. and Fox, K.J. (2011). Scanner data, time aggregation and the construction of price indexes. Journal of Econometrics. Vol. 161(1), pages 24-35, March 2011. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2010.09.003
Melser, D. (2018). Scanner Data Price Indexes: Addressing Some Unresolved Issues. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 36(3), pages 516–522. http://www.jstor.org/stable/44867994

title: Glossary
text:
This page contains the handbook glossary.



Introduction
The first challenge for any international guidance manual is to harmonise the terminology used. This is particular true in the world of consumer price statistics, where different countries and users use different terms to discuss the same concepts. In this glossary, we have not only included words/phrases that require defining, we also have tried to note where different terminology is sometimes used. We start this page by looking at some of the key areas that require definition, before moving onto the glossary in its more conventional sense. 


Definition of a product
One of the areas with the biggest difference in terminology is how different countries describe the individual products whose prices (and expenditure, if available) are used to compile consumer price statistics. For this wiki, we have used the following terminology.
Table 1: summary of terminology used to describe products












Lowest level (observation)
Aggregation over time
→ 
Average price for a specific time period (e.g. a month), a specific outlet and specific article code
Aggregation over outlets
→ 
Average price for a specific time period and specific article code, but over several outlets
Aggregation over article codes
→ 
Average price for a specific time period but over several outlets and article codes = Homogeneous product


Observation: at a specific time, from a specific outlet, for a specific article code, under specific terms of supply, and for which a price is observed




(if available)




Homogeneous product: set of individual products among which there are no significant quality differences and for which an average price is calculated;


Individual product: depending on context, this can refer to anything between an observation and a homogeneous product





Other words/phrases often used here include Global Trade Item Number (GTIN), item code and item. The glossary in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) Manual uses the term variety to mean "the individual product for which prices are collected during the collection period. It includes the detailed specification of the product or item observed". However, for this wiki, we have chosen to use the terminology article code for this purpose. We use the term variety to mean the different varieties of products you can get that have the same article code, for example different sizes or colours.


Glossary of terms
Table 2: glossary of terms



Term
Definition


Alternative Data


Data that differ from the traditional form of data typically used by National Statistical Offices (NSOs) by collection method (web scraped or bulk data delivery) or by type (Transaction records). This category can encompass transaction data, administrative data, or data collected through web scraping outside an NSO’s typical survey and collection framework. Some NSOs may have long histories of using data sources (especially administrative date) that may be considered novel and alternative by others.


Article Drift
Chain drift can be formalized in terms of the violation of the multi period identity test. According to this test one can expect, that when all prices and quantities in a current period revert back to their values from the base period, then the index should indicate no price change and it equals 1. For a worked example of chain drift please see Section Example of chain drift.




Article Code
The individual product for which prices are collected.


Chain Drift
Chain drift can be formalised in terms of the violation of the multi period identity test. According to this test one can expect, that when all prices and quantities in a current period revert back to their values from the base period, then the index should indicate no price change and it equals 1. For a worked example of chain drift please see Section Example of chain drift.




Consumption Patterns
A household's allocation of expenditures across different consumption categories, such as food, housing, clothing, and transportation, how consumers act, how loyal they are to brands and how they react to new products and services.


CPI
Consumer Price Index is a measure of the average prices of goods sold to consumers.


Elementary Aggregates
Elementary aggregates (EAs) represent the lowest level – both in the product and the geography dimensions – where price indices are first calculated using prices for individual products.




Homogeneous Product
See above. set of individual products among which there are no significant quality differences and for which an average price is calculated;




Individual Product
See above. depending on context, this can refer to anything between an observation and a homogeneous product




Non-Survey Data
Data obtained without the sampling methods typically used for traditional data used by NSOs.


NSO/NSI
National Statistical Office/ National Statistical Institute. In this wiki, we use National Statistical Office (NSOs) but both are valid.




Observation
See above. At a specific time, from a specific outlet, for a specific article code, under specific terms of supply, and for which a price is observed.




Periodic Resampling
Sources of time series data which are periodic measurements or observations.


Probability Sampling
The selection of a sample from a population that is random or by change.


Sampling Error
A statistical error occurs when a sample is selected that is not representative of the sample being studied and is known as a sampling error.


Scanner Data
Data ultimately derived from records created by retail checkout scanners. This is one form of transaction data.




Transaction Data
Data that reflect actual purchases. Observations may represent individual transactions or aggregations of sales at a product level. Data include transaction prices and a measure of sales volume (quantity or expenditure). See scanner data above.




Variety
The different varieties of products you can get that have the same article code, for example different sizes or colours.




Web scraping
A process of automated data collection where computer programs extract relevant data elements (such as list price and product details) from websites.

title: Method 3: Recommendation / Machine-assisted classification
text: Machine-assisted classification is still a manual classification technique and therefore the ideas in the manual classification chapter are still valid. The key difference is the addition of a recommendation system that supports labellers in identifying the most appropriate class. Every product is still manually scrutinised, but machine-assistance may improve efficiency and potentially quality by offering recommendations. For example, for a product sold in a supermarket, a labeller may be faced with hundreds of possible food and drink, pharmaceutical, household goods and clothing (amongst other) classes to choose from. The labeller may immediately recognise the appropriate class, then spend minutes navigating a complex hierarchical structure to choose it. The recommendation system used in machine-assisted manual classification provides a shortened list of options for the labeller to choose from, substantially improving the speed with which labellers can parse lists of classes to assign the most appropriate one.

title: Method 3: Recommendation / Machine-assisted classification
text:
Keyword-based recommender
The first potential option is a keyword-based recommender. This approach uses words within the product name, description and hierarchy to identify potential classes, similar to pattern based classification. For example, if the word “cola” appears in the product name or description, then the machine might recommend “fizzy drinks” and “pre-mixed spirits” as classes.
Table 1: Pros and cons of a keyword-based recommender







Pros
Cons



Relatively simple method to implement and understand.
Can work reasonably well when products are marketed by general descriptor terms rather than brand names. “Blue t-shirt” works well; but “Pepsi 2L” works less well.


The national statistical office will likely need to maintain substantial lists of keyword-to-class recommendations.
It may be difficult to identify more-abstract classes with this method. “Lemon and pea risotto” may serve “lemons”, “peas” and “rice” as recommendations, but not the potentially desired “ready meal” class.

title: Method 3: Recommendation / Machine-assisted classification
text:
Hierarchy mapping
Another option is to use hierarchy mappings. This approach recommends classes that fit a specific retailer hierarchy descriptor and is thus similar to rule based classification. For example, if the retailer hierarchy is “Bakery/Bread/Sliced loaves” then the machine might recommend “white bread loaves”, “wholemeal bread loaves” and “seeded bread”.
Table 2: Pros and cons of a hierarchy mapping approach







Pros
Cons



Relatively simple method to implement and understand.
Will likely require fewer rules/lists and is thus requires little investment
This approach can be relatively straightforward to maintain


Vague hierarchies (such as “Fresh/Dairy/Other”) and all-encompassing hierarchies (such as “Food cupboard/Christmas food”) may require a substantial number of recommended classes.
Hierarchy mappings need to be maintained with changes to the retailer’s hierarchy. NSOs should consider stability of the retailer’s hierarchy before pursuing this option.




Note that NSOs should choose an appropriate level of granularity with which to create these mappings. Mapping at a very high level is likely to result in the labeller still needing to work through a very large list of classes. By contrast, mapping at a very low level is likely to result in a lot of setup and maintenance work.

title: Method 3: Recommendation / Machine-assisted classification
text:
Machine learning
A third option is to use supervised machine learning (thus a toned version of method 4). This approach involves training a machine learning algorithm by using previously labelled data, then using this algorithm to make recommendations on future data. Labellers manually scrutinise each product, either choosing the appropriate label from a list of the machine’s predictions or correcting the machine if the appropriate label isn’t available.
If this approach is taken, it may be better to use a machine learning algorithm which can provide multiple predictions with associated probabilities (such as XGBoost and Logistic Regression) than an algorithm that can only provide a single prediction (such as Support Vector Machines). This allows labellers to observe several potential classes, rather than just the single class the algorithm considers to be the most likely. If NSOs choose to not review each unique product but only a sub-set and accept the ML model's recommendation, this can be considered method 4.
Note, a potential variant of the machine learning approach to leverage most of the process but stop short of training ML models, instead comparing a new product to classes using similarity score in vector space. To do this, first levergage the preprocessing step (see ML chapter for more details) to convert a product's text descriptions into a vector. Secondly, use similarity scores (such as cosine similarity), compare the vector of the new product with the average vector for the nearest categories. See Wall et al (2025) for an application of this for labelling (1).
Table 3: Pros and cons of a ML approach







Pros
Cons



Manual scrutiny provides a safeguard against erroneous machine predictions.
Probabilities allows the machine recommendations to be sorted, with the likeliest classes appearing first, which may improve efficiency.
Scrutinising and correcting the machine’s predictions with regular retraining may allow substantial improvements in the predictive power of the algorithm over time as training data size improves.


Relatively complicated to implement and understand.
It may be too resource intensive to both develop/maintain a machine learning algorithm and manually scrutinise every product.
Requires some manual labelling work to have already been completed for training the first model.

title: Alternative approaches to acquiring scanner data
text:
Suggestions of what to do if the NSO is unable to acquire scanner data directly from retailers



Alternative approaches to acquiring scanner data
In the case that the National Statistical Office (NSO) cannot obtain scanner data directly from the retailers, an alternative approach is to get the data from market research companies (CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods, 2020). Ref. (1) provides a practical example of this use case.
Usually in this kind of approach data supply will not be free and financial resources are necessary to purchase the data. Advantages of the approach may include the negotiation of data sets relating to different retailers from one or a few data providers. The supply of cleaned data already classified according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) classification can also be a benefit of this approach. This can lead to reduced costs than those incurred by the NSO to build all the infrastructure to perform all these steps on its own. 
Besides the cost for obtaining the data, other disadvantages in this process include reduction in the control of the data being received and the loss of flexibility in the negotiation of the data sets and variables of interest and possible changes in data content over time.
Eurostat's HICP - Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data recommends whenever possible, to obtain scanner directly from the retailers.

title: Method 4: Machine Learning classification method
text:
Machine Learning (ML) can be a stable solution for classifying unique products when an NSO starts to use new data sources at scale. NSOs typically use supervised ML methods whereby a manually annotated dataset is used to train a classifier to predict all new unique products as part of recurrent classification. ML models can make mistakes however, thus NSOs that apply ML at scale also need to set up a manual validation process where some of the new products are validated after the ML model classifies them in order to help track model performance, mitigate mistakes for price index methods downstream, as well as to create additional training datasets to retrain models to help keep their performance optimal. The complexity of setting all this up is not trivial, the technical skillset investments necessary to properly operationalize and maintain ML means that NSOs should apply ML when the scale and data quality requires it.
Two articles are also included in this section:

title: Method 4: Machine Learning classification method
text:
Preparing the data
The first step in training a supervised ML model is to assemble a representative dataset. This is sampled from the data that the NSO wishes to classify, such as a year worth of unique products of a scanner dataset. This includes creating a representative dataset that can be used to train (and tune through validation process) a model, as well a holdout test dataset on which to test that the classifier performs well. All datasets also need to have a correct label already provided, hence the NSO will need to manually annotate the data (i.e. using Method 0). Making sure that annotation is done to a high quality will pay dividends as mistakes in training or holdout datasets can impact model quality. If a dataset on which a model is being trained on (such as during initial classification) is large, a sample of all unique products can be taken and labelled. This sample should be representative of what the model will see in the out-of-sample data (i.e. in production). For instance, an NSO developing a price index method on an initial dataset of 13 months of data can sample the full 13 months, annotate all the records, assign the 13th month as the hold out dataset, and use the initial 12 months for training and validation. If the dataset is found to be imbalanced after annotation, approaches to mitigate class imbalance may be applied on the training dataset.
In terms of variables that are relevant for ML models, all variables typically availible from alternative datasets can be used. In practice however, the text data present in product descriptions (such as product name or its longer form description), retailer categories for the product, and product metadata (such as product size or brand) are most applicable. Depending on the quality of the text data in these variables, NSOs may wish to also mine information from unique product codes such as GTINs or UPCs. See Figure 1 for a visual on how a UPC can be mined to extract manufacturer and product information if product descriptions are imperfect.
Figure 1: Overview of mining UPC to get information from a record in Dominik's Finer Foods dataset (example taken from (2), see (3) for more on the dataset).

title: Method 4: Machine Learning classification method
text:
Data preprocessing
Upon selecting the dataset, and splitting it appropriately so as to not cause data leakage, NSOs need to preprocess data to convert it into numerical format necessary for ML models. Depending on the quality of the natural language present in the selected variables, this may leverage traditional Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques or more nuanced feature engineering methods. For instance, if natural language is available for product descriptions (typical of web scraped data where fuller and more descriptive text descriptions may be captured) NLP approaches such as stop-word removal, stemming/lemmatisation, tokenization are commonly applied (see (4) for an overview). In this case, NSOs may concatenate all the selected variables together into one long string and apply these NLP techniques. All approaches will need to be tuned to select the preprocessing most applicable to the data. For instance, the stop-word step may need to be tuned to not drop keywords that are relevant for classification if they represent information relevant to classification. If natural language is limited (which can be typical of more traditional scanner data, as is visible in Dominick's finer food data), more nuanced techniques such as extracting manufacturers and products may be required (as shown in Figure 1 above). In either case, specific n-grams can be created from the input descriptions (for example whole words, letters, or a set of them together, such as "juice" can be converted into "juice" (whole word), "juic", "jui", "jce", "ju", "jc", etc). 
Following this preprocessing, the data needs to be vectorized to turn the data into a form ML models accept. Several approaches can be used, ranging from simpler methods such as bag-of-words or term-frequency inverse-document-frequency (TF-IDF), to pretrained embeddings such as Word2Vec, Glove or FastText. There is no consensus among NSO research on most appropriate approach, hence a method should be selected that is most applicable to the use case.

title: Method 4: Machine Learning classification method
section: Model choice, model evaluation and what is good enough
text:
Model choice, model evaluation and what is good enough
Several supervised ML models can be used. Many NSOs have been able to obtain good performance with a simpler non-linear model types such as Support Vector Machines (5) and XGboost (6, 7), however there is no concensus on the topic and the decision should stay with the NSO depending on their specific case and the characteristics of the data being classified. NSOs can try other approaches if they see fit, for instanace, some research has also been done on semi-supervised methods (8). The main objective is to evaluate the model that is trained and tuned on a hold-out test set that represents an out-of-sample example once the model is running in production. NSOs typically use several evaluation metrics to support their assessment. 
The key objective in training and selecting an appropriate ML model is to minimize the amount of misclassification. As ML models are typically used at scale and potentially for several datatasets at once, they typically classify products to one of several categories. While a few of these categories may not be used for production needs (such as for catch-all categories), the majority of the categories will feed price indices. As misclassification has been shown to cause both bias and variance in price indices (9, 5, 6), the goal is thus to select a model that will minimize the amount of validation that is needed to correct these misclassifications. NSOs can also minimize the amount of validation necessary by training performant classifiers and optimizing them effectively (for instance prioritizing precision over recall in the evaluation of models, which has been found to be more applicable, see 9 and 10).
MLOps: additional requirements when applying ML
Developing a high performing ML classifier is the first step before designing the operational process to deploy and maintain ML in production. Originally raised by Sculley et al (2015), efficient operationalization of ML (also know as ML Operations or MLOps) requires a large number of additional aspects (see Figure 2 for visual). In a nutshell, MLOps is a set of best practices to build transparency, reproducibility, rigor, scalability and efficiency - when applying ML for production use cases. MLOps literature has grown and a large amount of guides are available to provide NSOs with training on the topic (see guides, such as by Google, books on the topic (14), and courses (15), and a recent summary applying MLOps to price statistics by Ritter et al (2024)). The below sections outline the key aspects from a conceptual point of view, with additional technical considerations summarized in Desinging the classification step: technical and reproducibility considerations (forthcoming).
Figure 2: Elements of ML operations systems, as summarized by Ritter et al (2024).

title: Method 4: Machine Learning classification method
text:
Design of the validation process
As ML models make mistakes and misclassification can cause both bias and variance in price index methods applied on the data, it is necessary to validate a proportion of the unique products once a model is deployed into production. If no validation were to happen, several consequences would occur over time. Firstly, NSOs would not know how much misclassfication bias or variance is entering their elementary price indices. Secondly, the NSOs would not know how performant their model was and if it was degrading over time and if it needed to be retrained (more on model retraining below). Thus it is key for ML methods specifically, to ensure that there is a validation process on a proportion of records after they are classified (see operational considerations section for more detail on the overall design). NSOs can start with a strategy of validating all new classified products and scale down to lower proportions as the maturity of the operational process improves and measurement error is decreased. It is not recommended to ever eliminate validation due to inevitable data and concept drift in production settings.
How NSOs should flag and validate (manually) a set of products is a topic of ongoing research. Notable methods include randomly (such as by stratified random sampling) in order to create a dataset that is representative and can objectively summarize ML model performance every single period. Other approaches are more effective for correcting measurement error in calculated indices. A notable method applicable to scanner data is focusing on the most economically important products in each category (such as by applying the cut-off-sample approach on turnover of the product) has been shown as applicable to scanner data by Spackman et al (2024), as is shown in Figure 3. Other notable methods include using confidence of the model to direct annotation resources to products the model is least confident in. This approach however is not perfect as the correlation between model confidence and true likelihood of being incorrect is not perfect (see Angelopoulos et al (2020) for more info). Overall, it is best to flag records both randomly to understand objectively what model performance is, as well as in a statistically biased fashion to minimize measurement error. Several methods were evaluated and an approach NSOs could evaluate was recently proposed by Spackman et al (2025).
Figure 3: Demonstration of reduction of bias on 4 product categories by applying cut-off sampling based on sales on Dominiks Finer Foods scanner data. Taken from Spackman et al (2024).

title: Method 4: Machine Learning classification method
section: Retraining models to deal with model decay
text:
Retraining models to deal with model decay
ML models are typically quite effective when applied out-of-sample, but rarely stay effective when they are used out-of-distribution. Thus if the distribution of data for new unique products a ML model is classifying shifts, then the model will no longer be as performant as originally. For instance, if the data distribution shifts and there is a change in the decision boundary between classes, models will become less accurate and there will likely be more misclassification between these classes.  This has been shown to apply in the case of price statistics with alternative data (5, 12), however unlike simpler methods (such as attribute based methods, which can fail very suddenly, such as if a retailer category changes), this can happen gradually, hence NSOs should set up processes to be vigilant of this risk. Several methods are availible for NSOs: an approach that preceeds regular classification and one that follows soon after. The former is to statistically evaluate whether there is a shift in the data distribution on each new dataset prior to classifying it, for instance with a KL divergence test. The latter involves classifying new unique products and then evaluating model performance after a subset was validated (using the validation process outlined above). As production timelines are likely to be tight, performance monitoring provides NSOs considerable actionable information. On the one hand, it will show how well the ML model actually performed and how much manual validation may now be necessary. It will also result in a small subset of annotated data that can be used to tune the model (or allocate additional resources to more sampling). Statistical tests may also be valuable, depending on how the NSO designed its validation process. As most unique products are classified in the month they are first detected but they do not enter price index methods, NSOs may be validating them only in the subsequent month. Thus statistical tests may provide an early warning signal to allocate resources earlier than performance based approaches would. 
Once model decay is detected and enough new data is labelled, a ML model can be retrained and deployed to replace the degraded model. While some initial experiments have shown that retraining on a quarterly basis (every 3 months) is sufficient (see Figure 4 for a visual), NSOs should evaluate their data and the amount of decay they see in the design of their ML Operations (MLOps) system.  
Figure 4: Experiment showing quarterly retraining as quite efficient. Taken from Spackman et al (2023).

title: Method 4: Machine Learning classification method
text:
Operationalizing an ML model
Technically, ML models require resources to support them. Technically, it is recommended that they operationalized as Reproducible Analytical Pipelines (RAPs); however, compared to simpler methods such as Method 1 or 2, ML models introduce additional operational and technical considerations (forthcoming), including the need for tools like MLflow to track provenance across datasets, models, and other artifacts. While some NSOs have developed cloud systems to operationalize their MLOps system (see 12 for an Azure MLOps system overview), NSOs can tune the design as appropriate for their use case.

title: Handbook on utilising new data sources in the production of consumer price statistics
text:
This Handbook provides an overview and reference framework for the use of new data sources in the production of consumer price statistics.

Developed by the UN Task Team on Scanner Data, it is intended for a broad audience, including national statistical offices, central banks, international organisations, and researchers involved in the development, implementation, or evaluation of consumer price indices. 
The Handbook covers a broad range of data sources - including transaction data such as scanner data, and non-transaction data such as web-scraped data - that differ to traditional collection in how prices are observed, recorded and accessed. It is intended to support both organisations exploring these data sources for the first time, and those seeking to refine or extend existing implementations.
This Handbook complements Chapter 10 of the CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods by providing detailed operational guidance on the use of alternative data sources in CPI production. It does not replace the CPI Manual, which sets out the underlying concepts, principles and governance framework for the use of alternative data sources in CPI compilation. 
This Handbook covers key stages of the CPI production process where new data sources may be introduced, including data acquisition, preparation, classification, index compilation, quality assurance, and dissemination. It brings together conceptual discussion, practical considerations, methodological options, and examples from country practices, with the aim of supporting informed decision-making rather than prescribing a single method or workflow.
There is no single “correct” approach to using new data sources in CPI production. The appropriate choices will depend on national circumstances, data availability, institutional arrangements, technical capacity, and user needs. Accordingly, the purpose of this handbook is to present the range of available approaches, highlight their strengths and limitations, and provide guidance to help users assess what is most suitable for their particular context.
While the primary focus of this Handbook is on consumer price statistics, many of the data sources, processes, and systems discussed may also support other areas of official statistics. Where relevant, considerations for broader statistical use are highlighted to support efficient and sustainable use of alternative data sources across statistical domains.
This Handbook draws on existing international manuals, methodological papers, and country experiences, while also improving the literature on topics where guidance is currently more limited, such as data acquisition strategies, classification challenges, and the handling of highly dynamic product universes. Given the rapid pace of methodological and technological developments in this field, the handbook is designed as a living document. It will be reviewed and updated over time to reflect new research, emerging best practices, and feedback from users.
Users of this Handbook are encouraged to support its ongoing development and improvement. Feedback may include suggestions on topics that could be expanded or added, identification of errors or areas requiring clarification, or proposals to refine existing content in light of new research or country experience. Such feedback will help ensure that this Handbook remains relevant, accurate, and responsive to the evolving needs of the international statistical community. Feedback can be provided through answering the questions on this form: UN Task Team on Scanner Data - e-Handbook Feedback Form.
This Handbook is publicly available and intended to be used alongside related training materials and other supporting resources developed by the UN Task Team on Scanner Data.


Contents:

Acknowledgements — The development of this handbook and associated training material is a testament to the hard work of many individuals who collaborated on drafting, reviewing and updating the content. 
Glossary — This page contains the handbook glossary.
Initial considerations — This section covers some initial considerations that NSOs are recommended to review before setting out to use alternative data sources in the production of consumer price statistics.

Overview of alternative data sources — This page contains a general introduction to each of the alternative data sources used to compile consumer price indices. 
Why use alternative data sources? Strategic motivations — Common reasons shared by NSOs as a driver for using these new data sources.
Key challenges and trade-offs — Alternative data sources introduce a number of challenges and trade-offs that National Statistical Offices (NSOs) must actively manage.
Key decision points — The adoption of alternative data sources involves a sequence of related decisions that shape both the technical and organisational direction of implementation.
Resource implications and organisational readiness — The adoption of alternative data sources typically requires a different mix of resources and capabilities compared with traditional survey-based price collection.

CPI production system requirements — Requirements for IT systems are dependent on the choice of data source, the implementation plan for each new data source and the availability and knowledge of staff with specialist IT skills.

Dealing with unexpected data gaps — This page contains information on how to deal with unexpected gaps in the supply of new data sources

Preparation of data — This sections summarises the general steps required to prepare these new data sources for use in price index compilation.

Product sampling for price index calculation — NSOs can either choose to use all available data from their new data source, or to use a sample of this data. 
Standardising the data — Data will need to be standardised before being used to calculate price indices.
Aggregation across time and outlets — Data are usually disaggregated by various dimensions. This page contains information on how products can be aggregated across time and outlets.
Identifying unique products — Data are usually disaggregated by various dimensions. This page contains information on how products can be defined from the given article codes.
Treatment of discounts and refunds — This page contains information on how discounts and refunds should be treated in the data.

Classification — The goal of this section is to provide guidance on the critical step of classifying new data sources and make them ready for price index compilation. 

Pre-conditions and deciding on appropriate classification methods — There are several factors that NSO typically consider when approaching or implementing classification, such as the scale and complexity of the task, whether this is just the initial phase of classification or recurrent classification in production, or the structure and quality of the data. Evaluating these factors is useful to select the method(s) most appropriate for each use case.

Note on variables applicable for classification — Several variables obtained during the acquisition process  are typically applicable for classification. 

Method 0: Manual labelling or validation of predicted labels — Manual classification involves each unique product being manually assigned a classification class. This is often described as labelling, and those who specialize in the task, labellers This method can also be used to validate classification done automatically by other methods. 
Method 1: Attribute-based classification method — Attribute-based classification involves classifying observations in the data by mapping structured variables or attributes available in the alternative data file to the necessary taxonomy classes. 
Method 2: Pattern matching classification method — Pattern based classification involves mapping individual records to the taxonomy classes of interest according to patterns present in their descriptive attributes. For instance, patterns in the categories of the alternative data, patterns in the product name, or specific keywords in the product description - could all be used to classify a set of individual records. 
Method 3: Recommendation / Machine-assisted classification — Machine-assisted classification is still a manual classification technique and therefore the ideas in the manual classification chapter are still valid. The key difference is the addition of a recommendation system that supports labellers in identifying the most appropriate class. Every product is still manually scrutinised, but machine-assistance may improve efficiency and potentially quality by offering recommendations. 
Method 4: Machine Learning classification method — Machine Learning (ML) can be a stable solution for classifying unique products when an NSO starts to use new data sources at scale. NSOs typically use supervised ML methods whereby a manually annotated dataset is used to train a classifier to predict all new unique products as part of recurrent classification. 

How to evaluate classification methods — There are numerous metrics that can be tracked and applied when evaluating how well a classifier performs. 
Working with class imbalance — Datasets NSOs need to classify are typically not equally distributed, as some classes have many records (i.e. unique products) while others have only a few. This requires additional steps to be taken when designing and testing classifiers. 

Operational best practices — Once NSOs select and develop an appropriate classification method, they have to implement it. This section includes articles on appropriate ways to operationalize classification.

Outlier filter — Outlier filters aim at excluding or correcting extreme price increases or price decreases, typically compared to the previous period, from the price index calculation

Extension methods — Extension methods can be used in combination with multilateral methods to ensure revision-free index series. 
Decomposition — In addition to measuring the aggregate price or quantity change, it is important to decompose the change into its contributions by individual commodities or groupings.
