title: Product sampling for price index calculation
text:
NSOs can either choose to use all available data from their new data source, or to use a sample of this data. In the first case, all sold items’ prices and quantities in all outlets are used in the price index calculation. Items are typically weighted to reflect their economic importance and an appropriate index formula is used (typically a multilateral index method). No product or outlet sampling is needed in this case. In the second case, a country may choose to sample from these new data sources in order to replace the existing collection. Some considerations on how to choose an appropriate product sample from these data sources are given here.


Product sampling with scanner data
The availability of quantities sold or revenues for each individual product in scanner data provides opportunities for product sampling strategies for price index calculation purposes. For instance, scanner data generally represents a census of the retailer’s outlets and products sold during a given period. The process of filtering these data down to those goods and services within the scope of a Consumer Price Index (CPI) is covered in the section "Classification". Thus, a retailer’s scanner data (once classified) provides a sampling frame for statistical sampling techniques for the selection of outlets and products in the context of the CPI price survey.
The scanner data sampling frame can be used to design a non-judgmental sampling strategy. Probability sampling methods for products selection in the context of scanner data are discussed in Ref. 2. The results suggest the systematic sampling proportional to expenditure as the best performing method with unbiased price change estimates and relatively low standard errors. The cut-off sampling method performed well also. This might indicate that in the case of a small sample size, the exclusion of low-selling products from the price index calculation does not significantly affect the index series. While this result gives support to the use of the cut-off sampling with scanner data, this method may not be appropriate for some product categories in some countries. The cut-off sampling method can be implemented using the revenue share as a measure of the relative importance of products in their product categories (see paragraphs 10.41-10.47 in CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods (2020)). For the maintenance of the sample over time, the revenue share could help identify potential candidate products for replacement or during a sample update.
The Eurostat's HICP - Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data (chapter 8) also discusses two sampling methods for scanner data processing: a static sampling approach and a dynamic sampling approach. These approaches are most commonly used to produce bilateral price index methods, but in some instances the dynamic approach can also be used as a way of preparing the data to feed into multilateral indices, see for example Chapter 5 in Ref. 1.
The static sampling approach is very similar to the traditional field collection sampling of the price survey except that the data collection is done centrally instead of in-store visits by interviewers. A representative sample of store locations can be selected using the store level total revenue calculated over a recent period with a reasonable length and the stores with the largest revenues selected in the sample. Then, within a store and a product category, a representative product sample is selected using sales data from a recent period with a reasonable length, for example the previous six or twelve months. As a selection criteria, one may include products that have been sold in each of the preceding twelve months (stability) and that have the largest revenue shares within their respective product categories (representativeness). A threshold may be set for the cumulative revenue share of the sampled products. Depending on the dispersion of sales within the product category, this threshold could be set at 40%, 50%, 60%, etc. Each month, prices are collected for the sampled products using the scanner data for that month.
Whenever a product is no longer available in the data set in a given month, field collection substitution rules are applied. Also, it may be desirable to replace a product as soon as its monthly sales become so low that it could no longer be seen as representative for its product category. It may also be acceptable to let products exit the market before replacing them in the sample. When a replacement is required, candidate products are identified based on product descriptions and sales. The selected replacement products should be equivalent to the disappeared ones in terms of quality. The previous month price of a replacement product could either be looked for in the previous month scanner data or imputed using a quality adjustment technique, similar to rules in place for the field collection. Sales data may be monitored over time and used to keep the product sample as representative as in the initial month the sample was selected. A simplified version of the static approach consists in a direct replacement of the field collection product sample with a sample of products selected from scanner data for a given retailer, using exactly the same sample of stores. The sample size and the sampled outlets remain the same under the field collection. It should be noted that when used in practice, there is sometimes additional resource requirements to identifying suitable replacements from the scanner data. The process by which replacements are chosen and quality adjustments are made where necessary, can also have a significant impact on the final index output. 
The dynamic sampling approach uses a set of filters and an algorithm to select a matched sample of products for each month and the reference month. The product sample comprises of products that are present in both the current month and the reference month and that represent a significant portion of sales in their respective product categories. The product sample may vary from one month to the next. Given the use of pre-set filters, the entire sampling procedure can be fully automated. However, an automated system cannot necessarily handle product relaunches well in the calculation of price relatives, because the relaunched products cannot be conveniently linked to the old products in an automated manner. Challenges raised by relaunches or other sources of product churn make the dynamic sampling approach unsuitable for product groups with a high turnover rate. The dynamic approach improves the quality of price indexes based on scanner data, compared to field collection price indexes or to the static sampling approach. In view of the low level of manual interventions, it is cost efficient. As a result, when the dynamic sampling approach is used, it is easy to extend the use of scanner data to more retailers. A detailed discussion on the dynamic sampling approach is available in section 8.3 of Eurostat's HICP - Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data .
While National Statistical Offices (NSOs) should attempt to use the full universe of scanner data whenever possible, they may decide to use the static or dynamic sampling method if the capacity of their systems and processing infrastructure is limited. Using a sampling method may represent the first stage of a gradual approach to the use of scanner data in the CPI. When some minimum data processing capacity, skill set and infrastructure become available, the NSO may eventually move to a multilateral index method based on the universe of all available products.


Product sampling with web scraped data
If the NSO follows the targeted approach for scraping with web scraped data (see section on Strategies available for in-house web scraping) then this will already form your product sample.
When bulk web scraped data are available for some product categories from some retailers, they provide opportunities to improve the accuracy of the CPI through enhanced coverage of product dimensions such as time and varieties. However, since there is no sale information in web scraped data, the economic importance of individual products in their respective product categories cannot be estimated. The two sampling approaches previously discussed in the context of scanned data cannot be employed. The CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods (2020) briefly discusses a few considerations for using web-scraped prices in the CPI calculation. For instance, web-scraped data can be used as a replacement for the field collection for entire product categories from one or more retailers. In this case, using price data for all available individual products is the option likely to be chosen. Indeed, it is not clear how a sample of products could be selected given the lack of information on products’ representativeness in their categories. 
Before using web-scraped data from a given retailer in the CPI calculation, it is important to verify if there are any differences between web-listed and in-store list prices (or, ideally, transaction prices) for this retailer. Any available information on possible differences between these two types of prices should be taken into consideration. The goal is to ensure that the web scraped prices used in the CPI calculation reflect in-store prices as much as possible. For example, if a retailer uses a regional pricing strategy, it is important to collect and use appropriate local prices in the price index calculation for the lowest level geographic regions.

title: Strategies available for in-house web scraping
text:
Points to consider if in-house web scraping is the chosen solution



Preliminary analysis
If the National Statistical Office (NSO) decides to perform the web scraping on its own, some points should be considered to define the best scraping strategy and the best web scraping tool to adopt or develop.
Once the candidate sites are identified, guidance on web scraping for Consumer Price Indices (CPIs) (see section 3 of Eurostat's "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP" for further discussion) recommends that before putting up any scraping tools the first strategy to follow is check whether there is an Application Programming Interface (API) available to extract the desired data. The use of an API of a given web source allows access to a structured database that allows the extraction of the source’s data with improved control and stability without the need to scrape. An example on the use of an API for CPI purposes can be found in Annex II of Ref. "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP" and section "Collection of data via APIs".
Another important issue to consider before scraping a site is to check what is the site policy regarding web scraping. Some websites have restrictions against being scraped and may even forbid it. It is a good practice to follow the site rules. Robots.txt contains the information about website policies concerning which areas that scrapers are allowed to search. This file can be accessed by typing the root of the website and adding '/robots.txt'. For instance, https://www.ecb.europa.eu/robots.txt. A more detailed discussion on legal issues on using web scraping for CPIs is discussed in the Eurostat's "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP". Examples of NSOs current practices are presented in Annex VII of this guidance. The web scraping policy of the ONS-UK is another interesting example on such practices, where permissions to web scrape are managed centrally to avoid duplication and reduce the risk of blocking.


Targeted versus bulk approaches
If an API is not available and scraping is allowed, the choice of the best tool will rely on some factors such as the amount and frequency of data to be collected from a given site and the number of sites necessary to provide an appropriate coverage of a given item of the basket. Regarding these issues, web scraping can be divided in two approaches: targeted and bulk ("Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP").
Targeted web scraping aims at collecting data whose attributes are predefined beforehand and hence applies to the collection of a limited number of items from a given number of websites. This is useful for when the goal is to sample from these new data sources in order to replace the existing collection, rather than use the full data set. The bulk approach aims at extracting a large volume of data without selecting a subset of items to price.
The targeted approach is commonly employed when the goal is to replace and improve the collection of items of the basket that are usually performed in a manual centralized approach by means of emails, phone calls, human inspection of websites, etc. For this kind of problem, it is desirable to have a more generic web scraping tool that can be used to extract data from different websites and with a few input and control parameters that can be defined manually by users. See Ref. (1) and (2) for some examples.
NSOs have been employing the use of so-called point-and-click functionality tools to perform targeted extraction of web data. Such tools are based on user-friendly interfaces where users need to provide a set of parameters of the sites to extract desired information. There are third-parties that offer those engines and some NSOs have been exploring such tools. A disadvantage of using third-party tools is that they are not designed for the specific needs of CPI collection. For instance, such services are usually not free of charge and not open source, hence changes in the underlying scripts according to user needs are not allowed. For further discussion see section 3 of "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP".

An alternative is to develop fit for purpose tools in-house. A nice example of such an approach is the RobotTool engine, developed by Statistics Netherlands for targeted collection of prices. In Ref. (2) the details for the creation and development of the tool are discussed. The tool is currently available at https://github.com/SNStatComp/RobotTool, where the license terms are also presented, although note that as of June 2022, this repo will no longer be updated to reflect changes on the internal CBS production version of the tool.
For bulk collection the best option is to scrape by coding since the manual work to predefine the data of interest would be too resource intensive. The computational efficiency is also a key point since coded scrapers will usually run much faster than point and click applications. The code shall automate the actions that would be conducted by a web browser such as, opening a webpage, clicking and scrolling, and selecting the elements of interest by means of a query. Techniques to be employed will rely on the sites being of a static or dynamic nature ("Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP").
Due to its free software character, R and Python are popular tools adopted for web scraping by coding. Also, they already offer dedicated libraries developed for this goal. Among the most used ones we can cite Rvest and RSelenium in R, whereas in Python some options available include urllib3, BeautifulSoup and Scrapy3. The use of Selenium is necessary whenever the site has a dynamical character which demands the action of a user interacting with the page in order to get a given information. Selenium mimics a human in performing such tasks. The RSelenium library deals with this in R. Selenium is compatible and can be installed in Python also (see here, for instance). 
In section 3 of "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP", there is a detailed discussion on the main software used for coding a scraper and in Annex VII a list of the tools currently adopted by different NSOs. A more general discussion on Information Technology (IT) requirements for these new data sources is available in the section CPI production system requirements.

Paper presented at the UNECE Meeting of the Group of experts on Price Indices. https://unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/stats/documents/ece/ces/ge.22/2016/Session_2_Netherlands_On_the_use_of_internet_data_for_Dutch_CPI.pdf

title: Quality change and hedonic estimation
text:
Quality bias
NSOs have largely focused on eliminating or at least reducing quality bias, measured price change attributable to a change in the set of goods and services used to calculate a price index rather than a change in the measurement objective (typically cost of living or cost of goods). Hedonic methods and other quality adjustments methods are used to reduce quality bias, which we define here as a measured price change attributable to a difference in the value of the product sets observed over two or more time periods used to calculate a price index. Both real-world markets and sampled datasets undergo significant churn as specific products and varieties enter and exit the market. When a shift in the value of the goods results in a change in the measured price level, this apparent price change is a result of quality bias.
Matched model indexes may differ from hedonic estimates in certain cases. Two of the cases of most interest are when the characteristics and pricing behavior of product entrants and exits differ substantially from “matched” products and when the number of matched products is low. The frequency of matched products may be particularly low when price comparisons are being made over a large time span. This is particularly likely to arise when constructing multilateral price indexes as discussed below. Matched model indexes in scanner data functionally use the overlap approach to quality change unless an intervention is made to prevent different versions of an item from being used in the price index during the same time period.
NSOs account for product updates that change an product identifier by "relinking" discontinued products to their successors or finding a similar "replacement" item and using the price change between the two versions of a product. A matched model price index that does not use item replacement or relinking will only reflect the price change for a specific product version. While this produces a "constant quality" measure–one that even accommodates new good improvements with the overlap approach, this matched model will omit any price change associated with a model update, and may also introduce product cycle bias (such as showing downward price change as the result of new products tending to be sold at full price and then exiting the market at a discount). When NSOs use relinking or item replacement to address these issues, they introduce quality bias which must then be addressed with adjustment methods. Williams (2021) shows that price change across model iterations or relaunches can be substantial and larger in scale than typical estimates of quality bias. NSOs also use "grouping" (see identifying unique products) to combine products with different identifiers into a homogeneous unit value that will be treated as a single good. Both "grouping" and "relinking" help to address product turnover. Grouping should be used when two identifiers are used for homogeneous products with little or no differentiation. Relinking should be when a product has strong life cycle effects.
Quality bias is often a secondary effect of an effort to use relinking across product relaunches and replacement to accommodate price effects related to a product's life cycle (ILO 2020, p. 179). Practitioners should consider how a quality adjustment method might be impacted by the life cycle effect as well. Ideally, any hedonic price measurement would be able to model and account for life cycle effects. When not accounted for, life cycles may introduce a bias. For example, take the case of staggered price change such as annually updated contracts. In the case of an annual contract, price change for a specific product or service will only occur at an annual frequency. A naïve specification may attribute differences in the price level between pricing regimes to differences in the characteristics. Hedonic imputation with estimates specific to a pricing regime (old vs updated contracts) may accommodate this aspect of price change.  One of the motivations for relinking, and otherwise moving beyond matched model price change, is to capture price change associated with product change. For a variety of possible reasons, sellers may introduce price change (or otherwise change pricing strategy) when updating a product or product lineup. In the case of such a market, a same version, matched model price index would fail to capture price change. In order to capture price change between the set of old and updated products, either relinking or hedonic methods must be used. Similarly, relinking methods are used to offset other life cycle effects including patterns of discounting where a product ends its life cycle at a clearance rate.

title: Quality change and hedonic estimation
text:
Changes in consumer surplus
The introduction of a new good may allow consumers to achieve higher levels of utility under the same budget constraint. Hicks (1940) provided the original motivation for hedonic imputation with the recommendation that entrant goods be accounted for by estimating a “shadow price” so high that none of the good would be purchased in the period prior to its introduction. However, welfare interpretations of hedonic estimates have proven problematic. Hick’s "shadow price" is incompatible with typical utility functions, notably CES. Feenstra (1995) presents a welfare interpretation of standard hedonic indexes, but the assumptions required are restrictive. Also, while hedonic methods capture improved features, standard approaches do not capture novel features or completely new goods (see Crawford and Neary, 2021).
Non-hedonic price measurement methods have been proposed to account for the benefits of new varieties. Standard hedonic methods do not capture changes in consumer surplus directly related to changes in variety. Feenstra (1994) and Feenstra and Diewert (2022) have proposed adjustments to account for changes in product variety. However, these methods may be sensitive to identifying assumptions and the demand model specification.

title: Quality change and hedonic estimation
text:
Imputation 
Hedonic imputation can be thought of more generally as a means of correcting weighting by imputing the price of missing observations when “missingness” is associated with distinct pricing behavior.  Hedonic imputation often focuses on the cases of entry and exit, but other factors may be associated with a probability of “missing” an observation that results in a segment of a product category being underweighted. In such cases, hedonic imputation essentially serves as a weight correction. Also, while the existing literature focuses on imputation for entry and exit rather than “temporarily” missing observation, the distinction may not be useful in scanner data context. When working with current period sales records, an NSO will often be unable to ascertain whether an item has been discontinued or could be expected to return.
While many hedonic studies have focused on the price of entering goods, following Hicks, Erickson and Pakes (2011) focus on the use of hedonic imputation to estimate prices that may have exited the market before a data collector was able to capture a price. They found price surveys systematically omit the end of a product’s lifecycle where prices tend to be substantially discounted, and therefore introduce a bias into the index. This specific issue is less of a concern when scanner data accounts for the complete set of transaction prices from a seller.

title: Choosing an index method
text:
This section contains information on how an NSO can choose a suitable index method. The choice of index method is an important part of implementing these new data sources in production. It can be split into two scenarios, one where expenditure data are available (this also includes the scenario of web scraped for when there are proxy expenditure weights available) and one where expenditure data are not available.

title: Working with class imbalance
text: Datasets NSOs need to classify are typically not equally distributed, as some classes have many records (i.e. unique products) while others have only a few. This requires additional steps to be taken when designing and testing classifiers. Specitically, this represents a challenge for automated methods (such as Method 4 or Machine Learning (ML)), as models could struggle when they don't have a lot of examples to learn from, thus typically misclassifying sparse categories. This chapter introduces approaches that NSOs could use to mitigate consequences that arise from such class imbalance problems.

title: Working with class imbalance
text:
Undersampling
Undersampling techniques aim to balance class distributions by minimizing majority class items. This can be done randomly or according to more sophisticated concepts. Tomek links for instance is one such commonly used sophisticated approach that finds and removes noisy and hard to classify observations to help find a more disrable decision boundary (see imbalanced learn site for more guidance). An undersampled dataset posses the advantage that it is more balanced among the classes/labels and that it may help to improve storage problems and runtime, especially when the training data set is huge. It has been proposed as good means of increasing the sensitivity of a classifier to the minority class. On the other hand, it is very likely that it discards potentially useful information in the data which can be important for building classifiers. In addition, the undersampled dataset can be biased in the sense that it is not an appropriate representative of the population.

title: Working with class imbalance
text:
Oversampling
An alternative is to oversample minority classes, which may be more appropriate for NSOs. Specifically, as minority classes in alternative datasets may be mostly represented by just a few items, undersampling would be inappropriate as a balanced training dataset can only be achieved by a huge loss of data, and thus a resultant compromise in the quality of the ML classification. Oversampling techniques aim to balance class distributions by adding items to the minority class. Thus, it is a good choice when the training data set does not possess enough data in each class. The minority classes are not necessarily supplemented by creating exact copies of the particular records in those classes, as more diverse synthetic samples can also be created by introducing small variations of the items. This rebalancing method has is advantageous in that no information is lost, however its overuse can increases the likelihood of an ML model overfitting through replication of parts of the minority class specific items. 
Random Oversampling
The simplest oversampling technique refers to random oversampling. It randomly selects examples from the minority class and adds them to the training data set until an approximately balanced set is achieved. This method is also applicable to the minority class' feature space. As an example, if ngrams are used for text classification, one can randomly draw and combine ngrams from the minority class and add the result to the training data set. It worth mentioning, that this approach increases the likelihood of overfitting since examples or features are merely duplicated and the feature space is not increased. NSOs may need to regularize more heavily in this case to make sure models generalize out of sample.

SMOTE
In contrast to random oversampling with replacement, which does not necessarily increase the recognition of the minority classes, Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (or SMOTE) tries to identify similar but more specific regions in the feature space for the minority classes. In other words, the minority classes are oversampled by synthetically creating new examples:

First, features of the minority class are chosen (green points in panel a of Figure 1).
Second, identify the k nearest neighbors (the black point in panel b of Figure 1 is a selected feature and whereas the yellow points represent its neighbors). One can determine the specific number of neighbors k arbitrarily or by using heuristics, such as the "elbow method".
Third, synthetic examples are generated. Intuitively, this is done by randomly placing a point between the selected samples and their neighbors (red point between the brown points in panel c of Figure 1). Technically, the difference of the minority class feature vector and its nearest neighbor is taken. Thereafter, the differences are multiplied by a random number between 0 and 1. The resulting vector of synthetic features is added to the minority class' feature vector. In the multiclass case, this procedure is repeated for each minority class.

Figure 1: How synthetic samples are generated with SMOTE. Each point represent a record in the feature space. See Schubach et al (2017) for more details.

Note, that SMOTE does not inherently consider feature relationships beyond simple interpolation. It assumes that linear interpolation within the minority class is safe and realistic, which may not always be the case. The method also assumes features are independent or loosely correlated, which is often not realistic in complex datasets. Thus, it is important to consider the nature of the relationship between features when generating synthetic data.

title: Implementation
text:
This page contains information on how to implement these new data sources into production. Once the research stage for any given data source has completed, there are a number of different steps to consider before moving to actual regular CPI production. This also depends on whether this is the first time of implementing these new data sources, or whether this is a phased approach where new categories/data sources are implemented over time (see Selection of categories). For example, a new production system can be built in a flexible manner to ensure that any future work to implement new categories can use this existing system and methods rather than requiring new development. The rough order of steps is presented below. Each NSO will of course have their individual circumstances to consider when planning this work.


Finalise a methodology


After testing the new data sources and methodology (summarised in the previous handbook sections), a final decision on the actual methods to be implemented in the regular CPI production must be made and how the new indices shall be integrated with the remaining indices (see Aggregation) based on other data sources and methodology. For information on how to introduce multilateral methods in regular HICP production, see Eurostat’s guidelines “Practical Guide on Multilateral Methods in the HICP” (chapter 10)


Build a production system
New methodology will most likely require that a new production system needs to be built (see CPI production system requirements). Prototype systems may have already been built in the research phase, but to move to production it is very important to have extensive tests that the new regular production system provides the expected results. Detailed documentation of the workflows and the different steps of production processes must also be created. In the line with producing the impact assessment, the system should be run in parallel for a certain time period to ensure it is stable and any bugs in the process have been found before moving it to live production. The production system should also include functionality to mitigate against scenarios where regular data is partly or totally missing from one or several retailers (see section Dealing with unexpected data gaps).


Adapt production process to incorporate these new data sources and/or methods
It is likely that when these new data sources are introduced, the production process will need to change. For example, the data may arrive more frequently (weekly rather than monthly) so the burden of running initial checks on these data could be more spread out through the month. Depending on methods chosen, the production team may need to spend more time on classifying the products, but may save time with no longer needing to run manual collections. Time will be required to train the production team if new systems and methods are being introduced (referring to the documentation produced for the new system).


Assess the impact of new methodology
Before implementation of CPI indices based on new data sources like scanner data it is important to assess the impact of the data source and new methodology. This can be done by performing a comparative study of the old and new methodology. The CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods (2020), paragraphs 10.116-10.121, discusses the importance of producing empirical results in relation to the implementation of multilateral methods. The indices should be run in parallel over a certain period of time, for instance a year, in order to study the methodology and produce and fully understand the empirical results.
The impact results of the new data source/methodology based on historical back data should emphasize both the effect on the all-item index as well as the COICOP groups affected. For instance, if scanner data is introduced for COICOP 01 Food and non-alcoholic beverages, the impact should be calculated for the all-item index, the aggregated COICOP group, as well as for lower levels.


Communication and publication
Introducing alternative data sources in the official CPI often means a major change and may provide real impact on the results. It is therefore important to provide adequate information to the users throughout the research and implementation phases. The information should be tailored both towards expert users as well as other users of the statistics by presenting both high-level summaries and more in-depth technical information. For the trust in the published CPI to continue it is important to ensure transparency and understanding of the methods used. Using scanner data and in particular multilateral methods are more complicated than traditional price index methodology and may present communication challenges for NSOs.
The results and the impact of the new method should be made available to all users, at the same time and according to a publication schedule announced in advance. Any significant changes in methodology must be fully explained and notified as far in advance as possible of the change being made. For more information on users need, see the CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods (2020) (paragraphs 10.116-10.121, 14.55-14.64). For an example of a publication explaining upcoming changes at (fairly) high level please see the Office for National Statistics' (ONS) publication Introducing multilateral index methods into consumer price statistics


Linking index series of new methodology to old series
When NSOs implement new methods based on alternative data sources like for instance scanner data in the CPI, the new series need to be linked to the old official series in order to have continuous CPI series. Due to the new methodology, the new index series are not directly comparable to previous index series and may show different price development. Also, switching the method from for instance an unweighted bilateral sample-based index based on scanner data to a multilateral index using all scanner data as well as both price and quantity information may result in differences in the price development.
The new index can be implemented in different ways. Some NSOs may present the change in methodology as breaks in the index series, others may present revised series even though many NSOs choose not to revise CPI once it is published. Making use of alternative data like scanner data often implies that NSOs do have historical back data of certain length which enables different chain-linking methods.
The three methods that can be used to link an index of new methodology to a previous official index are:

base month overlap method/base month linking
year on year linking method, linking on the same month of previous year
annual overlap method, where an entire year is used as an overlap period, also called an average year correction.

By using base month overlap method, the monthly change rates of the new index are preserved, but the year on year change rates may not be consistent with the change rates of the new index series. Using the year on year linking secures the year on year movements, but not necessarily the monthly price changes of the new index series during the first year. The annual overlap method ensures that the annual growth rate is identical in the new index series and the chained official index series. By using the annual overlap method, one therefore makes a level shift adjustment or an average year correction to the chained official index. The adjustment factor can be defined as the ratio of the averages of the indices of the old and new methodology over the months in the year before the new methodology is introduced. The monthly change rates will be equal to the indices for the new series, except for the first month of implementation. Antonio Chessa discusses the different chain linking methods in the paper “Extension of multilateral index series over time: Analysis and comparison of methods” (2021).
Depending on how different the price development is between the indices of the new and the old methodology, the choice of chain-linking method may potentially impact the results of the new chained official index during the first transition year of the new method. The European Central Bank Statistics Paper “Chain linking over December and methodological changes in the HICP: view from a central bank perspective” (2021) discusses chain-linking strategies in relation to the European Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) and methodological changes.

title: Quality assurance
text:
The use of alternative data sources in CPI compilation requires robust quality assurance procedures. 
While many of the quality principles applied to traditional price collection remain relevant, alternative data sources introduce new risks that must be managed carefully. These risks may arise from the scale and complexity of the datasets, the automated nature of processing pipelines, and the reliance on systems and processes that are outside the direct control of the National Statistical Office (NSO).
Quality assurance should therefore be embedded throughout the CPI production process. Rather than being treated as a single stage of validation, quality considerations should inform the assessment of potential data sources, the design of processing systems, the compilation of indices and the ongoing monitoring of outputs. Quality assurance procedures should be proportionate to the scale and complexity of the data source and should evolve as experience with the data increases. NSOs are encouraged to develop quality assurance procedures tailored to their own data sources, compilation methods and operational environments.


Quality frameworks
International statistical quality frameworks provide useful guidance for structuring this work. The United Nations (UN) has published the United Nations National Quality Assurance Frameworks Manual for Official Statistics (UN NQAF Manual), which provides guidance on establishing quality frameworks within national statistical systems. The manual includes specific guidance on quality assurance for statistics compiled using administrative or other non-statistical data sources.
Frameworks generally include a set of quality dimensions that can help structure quality assurance activities. For example, the Quality Assurance Framework of the European Statistical System identifies several principles relating to statistical outputs:

Relevance - The degree to which the statistical product meets user needs in both coverage and content.
Accuracy & Reliability - Accuracy is the proximity between an estimate and the unknown true value. Reliability is the closeness of early estimates to subsequent estimated values.
Timeliness and Punctuality - Timeliness refers to the time gap between publication and the reference period. Punctuality refers to the gap between planned and actual publication dates.
Accessibility and Clarity - Accessibility is the ease with which users are able to access the data, also reflecting the format in which the data are available and the availability of supporting information. Clarity refers to the quality and sufficiency of the metadata, illustrations and accompanying advice.
Comparability and Coherence - Comparability is the degree to which data can be compared over time and domain. Coherence is the degree to which data that are derived from different sources or methods, but refer to the same topic, are similar.

With the advance of modern methods and systems, including the potential use of machine learning and AI in the production of Official Statistics, some other dimensions of quality are also being considered and proposed. For example, reproducibility has been a key consideration in recent years (see for example, the Price Statistics Reproducibility Project), while explainability and robustnesses have also been proposed in the Machine Learning context (see A Quality Concept for the Use of Machine Learning in Official Statistics). 
All quality dimensions remain applicable when using alternative data sources for CPI production. In practice, however, their implementation requires particular attention to both the characteristics of the data source and the behaviour of the resulting statistical outputs. Quality assurance activities can therefore be considered across several stages of the CPI production process as described below. 


Source assessment
Before integrating a new data source into CPI compilation, NSOs should evaluate whether it is suitable for statistical use. This assessment should consider whether the data provide adequate coverage of the products, outlets or market segments represented in the CPI, and whether the concepts and definitions used in the data align with CPI requirements.
Other important considerations include the stability of product identifiers and classifications, the availability of metadata, and the sustainability of access to the data source. Because alternative data sources are often supplied by external organisations, changes in provider systems, business practices or data delivery mechanisms may affect the structure or interpretation of the data.
Exploratory analysis or pilot studies can be useful in assessing whether the data source provides sufficient coverage, stability and quality for CPI purposes.
Where alternative data are obtained from external providers, formal data sharing agreements or contracts are typically required. These agreements should specify the data schema, transfer frequency, delivery method and responsibilities for maintaining the data supply. It is also good practice to include provisions requiring advance notification of planned changes to data structures, definitions or delivery processes so that NSOs can make any necessary adjustments in advance. Where possible, any validation checks carried out by the data supplier should be agreed and documented.
More details of quality assurance at this stage of the process are provided in the Data selection and acquisition section. 


Data ingestion and integrity checks
Once a data source has been established, quality assurance should begin with checks on the integrity of incoming data deliveries. These checks confirm that the data have been received as expected and that their structure remains consistent over time.
Typical checks may include verifying the completeness of data deliveries, confirming that key variables and identifiers are present and correctly formatted, and monitoring the volume of observations received. Sudden changes in data volumes, missing variables or structural differences may indicate delivery errors or changes in provider systems that require investigation.
At this stage it is often useful to standardise incoming data into a common internal schema used for CPI processing. For example, NSOs may adopt consistent naming conventions and variable definitions for key fields such as price, quantity, product identifiers or transaction dates. Standardising the data structure helps ensure consistency across different sources and simplifies downstream processing.
Many NSOs implement automated validation pipelines or monitoring dashboards to track incoming data deliveries and flag anomalies. These tools can help detect missing data, structural changes or unusual shifts in data volumes as soon as the data are ingested.


Data preparation and processing
Quality assurance during data preparation focuses on ensuring that the data have been correctly processed and classified for CPI use. This stage often involves mapping products to the CPI classification, identifying missing or duplicate observations, and detecting extreme or implausible price movements. 
In the case of alternative data sources, particular attention may be required to manage product identifiers, product relaunches or changes in packaging and product characteristics. Because these datasets are typically large and require automated processing pipelines, reproducibility, documentation and version control are particularly important.
The systems used to process alternative data sources should also be appropriately tested and supported by the NSO’s IT infrastructure. Responsibilities for maintaining these systems, including the division of roles between statistical production teams and IT departments, should be clearly defined.


Index compilation and validation
After price indices have been compiled, quality assurance should focus on the behaviour of the resulting statistical outputs. This may involve analysing the volatility of indices, reviewing the contributions of individual products or retailers, and comparing results with indices produced using alternative methods or data sources.
Unexpected movements or structural breaks in the index may indicate issues in the underlying data or processing procedures. For example, changes in product coverage, filtering rules or matching algorithms may affect index stability and should be investigated carefully.
Before introducing indices derived from alternative data sources into live production, it is generally advisable to conduct impact analysis comparing the results with existing CPI series (see section on Implementation). Differences between the new and existing approaches should be understood and documented, and any methodological changes should be clearly explainable to users.
Some NSOs also use formal governance arrangements when introducing new data sources or index methods, such as internal review panels or external advisory groups (see as an example the UK's advisory panels for consumer prices - stakeholder and technical). These structures can provide additional scrutiny and help ensure that proposed methodological changes are robust and transparent.


Ongoing monitoring
The characteristics of alternative data sources may evolve over time as retailers update systems, websites change structure, or consumer purchasing behaviour shifts. Quality assurance should therefore include ongoing monitoring of both the underlying data and the resulting statistical outputs.
Monitoring activities may include tracking changes in product coverage, retailer participation or identifier structures, reviewing the stability of data deliveries, and periodically reassessing the representativeness of the data source relative to the CPI universe.
Where automated or machine learning approaches are used in data processing (for example in product classification or matching), additional monitoring may be required to ensure that model performance remains stable over time. Changes in product ranges or market behaviour may affect the accuracy of such models and periodic review may therefore be necessary. The section on classification includes a discussion on monitoring the accuracy of any machine learning models used over time.

title: How to evaluate classification methods
text: There are numerous metrics that can be tracked and applied when evaluating how well a classifier performs. This chapter provides an overview of common approaches using a Machine Learning (ML) classifier (i.e. Method 4 and in some cases Method 3) as the use case throughout due to their applicability and popularity with ML. These metrics however, could also be applied on classifiers created with other methods (such as Method 2) as long as there is a representative test dataset on which to evaluate classifier performance.

title: How to evaluate classification methods
text:
Binary classification
For simplicity, we start with a binary case with two classes.

Several metrics can be calculated from this:

Accuracy is the proportion of correct predictions out of all predictions made. Accuracy is also an indicator of the overall classification task (i.e. summarizes the situation for both positive and negative classes as one metric).

\[\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\text{correct predictions}}{\text{all predictions}}= \frac{tp + tn}{tp+tn+fp+fn} \]

Precision is the proportion of correct predictions out of all predictions estimated as positive. It is calculated individually for each class.

\[\text{Precision} = \frac{tp}{tp+fp}\]

Recall (also called sensitivity) is the proportion of true positives out of all positive observations. Similar to precision, it is calculated for each class.

\[\text{Recall} = \frac{tp}{tp+fn}\]
Ideally, we want a high precision and a high recall. Precision and recall do not necessarily both increase, they can also behave in opposite ways. Both can be combined through an F1 score:

F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. The F1 score shows how precise the model is, as well as how robust it is. If one of the two metrics is much lower than the other, then the F1 score is lower than the arithmetic mean of the two scores.

\[\text{F1} = \frac{2tp}{ (2tp+fp+fn)} = 2\frac{\text{precision}* \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}\]
Accuracy and F1 score are very commonly used scores to evaluate a classifier. Accuracy is very easy to interpret, but it also has weaknesses especially with heterogeneous distributed class sizes (or imbalanced data). Suppose you have one class with 99 observations and a second class with one observation. If the classifier always estimates the first class, it will have an accuracy of 99%, however it will always miss the second class, which is undesirable. 
Example 1: Suppose we have 10 items to be classified, 2 milk and 8 yogurts. If the classifier classifies one milk item correctly and the other milk as a yogurt and all yogurts correctly, we get the following scores. 

Accuracy = 9 / 10 = 0.9 or 90% correct
F1 for Milk = (2*1)/(2*1+ 0 + 1)= 2/3 = 0,5 = 66,7%
F1 for Yoghurt = (2*8)/(2*8+1+0) = 16/17 = 94.1%

In this example with unequal class distribution, accuracy is less suitable. F1 metrics also tell different stories depending on the class you calculate them for.

title: Why use alternative data sources? Strategic motivations
text:
Common reasons shared by NSOs as a driver for using these new data sources.
National Statistical Offices (NSOs) adopt alternative data sources for a range of strategic, methodological, and operational reasons. While the specific motivations vary across countries and institutional settings, several common drivers are apparent.
Importantly, the decision to use alternative data sources is rarely motivated by a single factor. Instead, NSOs typically face a combination of pressures and opportunities, and the relative importance of these may evolve over time as systems, skills, and user expectations change.


Improving timeliness and frequency
Alternative data sources can support more timely price measurement by reducing reliance on manual data collection and processing. Transaction data, APIs, and some administrative sources are often available on a regular and predictable schedule, while web-based sources can be collected at high frequency.
This can enable:

Faster production cycles,
More rapid incorporation of price changes, and
Greater flexibility in responding to shocks or sudden market developments.

For some NSOs, improved timeliness is a key motivation for initially piloting alternative data sources, even if full integration into headline CPI production occurs later.


Increasing granularity and analytical potential
Compared with traditional survey-based collection, alternative data sources often provide large volumes of detailed observations. This can allow NSOs to compile and explore indices at more granular levels (e.g. by product, retailer, or region) and to refine and/or expand its coverage (in terms of sectors of the basket and regions covered).
Greater granularity can support internal quality assurance, methodological research, and more informed communication with users, even where headline CPI outputs remain unchanged.


Supporting methodological development
The availability of detailed price and, in some cases, quantity information opens up methodological options that are difficult or impossible to implement with traditional survey data alone. In particular, transaction data can support the use of explicit weighting at the elementary aggregate level and facilitate the application of more advanced index number methods.
For some NSOs, the adoption of alternative data sources is closely linked to longer-term plans to modernise index compilation methods, rather than simply to replace existing collection mechanisms. This kind of strategy is recommended and the discussions presented in this Handbook are expected to support CPI compilers to have a thorough vision of the processes involved in the use of alternative data sources to also build their own strategic plans. 


Improving efficiency and sustainability
Alternative data sources have the potential to reduce the operational burden associated with large-scale price collection, particularly in categories where traditional surveys are resource-intensive or difficult to maintain.
Over time, automated data acquisition and processing can:

Reduce respondent burden,
Lower field collection costs, and
Improve resilience to staff turnover or external disruptions.

However, these efficiency gains are typically realised only after initial investment in systems, skills, and governance arrangements.


Enhancing coverage of rapidly changing markets
Some markets, such as consumer electronics, online services, or digitally delivered goods, evolve quickly and are challenging to capture using traditional survey approaches. Alternative data sources may allow NSOs to:

Detect new products more quickly,
Collect rich products attributes in a a cost-effective way that can be used for the construction of hedonic adjustments;
Better reflect changes in assortments, and
Reduce delays in incorporating market innovations into price indices.

This motivation is particularly relevant in environments characterised by high product churn or frequent changes in retail channels.


Supporting wider use across the statistical system
Although the primary focus of this handbook is on consumer price statistics, many NSOs are also motivated by the potential to reuse alternative data sources across multiple statistical domains. Where data access, concepts, and quality permit, a single data acquisition effort may support price statistics alongside other outputs such as business price statistics, PPPs, national accounts, short-term indicators, or analytical work.
This broader perspective can strengthen the strategic case for investment but also increases the importance of coordination across organisational units. Other uses of alternative data sources are considered in the section Other uses of alternative data sources.

title: Collection of data via APIs
text:
An alternative to automatically scraping data from web pages is to extract data directly from application programming interface (APIs)



API data collection
An alternative to automatically scraping data from web pages is to extract data directly from application programming interface (APIs). The Eurostat’s practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP (Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices) recommend checking for available APIs before setting up solutions for web scraping. The purpose of an API is to provide structured and controlled access to specific data or services. API is a set of procedures and communication protocols that provide access to data of an application, operating system or other services.
Compared to scraping web pages, extracting data from databases often means greater stability and less maintenance work. While web pages suddenly may change their layout and hence require corrections in the scraping code, the API solutions are often more stable and changes in the API structure are likely to be announced in advance. Extracting data from API can be an effective way to get large amount of data with less time spent on data collection. Some APIs are free to access and available for everyone, but in most cases access to API will require formal contracts with data owners and a pay-per-use approach.
An example of how APIs can be used in practice are for the collection of airfare prices (see section on Selection of categories). Some National Statistical Offices (NSOs) use an API in the data collection of airline tickets where requests with parameters on representative flights are sent to the API and the API returns information on prices and additional information related to the tickets (for example, flight number, departure and arrival time, booking category, etc.). The Eurostat practical guidelines suggest that the booking system Amadeus can serve as a good starting point to master using APIs.
Making use of available air travel APIs has the advantage that NSOs do not have to set up airline-specific API solutions, but only need to deal with one single data provider. On the other hand, it is important to check with data provider the actual market coverage and what information is provided in the API. It can also be advisable to check prices collected from the API against prices on the airline companies’ own web pages and to look closer into any discrepancies.
Measuring airfares presents a challenge as they are subject to a dynamic pricing structure, dependent on how far in advance they are booked and on availability. Furthermore, flights shall be included in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) when actually consumed, not purchased. As airline tickets often show strong price fluctuations it is important to separate between time of ordering and time of travelling. Making a schedule for the price collection of flights rests on a series of assumptions that must be adapted to the specific situation in each country. The prices should be recorded sufficiently in advance of departure to ensure they are representative of consumers’ expenditure and behaviour. Input from professionals from within the airline industry could be very useful when setting up such a schedule.
The data collection may be performed by using Python programming language and by making use of software packages that can be downloaded and imported, for more information see example in the annex II of Eurostat practical guidelines.
The collected API data can be monitored and checked for abnormalities in the same way as data collected through web scraping, see section on monitoring, validation and plausibility checks for web scraped data. 
In the training course 2 about data acquisition, in module 2.3  a general description is given of the main issues to face and the plan to implement to access data via API.

title: Standardising the data
text:
Data will need to be standardised before being used to calculate price indices.



Standardising the data
After the data are received by the National Statistical Office (NSO), it will need to be standardised in order to be processed through the statistical pipeline. Standardisation can include:

renaming column names so that common attributes are called the same across different retailers
reformatting the data so that attributes are saved in the same data type (for example, all dates are saved in date/time format)
creating new variables that can help with future processing

Scanner data sets typically do not contain a price variable. Instead, the price variable has to be calculated. An average price is obtained by dividing total turnover with the corresponding total number of units sold (the ‘quantity’ variable) for a given set of transactions.  Because this is an average price, it may be different from the price that would be observed by a price collector on a particular day, in a specific outlet for a specific product.
Different articles usually have different package sizes, weights etc.. The price and quantity variables could be transformed into a common, standard, measurement unit.  Consider the example presented in Table 1:

Some articles, especially certain fruits or vegetables but also some cheese, meat and fish are sold by weight. For those articles, the quantity variable is typically not measured by the 'number of transactions', but by the total weight sold (e.g. kilograms). In that case, the calculated average price is already standardised (for example an average price per kilogram). 
A standardised price could also be calculated for web scraped data. For example, for clothing multipacks, the scraped price could be transformed into a 'price per unit'.

title: Key challenges and trade-offs
text:
Alternative data sources introduce a number of challenges and trade-offs that National Statistical Offices (NSOs) must actively manage.
These considerations often cut across organisational boundaries and require balancing competing priorities rather than identifying a single “optimal” solution.
Importantly, many of these challenges are not purely technical. Legal frameworks, governance arrangements, skills, and user expectations all influence how alternative data can be used in practice.


Legal, ethical, and governance considerations
Access to alternative data is often governed by complex legal and contractual arrangements. Unlike survey data, where NSOs typically have well-established legal mandates, alternative data sources may involve:

Commercial data providers,
Third-party intermediaries, or
Data originally collected for non-statistical purposes.

NSOs must assess whether data access is legally sustainable over time, whether terms of use permit statistical reuse, and how risks related to confidentiality, privacy, and ethical use are managed. These considerations may constrain methodological choices or limit how results can be published or shared.


Stability, continuity, and dependency risks
Alternative data sources may be subject to changes outside the control of the NSO. For example:

Retailers may change product identifiers or reporting practices,
Websites may alter structure or restrict automated access or even be discontinued,
Data providers may discontinue or modify data deliveries.

These risks create a trade-off between innovation and robustness. Highly detailed or novel data sources may offer analytical benefits but increase vulnerability to supply disruptions, requiring contingency planning.


Methodological complexity versus transparency
Many alternative data sources enable the use of more sophisticated index methods. While these methods may offer desirable statistical properties, they can also:

Increase computational and system complexity,
Build the team skills to learn and use such methods;
Be harder to explain to non-technical users, and
Complicate internal validation and quality assurance processes.

NSOs must balance methodological refinement with transparency, reproducibility, and the need to maintain trust in official statistics. In some cases, simpler methods may be preferred during early implementation phases, even if more advanced approaches are planned longer term.


Timeliness versus revision policy
Some alternative data based methods, particularly multilateral index approaches, may imply revisions when new data become available. This can conflict with established CPI revision policies or user expectations of non-revised headline indices.
NSOs therefore face trade-offs between:

Using methods that make full use of available data, and
Maintaining stable, non-revised published series.

Splicing, window design, and publication strategies become critical choices in managing this tension. These are discussed further in Price index methods. 


Resource constraints and skill requirements
Although alternative data sources have the potential to reduce long-term costs, their adoption typically requires upfront investment. This may include:

New IT infrastructure,
Data engineering and coding skills,
Methodological expertise in advanced index number theory, and
Ongoing maintenance capacity.

NSOs must consider whether these resources are available internally, whether partnerships are required, and how knowledge is retained over time.


Organisational coordination and change management
Introducing alternative data often affects multiple parts of the organisation simultaneously. For example, data acquisition, IT systems, methodology teams, and dissemination units may all need to adapt.
A key trade-off is between incremental integration, where new data sources are phased in gradually, and more transformative approaches that redesign production systems end-to-end. Both approaches have merits, but they imply different risks, timelines, and management challenges.
These challenges and trade-offs mean that adopting alternative data sources is not simply a technical exercise. NSOs must make a series of deliberate decisions about scope, methods, governance, and resourcing.

title: Data requirements specification for scanner data
text: Key variables to ask for when acquiring scanner data.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for scanner data

title: Data requirements specification for scanner data
text:
Retailer/outlet identifiers
A retailer/outlet identifier is a unique code to identify each store of the retailer. This allows identification of each store at a more disaggregated level. Typically, the statistical office should aim at getting the scanner data at the most detailed level whenever possible, i.e., at the outlet location level. This ensures that price changes are estimated at the level at which they generally occur in the retail chain. It is also important that data from all outlets are included in the scanner data set of each retailer in each reference period, unless the retailer has reasons not to do so. When data are obtained for a sample of outlets only, additional data may be required for an appropriate weighting of the included outlets during the index aggregation. If results are to be aggregated for different regions or stores in the chain, a new code can be attributed relating to the aggregated stores. For a discussion on the conditions on the use of aggregated data for different stores of a given retailer, see section 3 of Eurostat’s guidelines “Practical Guide on Multilateral Methods in the HICP”.
In order to perform the geographical aggregation, if available, use of geographical data such as zip codes and/or longitude and latitude coordinates of the stores are recommended as they allow an efficient and accurate way to aggregate similar stores in a given region. More discussions on aggregation of outlets can be found in the section aggregation across time and outlets. Nowadays, a given retailer can also possess both an online and physical presence. In some cases the retailer can provide an additional variable distinguishing these characteristics.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for scanner data

title: Data requirements specification for scanner data
text:
Article identifier
A unique code to identify an article. Different kinds of article codes might be necessary in this process. The Global Trade Item Number (GTIN) code is the most elementary level to identify an article sold by a store, in principle, this could provide such a key. However, as discussed in the section on identifying unique products, due to multiple factors of market dynamics such as data churn and product relaunches, several GTIN codes can correspond to the same article (see for instance Table 1 in Eurostat's Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data). Therefore, it may also be useful to ask for the retailer identification numbers (for example, SKUs, or Stock Keeping Units) which are generally defined at a higher level and can capture relaunches in product varieties. For a detailed discussion of each of these codes, see section 4 of the practical guide.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for scanner data

title: Data requirements specification for scanner data
text:
Other retailer codes
Retailers generally have their own classification structures. Retailer hierarchies can provide useful information for the purpose of classification.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for scanner data

title: Data requirements specification for scanner data
text:
Articles descriptions
Text string describing the product associated to the article code, product characteristics (for example, in the context of groceries, this would include things such as package weight and unit of measurement like 500 grams), content of the package, tax rates and brand name. These variables can also be useful for applications such as CPI at constant tax rates and quality adjustment (Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data).
It should be noted that services might not possess codes that identify the articles (for example, package holidays or railfares). In this case the NSOs need to construct such kind of key after classifying and aggregating different articles via the use of the articles descriptions available.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for scanner data

title: Data requirements specification for scanner data
text:
Turnover
For a given retailer and period, the turnover per article code is necessary to derive unit prices. With this information, more aggregated turnover for broader grouping of products can be derived if necessary.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for scanner data

title: Data requirements specification for scanner data
text:
Quantities
For a given retailer and period, the quantities sold per article code are necessary to derive unit prices and to be used to derive weights for the products. More aggregated information on quantities for homogeneous products can also be derived.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for scanner data

title: Data requirements specification for scanner data
text:
Time period 
A time variable identifying the period to which the sales per article code refer. This will be related to the periodicity that data will be provided and the level of aggregation of the sales per article codes in the specified period. Ideally data should be sent from the retailers to the NSOs on a daily or weekly basis at most. Daily information is preferred since allows a more frequent control of data sent and the compilation of more refined monthly indices or even high frequency indices. However, this comes with an increase in IT costs for storage and processing due the larger amount of data involved. For practical purposes of compilation of monthly indices, weekly aggregated data can provide the desired information and this approach has been adopted in production by some NSOs. For more discussion on time aggregation, see the aggregation across time and outlets section.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for scanner data

title: Data requirements specification for scanner data
text:
Historical/back data 
Access to back data (at least from the previous year) is necessary to identify the article codes of interest for the CPI. Also, if multilateral methods are to be adopted, a longer series of back data is required to test the methods before implementation (see Eurostat's Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data). Back data can also be used for validation purposes of the data and methods as the results derived can be compared to the older CPI series derived via traditional approaches.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for scanner data

title: Data requirements specification for scanner data
text:
Other variables
If available, data identifying transactions between the retailer and other business can be used to exclude transactions that do not belong to the scope of the CPI. Information on product returns can also be used to exclude such transactions and to identify whether they are relevant for price development. Information on discounts can also be useful to allow for comparisons with existing methods where the take up rates of discounts (for example, multibuys and staff discounts) may not be known. See treatment of discounts and refunds for further discussion on this topic.

Experience from NSOs (Ref. 1, 2 and 3) show that different formats of the variables may be provided. In the negotiations with the retailers it is then important to try to standardize the data formats to be received from different providers to optimize the data transfer and processing.  
For more information, readers can find rich information on the data needs to deal with classification and aggregation of products in sections identifying unique products and classification. For the data demands necessary to adopt multilateral methods a nice description is presented in section 1 of Eurostat's “Practical Guide on Multilateral Methods in the HICP”. A detailed account on the specification of scanner data variables for different uses can be found in Section 5 of Eurostat's Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data). Section Example file structures for web scraped and scanner data of this wiki provides a comparison between what a typical file structure may look like for scanner data and web scraped data.

title: Common technical problems for in-house web scraping
text:
Overcoming some common technical problems for web scraping



Common technical problems for in-house web scraping
Data extraction from websites through web scraping techniques for production purposes in the consumer price index (CPI) compilation is challenging. Around 75% of the countries covered in the Eurostat questionnaire have experienced technical problems concerning web scraping, see "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP". While collecting information via crawlers for long periods several technical issues may arise such as, web site structural changes, internet protocol (IP) blocking, captchas, popups and even shut down of a website. A backup solution is advised in case of interruption while the scraping is not fixed and well-functioning again.
A good approach to prevent web scraping issues is to contact the website owners in advance of web scraping to ask about anti-robot policies and avoid getting your IP blocked. Establishing a good relationship with the retailers might also provide more efficient solutions like getting access via API or scanner data. Another advantage is to know beforehand upcoming changes on the website and be able to modify crawler’s code to prevent its malfunctioning.
In general, websites require a tailor-made scraper for its extraction. The maintenance of the web scraper requires dedicated staff to keep the programs working properly. Even small modifications on the websites like changes in the Xpath or css may lead to malfunction or inoperant crawlers. It is common that websites modify nodes from time to time as an anti-robot strategy. Using more stable Xpaths can prevent web scrapers from failing when such minor changes occur. Nevertheless, it is important to have in-house staff with programming skills and knowledge of the codes to deal with these changes.
It is preferable to scrape websites that usually do not have regular changes in its structure or HTML layout. It is not always possible to know in advance whether modifications will occur, but a good strategy is to perform some previous scraping of a target website some time before implementing the robots for CPI production. However, there is no guarantee that a website will not shut down as shown, for instance, in a case example in annex VI of "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP".

title: Low sales filter
text:
The low sales filter ensures that products with small expenditure shares do not unduly influence the index results.



Low sales filter
Even if they seem to be similar at first sight, a low sales filter has a different objective than a dumping filter. The low sales filter ensures that products with small expenditure shares do not unduly influence the index results. A commonly used low sales filter includes only those articles sold in two subsequent months which fulfil the following condition (Eurostat's HICP - Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data).
\[\frac{s_{i}^{t-1}+s_{i}^{t}}{2}>\frac{1}{nλ}\]
where sit is the expenditure share of product i in month t, n is the number of considered products and λ a parameter which can be considered as a cut-off value determining the total expenditure share that shall be covered. Typically, λ is set equal to 1.25 which means that only those of the most sold products will be considered which represent about 80% of the expenditures in the periods that are compared to each other (Eurostat - Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data). Depending on factors such as the market structure or the product life cycle, other values for λ might be better suited for various product groups. However, the value for λ should be chosen with caution as Bialek and Beręsewicz (2021) showed that the value for λ can considerably affect the index results. Care should also be taken for sellers with large product offerings since a substantial portion of their overall sales may be excluded with a low sales filter.

Applying low sales filter to weighted indexes may not be required since these indices allow every article to enter the index calculation according to its importance (in terms of turnover share) anyway. Therefore, weighted indexes are not prone to overrepresent articles with neglectable turnovers. Nevertheless, in order to save computation time, it might be helpful to use low sales filter also for weighted indices as they remove products before the more computational expensive index methods are applied. However, it should be investigated in advance whether the results with and without low sales filters are comparable.





References
Białek, J. and Beręsewicz, M. (2021). Scanner data in inflation measurement: From raw data to price indices, Statistical Journal of the IAOS 37, 1315–1336, http://doi.org/10.3233/SJI-210816
