title: Selection of categories
text: One of the initial steps in this process is the identification and selection of product categories to consider for the adoption of alternative data sources

title: Selection of categories
text:
Data source availability and properties
Source availability is an important point to take into account while exploring alternative data sources for CPI. A strategy can be developed to cover different sectors via different sources according to the sources properties and availability (Ref. 2, 12, 21).
Data acquisition challenges can differ according to the different data sources of interest. To have in mind the peculiarities to get access to each data source is an important point for NSOs to define the strategy for the selection of sectors to explore via alternative data sources as it might impact the planning of a schedule for study and implementation of these data. For instance, access to scanner data involves intense negotiations with the retailers and the first access to this source might take more time than web data.
When data is available for the same sector via different sources, scanner data should be preferred over web data with “similar” (prices and product descriptions) content as the former has superior data properties (Ref. 7, 8).
Scanner data sets are also superior to the web since it might provide a back series of data for initial research. Stability in the data supply should also be considered. Hence, access via stable sources or tools like APIs should be preferred over web scraping whenever possible (Ref. 8).
Since these data sources do not have a full overlap of the variables covered (see Example file structures for web scraped and scanner data), they can also be used in a complementary way for some circumstances. For instance, product attributes extracted from the web can be combined with scanner data for the development of more refined automatic models for aggregation and classification of products (clothing being a typical example) (Ref. 5) or for the use of hedonic techniques to deal with quality adjustment issues (for instance, in the sector of electronics (Ref. 10)).

title: Selection of categories
section: Representativity of the sector in the basket
text:
Representativity of the sector in the basket
This can take into account the representativity in terms of expenditures of the sector in the basket and/or the number of elements of the basket covered. The current burden in terms of price quotes manually collected to build a representative sample for the sector can also be a useful parameter to consider.
A strategy that prioritizes sectors with a higher degree of representativity is appealing as the efforts addressed will have a greater impact in the CPIs produced.

title: Selection of categories
text:
Representativity of the retailers
For the sectors chosen it is important that the alternative data sources available encompass retailers with important representation of the market of interest (see further discussion in the selection of retailer’s section). In this sense, sectors with a high degree of market coverage by a reduced number of retailers are appealing as they can minimize the data access demands while leading to more significant results in terms of CPI production.

title: Selection of categories
section: Methodological demands, human and IT resources
text:
Methodological demands, human and IT resources
As discussed in the Introduction to the new data source section, incorporation of alternative data sources into CPI can require lengthy data preparation processes and important methodological developments that are intensive in human and IT resources.
Some sectors can be more costly in this sense than others. As an example, treatment of groceries can be less demanding than clothing in terms of aggregation and classification of products (Ref. 20). Ref. 22 also suggests that scanner data for clothing can also be more subject to the effects of refunds than groceries which could require additional treatment.
Being aware of the methodological challenges that should be covered by different sectors is also beneficial in the choice of sectors to cover as this will have impact on the IT and human resources necessary to take into account such issues properly.
The decision on whether to use a sample or the whole data set (see Product sampling for price index calculation) of a given source also has different methodological and structural demands that should be evaluated by an NSO.

title: Selection of categories
text:
Groceries
The exploration of grocery scanner data is usually the first choice of an NSO (Ref. 1, 7, 13, 22). This sector is appealing for this since in many countries, especially in Europe, the market is highly concentrated in a small number of big retailer chains that have a high degree of market coverage. Furthermore, this is a sector with a high representativity in the CPI baskets and demanding in terms of collection. In this case, scanner data can allow a substantial reduction on the collection burden and still provide an expansion of the stores covered as all the stores of a given chain will be covered instead of a sample.
Studies on the use of web data for this sector can also be found (Ref. 2, 3, 13). However, one should be careful about the representativity of online purchases in this sector which are still lower compared to physical stores.

title: Selection of categories
text:
Clothing and footwear
Experiences on the use of both scanner (Ref. 6) and web data (Ref. 3, 6, 13, 27) can be found for these sectors. These are also among the main candidates first explored for CPI compilers studying alternative data sources. Again, important reasons for this choice amounts to the representativity of the sector, significative reduction of collection burden and improvement of coverage and methodology.
As this market tends to be more segmented than groceries, acquisition of scanner data for the number of retailers required that can provide a high degree of market coverage here can be more cumbersome. Also, the representativity of online purchases for these sectors are usually higher than the case of groceries. For these reasons, even though use of scanner data is encouraged, web data might offer a quicker first approach for this field and many countries are developing studies on this latter source (Ref. 3, 6, 13, 27).
As mentioned above it should also be noted that data classification and preparation can be more demanding here than for other sectors (Ref. 14, 20).

title: Selection of categories
text:
Transportation services
This can include air fares (Ref. 23, 25), rail fares (Ref. 8), taxi (Ref. 8), ride sharing services (Ref. 15) etc.
Use of alternative data sources here can provide a significative reduction in the manual collection burden (Ref. 23, 25) and/or increase the product coverage. The compilation of more precise CPIs that cope with companies pricing strategies such as dynamic pricing via reservation seats practices (see appendices IV and VI in (Ref. 8) for examples regarding train tickets and taxi services, respectively, and (Ref. 15) for a example regarding ride sharing services) can also be a by product from the use of alternative data sources.
The concentration of the sector is also another key feature since a high degree of representativity can be obtained via a reduced number of data providers. In the case of the web, this could involve scraping a reduced number of sites.

title: Selection of categories
text:
Accommodation services
Studies with both scanner (Ref. 29) and web data (Ref. 3, 13, 16, 19) can be found for this sector. And again, its choice is appealing due to possible improvement of the coverage of companies and products considered, and a significant reduction on the collection burden.
In the absence of scanner data sets available, the segmentation of the sector can be overcome via the use of booking sites that aggregates information from a large number of companies providing such services (Ref. 16, 19).

title: Selection of categories
text:
Electronics and household appliances
Improvement of the items coverage and development of more robust treatments of quality adjustment issues are some of the benefits of the use of alternative data sources for for this sector. Some experiences in this sector can be found in (Ref. 2, 10, 13, 23, 25, 30).
Combination of scanner and web data can be beneficial here as the web offers a source richer in product attributes that can be combined with scanner data sets in order to refine classification and hedonic models (Ref. 10).

title: Selection of categories
text:
Used cars and fuels
These sectors usually play an important role in the CPI basket in terms of expenditures. For the case of used cars, alternative data sources have shown to be useful to provide rich data sets that allow a cheap and effective way to compile quality adjusted indicators (Ref. 13). Sample coverage and refinement of CPIs for fuels can also be improved via means of alternative data sources as recent experiences have shown (Ref. 17, 24).

title: Selection of categories
text:
Centrally collected items
For some sectors of the basket for which data is centrally collected or alternative data sources such as the web are already used for manual collection (even not in a centralized manner), resources for the adoption of alternative data sources might not be so intensive since special data treatments or methodological changes might not be necessary in these cases and integration of the data into production can be more straightforward in an initial phase.
As an example, chart items such as CDs and DVDs, tickets for concerts, museums, books, etc that are manually collected on websites might have the manual process replaced by an automated one via the use of targeted web scraping techniques (Ref. 3, 9, 18).

title: Decomposition
text: In addition to measuring the aggregate price or quantity change, it is important to decompose the change into its contributions by individual commodities or groupings. The calculation of such contributions is an important tool for compilers to validate and interpret price index results (1, 3). NSOs find greater need for index decomposition methods when processing transaction data sets that usually contain in the order of (tens of) thousands of products. Methods that are able to identify the main drivers behind overall price change are increasingly important when dealing with such large data sets.

title: Decomposition
section: Multiplicative decomposition of the GEKS index

title: Decomposition
section: Additive decomposition of the Geary-Khamis index
text:
Additive decomposition of the Geary-Khamis index
\[P_{GK}^{t_{1}, t_{2}}=\sum\limits_{i \in G_{t_{1}, t_{2}}} \frac {s_{i}^{t_{1}} \sigma_{i}^{t_{2}} p_{i}^{t_{2}}} {\sigma_{i}^{t_{1}} p_{i}^{t_{1}}} + \frac{1}{P_{GK}^{0, t_{1}}} \sum\limits_{i \in G_{t_{2}} / G_{t_{1}}} \frac {s_{i}^{t_{2}} p_{i}^{t_{2}}} {v_{i}}\]
where \(\sigma_{i}^{t}=\frac {p_{i}^{t} v_{i}} {\sum\limits_{j \in G_{t}} p_{j}^{t} v_{j}}\).

section: Multiplicative decomposition of the Time Product Dummy (TPD) index
text:
Multiplicative decomposition of the Time Product Dummy (TPD) index
\[P_{TPD}^{t_{1}, t_{2}}=\prod\limits_{i \in G_{t_{1}, t_{2}}} \frac {(p_{i}^{t_{2}})^{s_{i}^{ t_{2}}}}{(p_{i}^{t_{1}})^{s_{i}^{t_{1}}}} (\exp(\hat\delta+\hat\gamma_{i}))^{s_{i}^{t_{2}}-s_{i}^{t_{1}}}\]

title: Different approaches to accessing web scraped data
text:
Approaches for setting up a web scraping project





Initial considerations for setting a web scraping project
In the last decade, the interest in the use of the internet as a source for the development and improvement of price statistics by National Statistical Offices (NSOs) has grown substantially. This is conducted by a combination of the rise in the representativity of e-commerce practices by consumers, substantial increase in the number of online retailers, and the possibility of NSOs extracting large amount of valuable information from websites possibly at reduced costs.
Behind the information that a browser displays for each web page lies a html-like structure that contains the information seen by users. Web scraping consists of building automatic tools that walk through the html and extracts information of interest buried in the html nodes and process them into a convenient structured format.
Data collection from the internet and its subsequent processing for producing statistics can demand different levels of Information Technology (IT) skills. These range from basic understanding of how an html page is structured, to knowledge of cloud computing and machine learning techniques (more discussions can be found in section 3 of Ref. (1)). This will rely on the amount of information to be extracted from the websites and processing procedures to clean and classify the data for the purposes of the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
A comprehensive and detailed description of the steps necessary for setting up web scraping for official statistics is presented in a reference framework proposed in the Eurostat "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP". This framework relies on three main phases: the site analysis phase, the data analysis and design phase, and the production phase.
In summary,

The site analysis relies on the identification and evaluation of the characteristics and data available at retailer’s sites fit for use by CPI purposes, and selection of the appropriate web scraping mechanism to adopt.
Data analysis and design relate to building the tools to extract web data and analysis of the information retrieved.
The production phase relates to implementation and maintenance of the scrapers into CPI routines.

Though data acquisition occurs in different phases, Ref. (1) suggests that it is crucial to decide at the beginning of the project who will be responsible for the scrapers in the long term at the production phase, since this is very demanding in human and financial resources. NSOs have taken a variety of approaches, from working with more centralised IT resources, to set up and maintain the scrapers, to having the web scraping team sit within the Prices production area.


Overview on approaches to be adopted
NSOs interested in using web data can choose between (i) developing in-house expertise and structure necessary for data extraction and processing; or (ii) contracting third party services. The adoption of the best approach should consider the goals of the NSOs in respect to the use of web scraping for CPI, resources available and the complexity of all the steps involved to set up web scrapers for the compilation of CPIs.
According to Ref. (1), to develop and maintain scraping by coding internally is usually the ideal option since this process is more flexible and allows to better handle data according to CPI needs. This approach also tends to be cheaper in the long run and the web scraping expertise developed by the internal personnel can be applied to produce official statistics in other areas beyond the CPI (Ref. 3).
However, due the complexity and costs involved in the development and maintenance of the robots for data acquisition, some NSOs may find more suitable to adopt an alternative approach and contract third party services that provide the desired information (Ref. 4, 5).  In this approach usually the NSO specifies the product categories and retailers of interest and the frequency to which data should be collected and sent to the NSO. Important things to include in the contract refers to the possibility of refreshing the sample by the addition of new retailers and basket items across time and to require a good coverage of data.
By the adoption of third party services, the NSO can also specify that the data is provided after cleaning and already classified according to the CPI needs. This means that according to the services adopted, the demands for internal infrastructure an NSO would have to create for the development, maintenance and processing of web data can be reduced.
One of the challenges of using web scraped data are that a back series of data are less easily available (unlike scanner data). Some NSOs have contracted third party services in the short-term to ensure data can be collected for analysis and research purposes while the process of building up in-house web scraping capability takes place. Once the in-house team is set up, the third party contract can be terminated.  
In the training course 2 about data acquisition, in module 2.2 a general description is given of the main issues to face and the plan to implement to access data via web scraping techniques.

title: Selection of retailers for alternative data sources
text:
This page contains information on how to identify suitable retailers who can supply these alternative data sources



Overview
The scanner data technology for retail transactions is now used by most businesses in the retail sector. While all chain retailers have adopted its use for all their transactions, some local businesses do not have it due to its cost as well as the small scale of their operations. Among those who use this technology, not all of them have in place the infrastructure and the equipment required to produce scanner data files that record details on all cash register transactions. As a result, some of the retailers included in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) price survey outlet sample may not have any scanner data available. Similarly, the websites of large retailers generally provide useful and detailed information, including prices and descriptions for the online products while smaller ones may only provide limited information (contact information, available product lines, etc). In addition, statistical offices may not have a control on which retailers will eventually be providing access to their data through these two types of data collection mode. Depending on each country’s legislations, the retailers’ participation may or may not be made mandatory in regards to the Statistics Act. Thus, in practice it may not be possible to move to scanner data or to web scraped for all the retailers included in the price survey’s field collection sample.
Whenever both scanner and web scraped data from a given retailer are equally accessible to a CPI program, scanner data should be preferred. Indeed, both types of data sources provide detailed product descriptions, even if the levels of detail are not exactly the same. Scanner data contain information for only products sold in the data reference period. Web scraped data contain information for all products advertised on the retailer’s website at the time of the website scraping, some of which may not have been sold during the reference period. For the CPI calculation, prices based on actual transactions are preferable to list prices available in web scraped data. In addition, the sales revenue available in scanner data can be used in the estimation of expenditure shares for lower level product classes of the CPI classification, which helps improve the basket weights. A good practical strategy is to pursue the search for both options simultaneously as their outcome may be uncertain. This section discusses key considerations that may be useful in the selection of retailers for scanner data acquisition or for web scraping.


Scanner data
The selection of potential retailers for scanner data acquisition can start from the list of retailers included in the existing CPI price survey (field collection, Internet collection, etc). Then, representativeness and market structure considerations can be used to set priority. The retailers’ representativeness in their respective retail sector can be assessed using a variable such as annual sales revenue. The same data sources used for the selection of the field collection store sample, including the business register and retail commodity surveys, can be used. As much as possible, these data sources must allow the estimation of sales revenue by product category and by type of outlet (large retail stores, small retail stores, Internet sales, etc.). Large retailers with large market shares in certain sectors should get a higher priority compared to smaller retailers with low market shares. Then, a list of potential retailers for scanner data acquisition can be formed and data acquisition discussions initiated.


Web scraping
For the selection of retailers for web scraping, those retailers that cannot provide scanner data should be prioritized. In contrast, retailers with a highly regional pricing rule should be avoided for web scraping as many web access points might be needed for scraping in order to accurately reflect actual price movements occurring in all regions of the country. The Eurostat’s manual “Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP” (chapter 4) discusses useful guidance and criteria for the selection of products for web scraping. Methodological considerations, for example related to the evolution of online sales for different product categories and different retailers need to be used in the selection of target product categories for web scraping. For instance, products that do not experience neither significant nor frequent quality change and products that are gaining popularity among online purchases are good candidates for a web scraping project. It is worth considering key website characteristics in the selection of retailers for scraping. These include representativeness of consumers’ habits, volume of data available, technical characteristics of the website, stability of the website, metadata information, etc.
It may be useful to mention the case of third-party retailers that sell their products through the websites of larger and well-established retailers via online marketplaces. These can be helpful in providing a single source of data rather than having to scrape multiple different websites. However, there are arguments in favour to restricting web scraping activities to only products offered for sale by the selected retailers who own their websites. For example, if the products whose prices enter the CPI calculation need to be offered by retailers with some minimum market share, then further analyses may be required to decide which of the third-party sellers can be considered for the scraping of the selected websites. Inversely, if the number of third-party retailers is relatively small and they can be identified as popular among consumers, then their product offers should be considered for web scraping. The treatment of third-party retailers with respect to scraping from a selected website needs to be conducted on a case by case basis.
Overall, because small retailers may not have a fully operational website or may not generate scanner data files for their transactions, it is not clear at which point a CPI program could terminate its field collection price survey and solely rely on scanner data or web scraped data collections, which are more cost-efficient. There is a need to monitor the trend in e-commerce among consumers as well as the evolution of the use of technology in retail. For more information on how to aggregate the different data sources (field collection, plus scanner and web scraped data, please see the section "Aggregation".

title: Aggregation across time and outlets
text:
Data are usually disaggregated by various dimensions. This page contains information on how products can be aggregated across time and outlets.



Introduction
Scanner data and web scraped data are usually disaggregated by article code, by time period and by outlet or retailer. The different units (lines) included in these data sets must therefore be further combined into new units that are meaningful for Consumer Price Index (CPI) compilation purposes. The below contents cover aggregation over time and outlets. Aggregation over article code is covered in the section Identifying unique products.


Aggregation across time
A decision must be made on the temporal coverage (see Ref. 5). For example, if scanner data is disaggregated by week, then the weeks must be combined in order to obtain monthly data. An average monthly price is obtained by dividing the monthly sales by the monthly quantities. In general, it is appropriate to calculate a unit value over the entire reference period when an article is sold at different prices to different consumers at different times.
Ideally, scanner data should cover as much as possible of the reference period. In Ref. (4), it is shown that aggregation over only one week of the month can be upward biased compared to aggregation over the full month. In practice, this also depends on the moment that the data is supplied, the time that is left before results are published and the temporal coverage and level of disaggregation of the supplied data. Very often, the data used for index compilation only covers part of the reference month (for example the three first full weeks of the month). Aggregation across the month can also be impacted by seasonal events such as Easter, which could fall in the first couple of weeks of the month in one year and the last week in the next year.
Aggregation across time is also an issue with web scraped data. Very often, data are scraped more than once per month (e.g. daily). It is desirable to collect prices at a high frequency if they are known to fluctuate a lot within a month (see for example Ref. (2)). From a conceptual point of view, a unit value price would be the desired price target. However with web scraped data, expenditure weights are not available (see section Deriving proxy weights for web scraped data). Therefore, the calculation of a true average price is not possible. The practical solution is to compile either an unweighted arithmetic or a geometric average of the scraped prices in a given month. Annex 5.5 in the CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods (2020) illustrates such calculations when integrating web-scraped data with field price collection.


Aggregation across outlets
An average price for an article code could be calculated at the level of an outlet, which means that prices observed in different outlets are treated as different units (individual products). This is consistent with the approach used in field price collection. However, in some cases the data provider only supplies the data by chain such that calculating an average price at the outlet level is not possible. But also if the data are available at the outlet level, it may be reasonable to combine outlets of the same retail chain or brand and calculate average prices by retail chain. The prices in the outlets of the same retail chain may be relatively similar, at least within a specific region of a country. Also, aggregating across outlets and using average prices by retail chain decreases the size of the data sets used later for index compilation. The decision on aggregating across outlets or not  is an empirical matter that can be tested (see Ref. 6).
An empirical study on the impact of the temporal coverage, and the impact of aggregating or not over outlets can be found in (3). Another example of the impact of aggregating over outlet type can be found in Subsection 6.5 of Ref. (1)

title: Dumping filter
text:
Dumping filters aim at eliminating the downward pressure of clearance prices on the index.



Introduction
Dumping filters aim at eliminating the downward pressure of clearance prices on the index. This is an issue especially when the index calculation is conducted at the variety level such as, GTIN or any other unique product identifier. In this case, new products will affect the results of the majority of the relevant index formulas only poorly or even not at all in the period of appearance. However, especially in the case of relaunches, these products should have an immediate impact on the index, which then in theory should balance out the downward pressure of clearance prices. A dumping filter can therefore be of help in cases where products leaving the market and products entering the market cannot be linked appropriately.
It has to be remarked that the efficiency of the dumping filter depends on the typical pricing strategy of the products for which the index is calculated. For example, a dumping filter will not prevent a downward bias of those products for which usually a price skimming strategy is applied (e.g. clothing or electronic devices which are often introduced at high initial prices and then dropped over time). For this situation, it is absolutely essential to build homogeneous products groups first (and not calculate on the GTIN level) (see section Identifying unique products) in order to capture the price increasing effect of product relaunches and the entrance of new products in general.
In general though, applying a dumping filter before the index compilation can be helpful even when items have been grouped together in a first step.


Dumping filter for scanner data
Dumping filters are designed to detect and delete clearance sales which are characterised by both a sharp decrease in prices and sales quantities compared to the previous period. Scanner data provide the information required to apply the dumping filter. Similar to the outlier filter, a dumping filter should be set with caution. It has to be noted that if both an outlier filter and a dumping filter are used, the threshold value for the tolerated price decrease should be higher for the outlier filter than for the dumping filter. Otherwise, the dumping filter has no impact at all.
The section on current practice has some examples of values which countries have chosen for the dumping filter. Products identified by the dumping filter in a month should also be excluded in the following months if price and quantity remain similar.
There is ongoing research into whether some indices suffer more from downward pressure from clearance prices than others (see section Methods for when expenditure data are available). Several analyses have revealed that especially the GEKS index reacts sensitive to product sell-offs (e.g. Chessa et al. (2017), and van Loon and Roels (2018)). However, while van Loon and Roels (2018) found only short-term deviations and similar long-term price trends, Chessa et al. (2017) found a longer lasting bias. This divergence in findings can possibly be explained by the fact that van Loon and Roels (2018) analysed the effect of clearance prices on multilateral methods without chaining (full window) whereas Chessa et al. (2017) applied the fixed base monthly expanding method to calculate the index series. Overall, the current evidence indicates that the impact of dumping filtering has stronger impacts on the GEKS index than on other multilateral indices such as Geary-Khamis (GK) or Weighted Time Product Dummy (WTPD).


Dumping filter for web scraped data
In contrast to scanner data, web scraped data do not contain information on the quantities sold for an observed price. Some research has been conducted in the recent years how clearance prices can be also detected when using web scraped data. In general, when proxy weights are determined for web scraped data, a dumping filter for scanner data can be applied to web scraped data in a similar way. In the case of web scraped data, the proxy weights could replace the quantities in order to determine together with the price whether a product has reached the sell-off phase.

title: Preparation of data
text:
This sections summarises the general steps required to prepare these new data sources for use in price index compilation.

Section contents:

Product sampling for price index calculation — NSOs can either choose to use all available data from their new data source, or to use a sample of this data. 
Standardising the data — Data will need to be standardised before being used to calculate price indices.
Aggregation across time and outlets — Data are usually disaggregated by various dimensions. This page contains information on how products can be aggregated across time and outlets.
Identifying unique products — Data are usually disaggregated by various dimensions. This page contains information on how products can be defined from the given article codes.
Treatment of discounts and refunds — This page contains information on how discounts and refunds should be treated in the data.



Overview
The main objective of this step is to prepare these new data sources for use in price index compilation.

The format of the files or the variables included in the data sets may not be exactly the same for all data providers and new variables must be derived (see Standardising the data).
These data are usually disaggregated by article code, by time period and by outlet or retailer. The different units (lines) included in these data sets must therefore be further combined and new units must be constructed. Three dimensions must be considered when specifying the individual products: the time and outlet dimensions (see Aggregation across time and outlets), and the product dimension (see Identifying unique products).
Further adjustments may be needed to take into account for example, discounts or refunds (see Treatment of discounts and refunds).

These steps may be applied to all the data, or only to a subset of the data that has been previously selected to be in scope of the index calculations (see Product sampling for price index calculation).
The prices, weights and other information of these new units (called ‘individual products’) will then be the input of any further steps in the production process. Data preparation essentially corresponds to step ‘5.5. Derive new variables and units’ in the Generic Statistical Business Process Model.

title: Identifying unique products
text:
Data are usually disaggregated by various dimensions. This page contains information on how products can be defined from the given article codes.



Aggregating article codes
After possibly aggregating across time and outlets (see Aggregation across time and outlets), an average price by article code is available. In some cases, these article codes may be too detailed for price index calculation because of relaunches, or because article code churn is very high (see for example Ref. (4) for discussion on this by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
For example, let us suppose that a first article code has a price of 20 euros in period 1 and becomes unavailable from period 2 thereafter. A second article code of the same quality (a ‘relaunch’) has a price of 25 euros and is only available from period 2 onwards. A price index based on matching article codes would miss the price increase from 20 euros to 25 euros.
In some product categories, such as clothing and footwear, the article codes frequently appear and disappear making it difficult to match them across time and therefore price changes are not adequately measured.
There are different strategies to cope with new and disappearing article codes.

Linking - an outgoing article code is linked with an incoming article code so that their prices can be directly compared, possibly applying a quantity adjustment if package size has changed (see Ref. (1) for linking article codes for clothing and Ref. (4) for application of relaunch linking to groceries).
Grouping - different articles with similar characteristics are grouped together and the average prices for these groupings are followed over time. (see Ref. (3) for creating homogeneous products for sports equipment). There are trade-offs in creating groupings (homogenous products). If a grouping is too broad, this can lead to unit value bias (and high volatility) as the individual articles are not strictly comparable. On the other hand, defining the grouping too narrowly may lead to a lack of matching between outgoing and new or returning articles. The multivariate adaptive regression splines (MARS) method (see Ref. (2)) can be used as a tool for finding a compromise between these two objectives.
Quality adjustment and hedonics - the prices for the new and disappearing articles are imputed in the periods when they are not available with the help of a hedonic function. For additional detail, see the section on Quality change and hedonic estimation.

Table 1 below summarises some of the key advantages and disadvantages of using these strategies.
Table 1: Key advantages and disadvantages of using linking, grouping and hedonics strategies.








Approach
Advantages
Disadvantages


Linking
Captures relaunches
Identification of article codes to be linked can be difficult


Grouping
Increases matching over time
Unit value bias can occur


Hedonics
Explicitly adjusts for quality changes
Product characteristics are required



All three strategies require some kind of metadata on product characteristics. Such metadata can be obtained as follows:

Extract relevant information from the text strings (such as the brand).
Calculate distance measures between the text strings.
Use the metadata directly provided in the data (e.g. retailer classifications, structured product characteristics).
Use additional information on product characteristics provided by market research companies.
Scrape additional product characteristics on the web for the article codes included in scanner data.

title: Method 2: Pattern matching classification method
text: Pattern based classification involves mapping individual records to the taxonomy classes of interest according to patterns present in their descriptive attributes. For instance, patterns in the categories of the alternative data, patterns in the product name, or specific keywords in the product description - could all be used to classify a set of individual records. This approach is typically used when attribute based classification is not sufficiently detailed but it is not necessary to make the extra investment to develop or maintain more complex methods. This method can also be considered an attribute-based method (thus an alternative to method 1) where specific patterns in the unique products' characteristics need to be matched to classify, rather than a handful of structure attributes (such as product categories).

title: Data sharing agreements
text:
Data sharing agreements can help provide structure to data flows between a supplier and NSO



Data sharing agreements
Before setting up a data sharing agreement, it is important to assess any current legislation and/or the existence of any statistics acts. Some National Statistical Offices (NSOs) may acquire data for statistical purposes through the statistics act. 
Nevertheless, due to the importance of the production of Consumer Price Indices and other official statistics from scanner data, it is recommended that the NSO establish a formal agreement of the data sharing terms with the retailers. To put these points into formal grounds is key to guarantee that there will be no undue interruption in the data supply and the stability of the content received. Some NSOs may have dedicated legal teams who can advise on the legal environment and the specific wording of any data sharing agreements or contracts.   
The terms of the agreement shall contain information on:

the data content and reporting formats to be transferred
timetables for the transmissions
uses of the data by the NSO
confidentiality terms (including data storage and security)
delivery charge conditions
duration of the agreement
notification on delivery faults/changes in the data specification by the retailer etc
main contacts (in case of any issues with data supply for example)

The Annex in Eurostat's HICP - Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data provides some examples of draft contracts employed by different NSOs

title: Extension methods
text: Extension methods can be used in combination with multilateral methods to ensure revision-free index series. Multilateral methods can be used to calculate price indices for each period (month) in a time interval (window). A big advantage of these methods is that the resulting indices form a transitive series, which means that such series are free of chain drift (see Example of chain drift). Transitivity can be achieved on a fixed time window. However, index series have to be extended to the next month when statistical offices receive new data. In addition, the extension of current series must be carried out in such a way that price indices that were already published are not revised, which would be impractical and undesirable for many users of consumer price statistics. Extension methods can provide revision-free index series, although it is also important to note that by their nature any series produced using these methods are no longer free of chain drift. There are a number of different extension methods that can be applied.

title: Extension methods
text:
The movement splice method
According to the movement splice method (5, 8, 9), a price index for the new month is calculated by chaining the month-on-month index for the last month of the shifted window to the index of the previous month (the last month of the previous window). The movement splice method can be described by the following recursive formula:
\[P_{M S}^{0, t}=P_{M S}^{0, t-1} \cdot P_{t-T, t}^{t-1, t}\]
where \(P\) is any multilateral price index formula, the subscript specifies the time window and the superscript contains the period (\(t\)) for which the index is calculated and the linking period (\(t-1\)). Figure 1 below gives an illustration of the movement splice method for 13-month windows.
Figure 1: Example of how the movement splice method would work for a 13-month window.

title: Extension methods
text:
The window splice method
The window splice method proposed by Krsinich (2014) is used to calculate the price index for the new month by chaining the indices of the shifted window to the index of \(T\) months ago (i.e. to the index of 12 months ago for windows of 13 months). The index series that results from the current window is linked on the last recalculated index of \(T\) months ago. Price indices generated by window splice can be expressed by the following general formula:
\[P_{W S}^{0, t}=P_{W S}^{0, t-1} \cdot \frac{P_{t-T, t}^{t-T, t}}{P_{t-T-1, t-1}^{t-T, t-1}}\]
An illustration of the window splice method is presented in Figure 2 below. The process underlying this method is illustrated in a different way compared with the above figure for movement splice because of the greater complexity of window splice (due to the linking on recalculated indices).
Figure 2: Demonstration of the window splice method

title: Extension methods
text:
The half splice method
De Haan (2015) suggested that the link period \(t_0\) should be chosen to be in the middle of the first time window and the Australian Bureau of Statistics (2016) called this the half splice method for linking the results of two time windows. In other words, according to this method, the half splice happens at \(t_0 = (T+1)/2\) if \(T\) is an odd integer and at \(t_0=T/2\) otherwise. A recursive formula for the half splice method is as follows: 
\[P_{H S}^{0, t}=P_{H S}^{0, t-1} \cdot \frac{P_{t-T, t}^{t-t_{0}, t}}{P_{t-T-1, t-1}^{t-t_{0}, t-1}}\]
Also the half splice method links on the last recalculated index.

title: Extension methods
text:
The mean splice method
The mean splice method (Diewert and Fox, 2018) uses the geometric mean of all possible choices of splicing, i.e. all months \(\{1, 2, ..., T\}\) which are included in the current window and the previous one. The general formula for the mean splice method can be written as:
\[P_{G M S}^{0, t}=P_{G M S}^{0, t-1} \cdot \prod_{t_{0}=1}^{T}\left(\frac{P_{t-T, t}^{t-t_{0}, t}}{P_{t-T-1, t-1}^{t-t_{0}, t-1}}\right)^{\frac{1}{T}}\]

title: Extension methods
text:
Splicing methods on published indices
Chessa (2019) suggested that there is in fact a different approach to splicing, which is to use published indices to link index series of subsequent time windows (3). Successive window shifts generate a sequence of recalculated indices alongside the initial published index in the same period. Similarly to recalculated indices, the published indices may serve as the index on which a new index series can be linked.
Linking on recalculated indices leads to published index changes that do not correspond with any of the period on period indices of the transitive series on successive time windows. Linking on recalculated indices in past periods may therefore result in serious drift, as can be observed in series calculated with window splice (3, 12). In order to control drift in the published index series over certain time intervals (e.g. over 12-month periods), the aforementioned studies recommend to link on published indices. This ensures that period to period changes in the transitive series of the time windows will be preserved in the published series, allowing to control drift to a certain extent. However, also the location of the linking period matters when linking on published indices. For instance, movement splice is an example of a method that links on published indices (i.e. on the index of the previous month), but also this method may generate considerable drift as it is basically a period on period chaining method (3, 12).

The window splice method on published indices (WISP)
The recursive formula for the window splice method based on published indices may be written as follows:
\[P_{pub}^{0, t}=P_{pub}^{0, t-T} \cdot {P_{t-T, t}^{t-T, t}}\]
An illustration of the WISP method is presented in Figure 3 and Figure 4 below. The difference between the methods can be shown here in the placement of the X linking months, which in this diagram are all on the first line in comparison to the diagram above where the linking happens on the subsequent calculated indices. 
Figure 3: Demonstration of the window splice method on published indices

Figure 4: Alternative demonstration of the window splice method on published indices



The half splice method on published indices (HASP)
Chessa (2019) uses the HASP method with a 25-month window, but in general any time window length can be considered in this approach. The recursive formula for the half splice method based on published indices (HASP) can be written in a similar form as for WISP:
\[P_{pub}^{0, t}=P_{pub}^{0, t-t_{0}} \cdot {P_{t-T, t}^{t-t_{0}, t}}\]
An illustration of the method HASP with a 25-month rolling window is shown in Figure 5.
Figure 5: Demonstration of the HASP method on published indices with a 25-month rolling window.



The mean splice method on published indices (MESP)
The recursive formula for the mean splice method based on published indices may be written as follows (Eurostat, 2020):
\[P_{pub}^{0, t}=\prod_{t_{0}=1}^{T} (P_{pub}^{0, t-t_{0}} \cdot {P_{t-T, t}^{t-t_{0}, t}})^{\frac{1}{T}}\]

section: The Fixed Base Monthly Expanding Window (FBEW) method
text:
The Fixed Base Monthly Expanding Window (FBEW) method
The Fixed Base Monthly Expanding Window (FBEW) method (Chessa, 2016) uses a time window with a fixed base month every year (December of the previous year). The window is enlarged every month with one month in order to include information from a new month. The FBEW method starts with two months in January, extends to three months in February and reaches the full window length (13 months) in December of the present year. The method is illustrated in Figure 6 below.

The Fixed Base Moving Window (FBMW) method
Lamboray (2017) considered a modification of the FBEW method by substituting the expanding window by a fixed-length rolling window, which gives rise to the so-called Fixed Base Rolling Window (FBRW) method. Also the FBRW method used a fixed base month and fixed base indices derived from the rolling windows are linked to the published indices in the fixed base month (December of the previous year in practice). title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
This page contains a general introduction to each of the alternative data sources used to compile consumer price indices.
Statistical agencies have traditionally relied on surveys to collect the price and expenditure information used in the production of consumer price indices (CPIs). These survey-based approaches typically involve the selection of a sample of retailers and items, with prices collected at discrete points in time. While well-established, such approaches can be resource intensive and may be slow to reflect changes in consumption patterns, particularly in markets characterised by rapid product turnover.
Increasingly, National Statistical Offices (NSOs) are exploring the use of alternative data sources to complement or replace survey-based price collection. Alternative data sources differ from traditional surveys not simply in scale or timeliness, but in the way price information is generated, observed and accessed. From this perspective, alternative data sources can be usefully grouped according to whether prices are observed through realised transactions or through posted or administered prices. This distinction is important because it has direct implications for index compilation methods, weighting, and representativity, as discussed later in the Handbook.
At a high level, alternative data sources relevant for consumer price statistics can therefore be characterised as follows:
Most alternative data sources used in practice fall predominantly into one of these categories. Once data are acquired, many downstream processing steps, such as cleaning, classification, validation, and index compilation, are conceptually similar across sources. However, the availability (or absence) of quantity or expenditure information is often a key determinator in the choice of sampling, index number methods, and aggregation strategies.
The main types of alternative data sources that can be considered within this framework are described below.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
Scanner data
Transaction‑level data, or data aggregated over short time intervals (for example, daily or weekly) or to defined units such as retail outlets or product identifiers (for example, GTINs), obtained from retailers’ point‑of‑sale systems either directly or via third‑party providers. These data typically include product identifiers, prices, quantities and turnover and can cover large shares of household retail expenditure for some product groups.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
E‑invoice data
Electronic records generated for administrative or tax purposes that document transactions between sellers and buyers. Depending on national systems, e‑invoice data may provide item‑level price information with varying levels of product detail, quantities or values. Where sufficiently detailed and accessible for statistical use, these data may support CPI compilation and related weighting or validation activities.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
Administrative transaction data
Transaction‑based data collected for regulatory or operational purposes, such as utility billing systems, regulated tariffs linked to consumption, or other administrative systems that record realised payments or charges experienced by households. While such data may follow administrative concepts, they can provide consistent and timely transaction prices where alignment with CPI pricing concepts is satisfactory.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
Other electronic transaction records
Including, where appropriate, data derived from payment systems, loyalty‑scheme databases, digital platforms or other electronic transaction environments (including emerging data sources such as those from IoT enabled device data such as smart appliances, connected home devices and wearables), provided the data record actual purchases and meet CPI conceptual and quality requirements. The structure, coverage and accessibility of these data vary widely across countries and markets.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
Web-scraped data
 Web scraping refers to the automated collection of prices and product information from online retailers and service providers. These data typically capture list prices rather than transaction prices and generally do not include quantity or expenditure information.
Two broad approaches to web scraping are commonly distinguished:

Targeted web scraping, which collects prices for a predefined set of products or characteristics, often to replace or supplement existing survey collection; and
Bulk web scraping, which aims to extract large volumes of price data without prior selection of items, enabling broader coverage and exploratory analysis.

Web-scraped data can substantially increase the number of price observations collected and allow for more frequent price measurement, often at lower marginal cost than manual collection. NSOs considering web scraping are strongly encouraged to engage with data providers where possible, as agreements with retailers can reduce the risk of access being blocked and improve data stability over time.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)
In some cases, online prices and product attributes are accessed through APIs provided by platforms or data providers rather than through direct web scraping. From a statistical perspective, API-based data access can be preferable to web scraping, as APIs are generally more stable, less sensitive to changes in website structure, and less burdensome for data providers. However, in terms of content, API data are often similar to web-scraped data, typically providing list prices and product attributes but not quantities or expenditures.
The feasibility of API access depends heavily on institutional arrangements and agreements with data providers, and NSOs should assess both the technical and legal implications before adopting this approach.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
section: Online listings and advertised price data
text:
Online listings and advertised price data
Prices and product characteristics derived from listing platforms or classified advertisements, where goods or services are offered but transactions are completed outside the platform (for example, car sales or property rentals). These data may be collected automatically or provided directly by the platform. The listed price may differ from the final transaction price, and while indicators of market activity (such as listing duration or removal) may be available, they do not constitute direct measures of transactions.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
Administrative non‑transaction data
Prices or tariffs set or published by administrative bodies, regulators or public authorities, such as regulated fees, charges or official price schedules. These data record prices as set rather than prices paid in individual transactions and typically lack information on quantities or expenditures. Their suitability for CPI compilation depends on the extent to which the administered price aligns with the price faced by households.


Caution: Use of bulk non-transaction data in CPI compilation
Bulk non-transaction datasets often provide large volumes of price observations but typically lack reliable expenditure or quantity information. In the absence of such information, NSOs may be unable to apply weighted index methods or to construct a demonstrably representative product sample, which can introduce bias or instability in CPI estimates. In addition, the ongoing maintenance of web-scraping systems, changes to website structures, and legal or contractual constraints may affect data continuity and sustainability. NSOs should carefully assess these methodological, operational and legal considerations before adopting bulk non-transaction data for CPI production. Details of these constraints are provided in later sections of this handbook.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
Coverage and representativeness
Some alternative data sources, particularly transaction data, can provide detailed information on prices and quantities for a large share of consumer purchases within participating retailers. This can improve representativeness at detailed levels and support the use of explicit expenditure or quantity weighting.
Non-transaction data sources, such as web-scraped or API-based price data and online listings data, typically provide extensive coverage of listed products and prices but may not include information on how frequently those products are purchased, this may disproportionately represent products that are frequently listed or heavily marketed online, regardless of how often they are actually purchased.
When quantity or expenditure information is unavailable, price indices derived from these data implicitly treat all observed products as equally important. This can result in indices that over-represent niche, premium, or rarely purchased products and under-represent commonly purchased items. While proxy weighting approaches have been proposed, identifying robust and conceptually appropriate proxies remains challenging and is an active area of research.
Administrative data may offer comprehensive or near-census coverage for specific services or regulated prices, but may be limited in scope or frequency and may not align perfectly with CPI concepts without adjustment.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
Methodological implications
The characteristics of each data source influence the choice of data preparation methods, index number formulas, and aggregation strategies. The availability (or absence) of quantity or expenditure information is particularly important, as it affects whether weighted or unweighted methods can be used at the elementary aggregate level.
Alternative data sources may also exhibit features such as high product turnover, frequent product relaunches, or changes in item definitions over time. These features can complicate product identification, matching, and quality adjustment, and place additional demands on data processing and index compilation systems regardless of the data source used.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
Operational and sustainability considerations
Compared with traditional survey-based collection, alternative data sources introduce different operational dependencies. Transaction data such as scanner data and administrative transaction data often rely on sustained cooperation with data providers or other public authorities, while non-transaction data such as web-scraping collection depends on stable technical access and clearly defined collection arrangements.
The long-term availability and continuity of alternative data cannot always be guaranteed. Changes in business practices, data systems, legislation, or technical interfaces may affect data supply over time. NSOs should therefore consider sustainability, contingency planning, and the implications of data changes for index continuity and comparability. Web scraping relies on automated extraction from retailer websites, which may change without notice or restrict access over time. APIs and data-sharing agreements may provide greater stability but require sustained cooperation with data providers.
When inserting the use of alternative data sources into production it is important and highly recommended that NSOs consider a feasible fallback plan to mitigate possible data gaps in the acquisition process.

title: Overview of alternative data sources
text:
Legal, ethical, and governance issues
The use of alternative data sources raises legal and ethical considerations related to data access, confidentiality, intellectual property, and compliance with national and international regulations. These considerations apply across data sources, though the specific risks and mitigation strategies may differ.
Clear governance arrangements, transparency about data use, and, where appropriate, formal data-sharing agreements are essential to ensure that alternative data are used responsibly and sustainably in official statistics. Further discussion on deriving a formal agreement for scanner data can be found in the section Data sharing agreements and in the training material for the module on data acquisition.

title: Aggregation
text:
This page contains information on how alternative data sources can be aggregated with existing data sources



Overview of aggregation approaches
Integration of alternative data sources into the CPI production system can require changes in several aspects. The degree of such changes will rely on factors such as the characteristics of the data source to be implemented, the approach adopted (targeted or bulk use of the data), the peculiarities of the classification/aggregation system used to compile the CPIs at different levels and the availability of weight sources for the creation and refinement of the different CPI aggregates.
As an example, incorporation of a targeted approach that aims to replace the traditional collection of a sample of products with a similar sample taken from the alternative data source may require fewer or no changes. In contrast, more fundamental changes to the amount of data will usually need changes to the aggregation system as well, such as an update in the classification structure of the CPI.
In this regard, the integration of alternative data sources in the CPI aggregation structure may involve the creation of new retailer-specific elementary aggregates (EA). Elementary aggregates represent the lowest level – both in the product and the geography dimensions – where price indices are first calculated using prices for defined products. The section Aggregation across time and outlets defines how individual price quotes may need to be aggregated to calculate price quotes for defined products in view of the frequency of the CPI.
Once calculated, the Eurostat’s guidelines “Practical Guide on Multilateral Methods in the HICP” (chapter 6) and "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP" (p. 18) discusses the integration of these elementary aggregates into the CPI aggregation structure. It has been discussed in the Eurostat's "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP" that the creation of the aggregates for the type of data sources at different levels of the classification structure can impact the potential use of the data sets. There are different experiences reported in the literature on how the CPI classification structure can be modified in order to incorporate such new aggregates. A summary of some of these approaches are described below.
One option is to introduce a new aggregation level corresponding to the types of data sources (for example, scanner data, web scraped data, field collection, administrative data, or other) just below the lowest level of the CPI commodity classification structure for which CPI basket weights are available (typically 5-digits European COICOP classes). This new aggregation level is between the lowest European COICOP level and any national refinement classes used for product categories; see Figures 1a and 1b of the illustrative examples below. This option has been discussed in Statistics Belgium (Redefining what products are in the context of scanner data and web scraping, experiences from Belgium) and in the Eurostat's HICP - Practical Guide for Processing Supermarket Scanner Data and is referred to as "integration at ECOICOP5 level".
Another option is to introduce the data source types under any national refinement classes used for product categories below the 5-digits European COICOP classes; see Figure 1c of the illustrative diagram below for a case example that has been considered by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) (Introducing alternative data into consumer price statistics: aggregation and weights). This has been discussed in the Eurostat's Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP where it is referred to as "integration at a product category". Note that a geographical breakdown is also considered in Figure 1c before the aggregates for the sources are introduced. 
Whatever option is chosen, product categories can then be defined for each type of data source, and even for each retailer within a data source type. Figure 1c shows an example of these product categories, identified here as "consumption segments". This structure allows consumption segments to be adapted to the data source type or to the retailer, depending on their product range. A price index can be calculated for each retailer and for each type of data source for the lowest level classes of the COICOP classification. The indices for all types of data sources are then aggregated to obtain the price index for the lowest level commodity class; retailer or data source type weights may be needed at this stage. An important consideration here is the level at which the indices are published. If they are currently published below COICOP5, it may be necessary to ensure that the same consumption segments are used for all data sources and those consumption segments define the level at which indices are published (see Figure 1c below).
A simplified view summarizing the approaches presented above can be seen in Figure 1d. Figure 1d illustrates two different possibilities of creation of such aggregates at the ECOICOP 5 or at the products level. The former is more appropriate for the bulk use of alternative data sources as it allows a broader and more extensive use of the data sets as all the products within this category could be considered. For integration at the product level, only this kind of classification structure could be considered.
In addition, since the alternative data sources contain prices for a large number of individual products, potentially covering all geographical regions of the country, a classification level corresponding to regions can be introduced and used in the index calculation, so that the relative importance of regions are explicitly taken into account in the national index calculation. A by-product of this allows for the possibility of regional indices to be calculated as an additional output.
Next we discuss the weights required to aggregate indices within the same type of data source and across different types of data source.


Weights for aggregation within the same type of data source
For the aggregation of indices based on scanner data, total sales information available in scanner data for each individual product can be used to estimate weights for the product categories. First, retailer-specific elementary indices based on multilateral index methods can be calculated using data from each scanner data retailer. For example, some retailers may have different types of stores such as convenience to larger supermarkets (see Figure 1c). Elementary indices can be stratified by this outlet type (see Aggregation across time and outlets). Second, the retailer-specific elementary indices can then be aggregated to obtain elementary indices using a weighted arithmetic average. For a given scanner data retailer, total sales for products that belong to a product category and a geography (and outlet type, if chosen) in a given month can be used as weight for that retailer in that month in the aggregation of retailer-specific elementary indices into a scanner data elementary index for the considered product category.
For the aggregation of indices based on web scraped data, due to the lack of total sales data, we may only rely on market shares derived from retail trade surveys or administrative data to aggregate retailer-specific elementary indices into elementary indices based on web scraped data.


Weights for aggregation across different types of data source
Another key point is that weights are needed for the different types of data sources to aggregate data source type-specific elementary indices into higher level price indices (see Figures 1a, 1b and 1c). For example, if field collection data and scanner data are to be aggregated for a consumption segment, we need to estimate the market shares of the retailers covered by the scanner data index as well as the market shares of all retailers represented by the field collection data. If the field collection is based on a sample of retailers, the market share of the entire subpopulation of which the sample is representative needs to be estimated.
Typically, NSOs have to aggregate price indices based on scanner data, web scraped data and field collected data for a given product category. They need to identify relevant data sources for the estimation of data sources' market shares for each product category. Among the possible data sources for the market share estimation, retail trade surveys may be useful. This type of survey has the potential to provide regional data. The commodity categories for which sales data are estimated from retail surveys may be higher than the published CPI goods and services categories. In this case, other data sources such as scanner data or third-party estimates may be used to redistribute sales estimates to lower level product categories. The business register may also provide some general information on retailers' operations, but generally it gives the total revenue for each retailer operating in the country. There may be no geographic or commodity breakdown of the revenue data, which does not make the business register a suitable data source for this weighting issue. In some cases, useful administrative data may be available from a third-party data provider. In all cases, NSOs need to assess the data quality, the coverage as well as the relevance of the various data sources available to ensure good quality weight estimates.

text:
Chain drift occurs when an index does not return to unity when prices in the current period return to their levels in the base period. The problem is mostly caused by sales (that is, highly discounted prices) of products. An example will illustrate the problem.
This example is taken from the upcoming publication: Consumer Price Index Theory chapter 6, Ref. (1).

title: Dealing with unexpected data gaps
text:
This page contains information on how to deal with unexpected gaps in the supply of new data sources



How do unexpected data gaps occur
Unexpected data gaps can occur for several reasons. First, the data provider (retailer) might change the structure of its data such that the data processing in the statistical offices no longer works. Second, scanner data deliveries may fail due to technical problems on either the transmitting or receiving side. Third, the worst case scenario arises when the data provider decides to stop its data deliveries.
In the case of web scraping, similar problems can happen. Changes to a retailer's website, such as revisions to the site's layout or structure, may require changes to established web scraping code or even completely new development. Moreover, technical problems in the statistical offices might interrupt the data scraping. Finally, it might also happen that retailers block the web scraping efforts of the statistical offices.


How can unexpected data gaps harm the production process
In the best case, while there may be a delay in the data, in certain scenarios missing data can be delivered retroactively such that they can still be used for the calculation of the final results with no noticeable impact. Generally, the longer the reporting period, the better are the chances that missing data will arrive in time. Therefore, a quarterly CPI has some advantages here over a monthly published CPI.
In case that the missing data do not arrive in time, i.e. before the deadline of the CPI production, there still might be sufficient data available in order to maintain the regular CPI production. For example, a monthly CPI calculation might be based on scanner data of the first two weeks of the month. If some scanner data are missing only for the second but not the first week, it is still possible to produce index results even though they will be probably of poorer quality.
In cases where data is not available from only one or a few specific retailers, it is reasonable to conduct some imputation based on the data or rather index results of the remaining retailers. When data are not available for the majority or even all retailers, more complex solutions have to be applied which require some preparation in advance (see next section). If historic data are required to calculate indices as in the case of multilateral methods, missing data should be requested by the statistical offices even if the deadline for the current reporting period (to which the missing data belongs) has already expired.
In contrast to scanner data, web scraping data are definitively lost when this kind of automated survey fails at a certain point of time. However, since web scraping can also be conducted at another point of time, the harm that arises depends on how fast problems are detected and whether there is enough time buffer to solve them. This is why it is very important to monitor the ongoing quality of web scraped data (see section Monitoring, validation and plausibility checks for web scraped data).


How to mitigate the harm of unexpected data gaps
The best way to mitigate the harm of unexpected data gaps is to mitigate the risk that unexpected data gaps arise at all. For scanner or admin data, it is highly recommended to either enter into data sharing agreements with the suppliers (either voluntary or contractual) and/or to implement a legal mandate requiring suppliers to provide transaction data to statistical agencies. Independent from the legal situation, a data sharing agreement is always helpful to enable a partner-like connection between the supplier and the statistical office. Typically, data sharing agreements specify that the statistical office will be informed in advance whenever the structure of the data will be changed by the supplier. This will help the statistical office to avoid facing unexpected data gaps.
For web scraped data, retailers scraped by the statistical offices should be informed in a timely manner. This will help to avoid the retailer blocking the statistical office’s web scraping activities. A data sharing agreement could further arrange for the statistical office to be informed of upcoming website redesigns. In any case, the time slots for web scraping should be set appropriately, meaning that there is enough time buffer to try the price collection another time (either manually or automated by web scraping) if the regular web scraping fails.
Monitoring the data arrival is another important measure to be aware of unexpected data gaps as early as possible increasing the chance to solve technical problems timely. Since the time slot to fix technical problems might be very short (especially for monthly published indices), it is recommend to maintain regularly a contact list containing all relevant contacts, both internal and external. This will speed up the process of solving technical problems whenever they occur. For web scraping, it is even more important to ensure the data quality at the time of scraping in case of errors identified (see section Monitoring, validation and plausibility checks for web scraped data).
If, nevertheless, no data are available at all that can be used for the CPI production of the current reporting period, a backup plan is required to impute the missing prices or rather indices. If scanner data from only a few retailers are missing, the index changes of the remaining retailers could be used for imputation of missing elementary aggregate indices. The way of imputation may depend on the implemented aggregation strategy and the market coverage achieved by the different data sources. In case that this way of imputation is not reasonable or possible, an alternative plan (prepared in advance) should be activated. Three possible solutions are presented here:

Price collectors: This option can be implemented relatively easily when price collectors still visit some of the stores of the retailer whose scanner data are missing. Then, a sample of products sold during month m-1 (last month for which scanner data are available) could be drawn from the stores that are usually visited by the price collectors (for the residual price collection). Price collectors record prices which are used to produce indices whose change is then used for imputation. Given that price collectors no longer visit the stores of the retailer whose scanner data are missing, price collectors might also be acquired by third party companies at short notice. However, this requires that a contract between the statistical office and the third party company has been concluded in advance. Alternatively to the collection of shelf-prices, "manual" online price collections can also be conducted to maintain the index production.
Web scraped indices: Parallel to processing scanner data, web scraped indices could be established. In the scenario that the scanner data are not available, the changes of the web scraped indices could be used for imputation purposes.
Indices/Data provided by third party companies: Statistical offices could try to engage third party companies such as market research companies to calculate the required price indices or to provide the missing data when the statistical office faces an unexpected data gap. It has to be determined, established and contracted in advance what the third party company shall provide in such an emergency situation.

All three proposals are for imputation purposes and should not be considered as a long term solutions in the scenario where scanner data deliveries are ceased permanently. Fortunately, NSOs that are already working with scanner data have not yet experienced very severe data gaps. This is mainly due to a good relationship to the retailers which should always be the aim of a statistical office.

title: Monitoring, validation and plausibility checks for web scraped data
text:
Recommended checks to carry out on incoming flows of web scraping data



Monitoring, validation and plausibility checks for web scraped data
Contrary to scanner data where the data sets are stored by the retailers and backup files are available, web collection does not allow recovery of past data. Hence, caution should be taken to evaluate if the collection is being performed appropriately to minimize and avoid mistakes and data losses.
Automatic monitoring of data collection is advisable especially when performing bulk web scraping where timely identification of problems is more challenging. It is useful to build a monitoring dashboard with automatic checks for control and validation of the extracted data. Useful checks noted within Eurostat's HICP - "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP" include the following

check if data size agrees with previous collections
check if the list of datasets and attributes are as expected
check for duplicate records
check the total number of items and levels of product churn each month
check number of items found which have values equal to zero
checks for suspicious values and outliers, and
checks for the number of items that were not classified.

Whenever possible, automatic solution to problems identified is advisable and a report with the mistakes found should be generated allowing further analysis of the main problems by experts (Ref. (2)). Early identification allows faster actions and reduces the impact of the problems for Consumer Price Index (CPI) compilation.
Section 5 of Eurostat's HICP - "Practical guidelines on web scraping for the HICP" and section 4.3 of Ref. (1) provide more details and experiences on the subject.
