title: Multilateral price index methods
text: This section presents the basic, commonly known formulas of multilateral price indices.Like the Bilateral price index methods section, it does not include a broader discussion of the legitimacy of using individual indices. For more information on choosing an index method, see the Choosing an index method section.

title: Multilateral price index methods
text:
The GEKS-Fisher method
Typically, the GEKS method uses the superlative Fisher price index (and is commonly referred to as just the GEKS) resulting in the following formula:
\[P_{G E K S}^{0, t}=\prod_{\tau=0}^{T}\left(\frac{P_{F}^{\tau, t}}{P_{F}^{\tau, 0}}\right)^{\frac{1}{T+1}}\]

title: Multilateral price index methods
section: The GEKS-Törnqvist method (also known as CCDI)
text:
The GEKS-Törnqvist method (also known as CCDI)
The GEKS idea was extended with the Törnqvist index as a base in the context of making quantity comparisons across production units (1), and subsequently as a method to make price comparisons across production units (16). Consequently, the the multilateral price comparison method involving the GEKS method based on the Törnqvist is now sometimes referred to as the Caves-Christensen-Diewert-Inklaar (or CCDI) (10). The corresponding price index can be expressed as follows:
\[P_{C C D I}^{0, t}=\prod_{\tau=0}^{T}\left(\frac{P_{T}^{\tau, t}}{P_{T}^{\tau, 0}}\right)^{\frac{1}{T+1}}\]
To note, the CCDI method is equivalent to the GEKS method with Törnqvist indices as bilateral indices. If prices are imputed when they are unavailable, for instance, because products were not sold in certain periods, then the CCDI method is referred to as "imputed CCDI". Examples and applications of the imputed CCDI method are described by de Haan and Daalmans (2019).

title: Resource implications and organisational readiness
text:
The adoption of alternative data sources typically requires a different mix of resources and capabilities compared with traditional survey-based price collection.
While long-term efficiency gains are often cited as a motivation, most NSOs experience an initial increase in resource demands during research and implementation phases.


Staffing and skills
Alternative data sources often require new technical and methodological skills, particularly in areas such as data engineering, programming, database management, and advanced index number methods. NSOs may need to assess whether these skills are available internally, whether targeted training is required, or whether external expertise should be engaged during early phases.
At the same time, institutional knowledge of CPI concepts and production processes remains essential. Successful implementation often depends on effective collaboration between methodologists, subject-matter experts, IT specialists, and dissemination teams, rather than on technical expertise alone.


Systems and infrastructure
Working with large or high-frequency datasets may require new or adapted IT infrastructure. This can include secure data transfer mechanisms, storage solutions capable of handling large volumes of data, and processing environments that support automated workflows.
NSOs should consider whether existing systems can be extended incrementally or whether new platforms are needed, particularly where multiple alternative data sources are being integrated simultaneously. Decisions on system design should also take account of maintainability and long-term support. More information can be found in the section CPI production system requirements.


Time and implementation effort
Implementing alternative data sources is rarely a rapid process. Research, testing, validation, and parallel running with existing systems can take considerable time, particularly where methods or systems are unfamiliar. NSOs should allow sufficient time for experimentation and learning, and avoid underestimating the effort required to move from pilot studies to live production.
Phased implementation, starting with selected product groups or data sources, can help manage this transition and spread resource demands over time.


Partnerships and external dependencies
Many alternative data sources rely on cooperation with external data providers, aggregators, or other public authorities. Maintaining these relationships may require ongoing engagement, negotiation, and coordination, particularly where data access arrangements evolve over time.
NSOs should consider how responsibilities for managing external relationships are allocated internally and how continuity is ensured if key contacts or agreements change.

title: Designing the classification step: operational considerations
text: This section provides context about where and how the classification step fits into the rest of the pipeline processing alternative data to create elementary price indices, as well as some important considerations and options when setting up the classification process. This article can also be seen as a companion to the pre-conditions to classification section, helping the NSO design the operational process for the individual or blended method that will be chosen.

title: Designing the classification step: operational considerations
section: Filtering out aspects of a retailer file not necessary
text:
Filtering out aspects of a retailer file not necessary
While NSOs approach alternative data with goals of using all the data for price indices, the alternative data received may not fully align with the set of elementary aggregates that will be calculated with this dataset. Specifically:

There may be aspects of the alternative dataset provided that may not fall into the scope of the CPI or be desirable for production. This could include cases such as the volume of data for the specific strata is just too small to be meaningful and representative. Alternatively, there may be a case where specific aspects of the provided dataset are not of interest or needed for the CPI. (2) 
Where the NSO is following a gradual adoption strategy of this dataset for production, and hence the proportion of the retailer dataset used for production expands over time.

In these cases, it may be useful to select an approach where the data is cleanly stratified to allow the NSO to focus on the proportion of interest. In this case, the NSO has two approaches that can be adopted (see Figure 1 for visual):

Option 1: The NSO may set up a two pronged ‘classification’ approach, whereby the ‘out-of-scope’ data within each file is first filtered out, and only the ‘in-scope’ data is classified further to the categoires of interest. This approach may be preferred if the filtering can be done in a very robust and stable way, such as with Method 1 or Method 2, and in essence acts as a separate simpler classifier that precedes the main classifier that actually supports production needs.
Option 2: the NSO may aim to classify all the data in the dataset using one classifier, aiming instead to only use categories that are needed afterwards. This approach may be preferred either if the data does not allow a clean way to filter out data points (say method 1 or 2 cannot be reliably used), or if the in-scope and out-of-scope categories will shift over time (such as due to the NSO following a gradual implementation strategy for the retailer dataset). The latter may be the chosen approach simply because it is simpler to maintain and update one classifier rather than two.

Diagram 1: Approaches to implementing classification in production

More specific consideration of both options can be seen here:








Option
Pros
Cons


Option 1: use a filter stage preceding the main classification stage

This approach would result in a stable and cleaner set of data that may need to be classified by the actual production classifier, which could make the task of creating the production classifier slightly simpler.
This may also target NSO resources validating classification output to only what is in-scope (as the filtered-out products may be skipped), which would require fewer validation resources.


This approach means that the NSO needs to maintain both filtering and classification sub-steps together and be mindful of the decline of performance of the actual classifier if the filtering sub-step were to fail. Specifically, the classifier may fail or perform poorly as it may suddenly not see the same data distribution as it is used to.
Furthermore, were the filter sub-step to start failing gradually, the NSO may not immediately notice why misclassifications occur and may need to spend more time disentangling performance issues to isolate the cause of the issue.



Option 2: Using one classification sub-step instead

This approach may simplify classification as there is only one classifier that is built for the production process.
It may also be more naturally aligned to using the whole dataset (or most of the dataset) for multiple purposes, which could be aligned to the gradual adoption strategy and would simplify the effort for the NSO. For example, the NSO begins by classifying all the data and focuses on using only a proportion of the data for the production CPI. The other data is also validated on a recurrent basis and could be used for research (and parallel runs) for additional price indices that the NSO could adopt when it is ready (3).
Finally, classifying all the data and at a low granularity may be valuable if one retailer dataset is used for multiple statistical outputs (forthcoming). In this case, after the classification step, the NSO may utilize a concordance to map the classified taxonomy codes to a higher granularity taxonomy that is used for the specific price statistic (4).


Depending on how this approach is implemented, this may require more resources for the NSO to validate all the records rather than just the in-scope ones of interest at the time.

For instance, if the classifier predicts each class and an advanced classification method is used (methods 3 or 4 for instance), then validation of a proportion of the data is recommended (6). In this case, the NSO may need to validate a proportion of all the data to support evaluation and updating of the classifiers.
Note, this may be mitigated if the NSO chooses to classify to ‘junk’ or ‘catch-all’ categories – as it may not be necessary to validate all the records in these categories (6). Furthermore, this approach may lead to a more complex classifier, as it would need to deal with a more complex dataset and classify to many more categories.





This separation into two conceptual options may be more a theoretical excersise and a mix may be used in practice. For instance, an NSO begins with with the first approach, however find that it is challenging to maintain or that option 1 still does not cleanly 'filter out' all records that are not of interest. In this case, a mix of two options may be maintained for a short time before the NSO concludes that option 2 is operationally simpler to maintain.
crumbs: Designing the classification step: operational considerations

title: Designing the classification step: operational considerations
text:
The classifier
The classifier sub-step, depending on the method used, applies one of the methods, or blend of them, to classify all new unique products to the taxonomy codes used in production. All products may be used as an input for a price index, or the output of this classification may be a  frame for which sampling is done. In either case, as classification often needs to be maintained (see subsequent sub-step), NSOs often aim to develop the classifier in a modular way so as to update it without impacting the later systems. In this sense, the classifier is a ‘product’ that can be evaluated in production using applicable metrics on all newly classified records (i.e. out-of-sample performance), and updated (or retrained if this uses advanced methods such as Method 4).
crumbs: Designing the classification step: operational considerations

title: Designing the classification step: operational considerations
text:
Validation follows classification
Following the classification method chosen or a blend, NSOs are strongly recommended to perform a validation step (5,7,8). While most commonly utilized with advanced classification methods (methods 3 and 4), this step can be used for all classification methods, such as Method 2 (see the feedback arrow in Diagram 1). In this step, it may be advisable to validate all, or a relevant proportion of the unique records (9). This step is critical to support robust evaluation of the classifier on an out-of-sample dataset, as well as to create additional validated data that can be used to retrain advanced classification models. Indeed, this step is critical within the Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) literature as model retraining is necessary to maintain performance over time (6,9).

text: Manual classification involves each unique product being manually assigned a classification class. title: Method 0: Manual labelling or validation of predicted labels
text:
The labelling environment
To perform labelling, National Statistical Offices will need to make a judgement on how much time to put into the design and development of their labelling environment based on the extent to which it will be used. Alongside labelling, the environment will need to account for work allocation, quality assurance and collation of completed labelling work.
For smaller classification tasks, work could be performed within spreadsheets. This may not be ideal for prolonged use due to several quality concerns. Allocation and collation of work is likely to be manual and time-consuming. Spreadsheets will not display information in a user-friendly way by default which may mean a lot of time spent by labellers interacting with the spreadsheet to obtain the information they need. Labellers may need to manually type classes and this can cause grammatical, spelling, or case-sensitive errors which will need to be corrected as part of a quality assurance process. If labelling is done long-term, these quality issues and inefficiencies may stack up and cause costly relabelling exercises.
Alternatively, NSOs may invest into designing applications for labelling. An example of a web browser-based application developed within the Office for National Statistics (UK) is shown to the right. This bespoke approach has been designed to meet the NSOs labelling requirements:

Information is displayed for labellers in a user-friendly way.
Labellers select classes rather than manually typing, improving efficiency and reducing errors.
Automatic saving avoids loss of progress through program crashes.
Labellers can use a navigation/search menu to search through available classes.
Offers labellers a help menu for training and advice.
When using machine-assisted manual classification, the program displays and allows selection of machine recommendations
The process of assigning products and collating and uploading labels is performed automatically by the back-end part of the system.

title: Deriving proxy weights for web scraped data
text:
Web scraped data does not contain expenditure information. In some cases, proxy expenditure weights can be derived.



Introduction
In contrast to scanner data, web scraped data are not transaction data which means that they do not contain information on the quantities sold. Especially in the dynamic universe of online trading, it would be important to know if a price that has been observed is really relevant in terms of the number of transactions that have been taken place at this price. Research has shown this is rarely the case and while consumers purchase a variety of products, they exhibit strong preference for only a small subsection of the available products and brands within any item. Antoniades et al. (2019) on distribution as expenditure found that typically sales distribution is so skewed, that based on their calculations total sales of the top 2% of grocery products per item accounted for as much as the total sales of the bottom 96%. 
The lack of information on the quantities sold entails two issues that have to be dealt with when web scraped data are used to compute price indices, aggregation of prices across time and how proxy expenditure weights can be calculated and used in the calculation of price indices.


Aggregation of prices over time
First, a decision has to be made on how different prices for the same item are aggregated over time (for example for a month or a quarter). Usually, the prices observed at different times of the month (or quarter) are aggregated to an unweighted (equally) weighted average price, which reflects the assumption that the buying behaviour with respect to a specific item is more or less independent of the price. Even though this is likely to be a too strong assumption, past research projects such as Chessa & Griffioen (2019) did not find severe differences between unit values based on scanner data and the respective average prices based on web scraped data. As expected, unit values were often found to be lower or equal compared to the average web scraped prices. Different factors may offer an explanation for this observation, such as different forms of discount that may enter transaction prices which cannot be scraped (e.g. discounts for customer card holders) and also increases in the numbers of items sold during discount periods. It is important to keep in mind that there seem to be only a few examples of such comparative studies (perhaps due to the difficult in sourcing different data for the same retailer), and that the cited study applies to a web-only shop. Further research could be conducted to verify whether the unweighted average price is appropriate also for products and/or retailers with both physical outlets and web shops, and for products/retailers with a very dynamic pricing strategy. In this context, it is worth mentioning that for the purpose of calculating the Consumer Price Index (CPI), the prices which are used for the index calculation must not necessarily reflect the true price level but the true price development. This means that the bias of the average price level could be greater than the bias of the change in the average price level.


Calculation of proxy weights
Second, the lack of information on quantities sold is an issue when it comes to price index calculations. ONS (2020) found that unweighted indices may suffer from a notable bias compared to their weighted counterparts. In order to mitigate this bias, some research has been conducted on deriving proxy weights for web scraped data. Two different approaches have arisen which are introduced in the following paragraphs.
Chessa & Griffioen (2019) used the number of times an item was scraped as a proxy for the quantities sold for this item. In their study, they compared web scraped data and scanner data from the same retailer. The website of the retailer was fully scraped which means that an item could have been scraped on different "routes", i.e. when navigating from the main menu through the various submenus. For example, an item from the retailer analysed by Chessa & Griffioen (2019) could be found in the sub menu "mens’ clothing" but also in the sub menu "sales". Chessa & Griffioen (2019) observed in their data a remarkable correlation between the number of prices scraped with this technique and the quantities sold based on the scanner data of the same retailer. The price indices calculated with these proxy weights were much closer to the benchmark prices indices based on scanner data than the unweighted price indices. Even though the results were promising, the authors recommended to verify whether these findings apply also to other retailers.
A different approach was conducted by Touzani & van Buskirk (2015) and ONS (2020). They used the popularity rankings defined by the order (or rather position) of where products are published on the website of a retailer. Thereby, they assumed that the cumulative distribution of the rank order was equal to the cumulative distribution of the number of sales. Given a log normal distribution, a truncated log normal distribution and a Pareto distribution, ONS (2020) determined the required distribution parameters by a maximum likelihood estimation based on summary statistics which were available in a scanner data set of the same retailer. In a next step, the sales quantities were derived from the equation of the cumulative distribution function of the rank order on the website and the suggested cumulative distribution function of the quantities sold. These approximated sales quantities were then used in a final step to calculate price indices. The results indicated that especially the truncated log, normal distribution could reduce the bias as measured with respect to the scanner data indices in comparison to the unweighted index series. It is important to note that this kind of approach requires the retailers to provide summary statistics, which means that some kind of cooperation with a retailer is needed and it relies on the (strong) assumption that the order in which products appear on retailers’ websites is reflective of quantities sold. For some retailers, it is possible to sort by "popularity" which could infer this relationship. However, for some retailers this option is not possible and they either don't allow sorting, or use the vaguer term "relevance". In some cases, retailers may influence the order to ensure that those products with larger profit margins sit at the top of the list rather than those with high quantities sold. This means that this approach should be used only when it can be reasonably assumed that the position of the product on the website indeed reflects the order of quantities sold because otherwise, there is a danger that the bias gets even worse compared to an unweighted index.
Possible alternatives for deriving proxy weights also include (research still ongoing): scraping the number of reviews for each product as a proxy for expenditure, testing the market share approach outlined in Antoniades et al. (2019), and using the theory of "price banding". The principle around the price band approach is a simplistic one, that producers know the optimum price they can sell their product to maximise sales. We can deduce that the more products around a certain price point will contain the highest selling products of the item, because more producers recognise the price as the optimum selling price. In practice, this means that each item is split into multiple price bands and each product can then be assigned to a band based on its price. The bands are then ranked from most products to least, with the products in the most populated price band receiving more weight than the products in the less populated price bands. As these research projects complete, we will link to the published results on this page.


Alternative approaches
Apart from these approaches to calculate proxy weights, one could also think about other ways to reduce the bias of unweighted indices for web scraped data. One option could be to use a bestseller approach where a certain number of the most popular items would be selected for the price collection via web scraping. The required bestseller lists could be searched on product specific websites or magazines. This approach would exclude items rarely sold from the price collection, which again might increase the representativity of the index results. Another approach that could be investigated is the use of weights from external sources. Even when these weights might not be available on the item level, they could help to distinguish more relevant from less relevant product groups (in terms of expenditure shares) such that an implicit or explicit weighting could be applied at the level of product groups. For example, weight information may be available at the brand level for technology products that could then be used to approximate the weight for individual items.
This is an area of ongoing research and it is clear that more work is necessary to shed more light on the issue of deriving proxy weights for web scraped data.





References
(1) Antoniades, A., Feenstra, R.C., and Xu, M. (2019) Using the Retail Distribution to Impute Expenditure Shares https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2020/preliminary/paper/r3FSyhnB
(2) Chessa, A. and Griffioen, R. (2019) Comparing Price Indices of Clothing and Footwear for Scanner Data and Web Scraped Data. https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques/4203548?sommaire=4203556
(3) ONS (2020) Using statistical distributions to estimate weights for web-scraped price quotes in consumer price statistics https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/articles/usingstatisticaldistributionstoestimateweightsforwebscrapedpricequotesinconsumerpricestatistics/2020-09-01
(4) Touzani, S. & van Buskirk, R. (2015) Estimating Sales and Sales Market Share from Sales Rank Data for Consumer Appliances https://www.researchgate.net/publication/272830600_Estimating_Sales_and_Sales_Market_Share_from_Sales_Rank_Data_for_Consumer_Appliances

title: Data filtering and missing prices
text:
This section covers some common methods used to filter the data before it is used to calculate indices, as well as a summary of how missing prices should be treated.

Section contents:

Outlier filter — Outlier filters aim at excluding or correcting extreme price increases or price decreases, typically compared to the previous period, from the price index calculation
Dumping filter — Dumping filters aim at eliminating the downward pressure of clearance prices on the index.
Low sales filter — The low sales filter ensures that products with small expenditure shares do not unduly influence the index results.
Current practice of data filtering — This page contains a summary of how NSOs currently approach data filtering.
Treatment of missing prices — This page contains information on how to treat missing prices through product-level imputation methods.



Overview
The scale of these new data sources mean that new methods are required to automatically identify and remove erroneous observations, as the traditional manual scrutiny of flagged observations is not feasible. Traditional data filtering often focuses on removing observations that are thought to be the result of erroneous data collection or that have a large impact due to small sample sizes.
New data sources tend to be much larger than conventionally collected surveys and reduce standard error due to sample size. Given the nature of scanner data, it is also less prone to ad hoc data collection errors compared with web scraped data, although some errors still can exist. Filters for non-survey data may be useful for addressing these issues with the dataset (for example, decimal point issues) and ensuring the reliability of the index results.
When processing new data sources for consumer price indices, three types of data filters that are applied directly to the product level data have been established as best practice:

outlier filter
dumping filter
low sales filter

The outlier filter focuses only on extreme price increases or decreases whereas the dumping filter and low sales filter additionally take the development of sales quantities into account. The settings of these data filters depend not only on the index formula that will be used but also on the type of data these filters are applied to. Typically, these data filters are used directly before the index calculation. Thereby, the order of filtering may have an impact on the index results. Usually, the outlier filter is applied first and then the dumping or low sales filter. For more detail on how these filters relate to the choice of index method and data source, please see the specific pages linked above. 
For products identified as outliers it may be appropriate to consider imputation. For those products filtered out by the dumping or low sales filter, these should not be imputed. 
Since web scraping data comprise of information only on prices but not sales quantities, the dumping filter and low sales filter cannot be applied in the typical manner. However, there is currently ongoing research into methods to estimate the expenditure shares of web scraped articles.
Over time, it is important to monitor whether the applied data filters are set appropriately. For example, it should be checked periodically if the share of filtered products is too high or if some certain product groups are filtered out systematically and unjustifiably. In this case, the data filters should be adjusted or there should be an option implemented into the production system, which allows the data filter to be overruled.
Data filtering is an area of active research and it is likely that different data sources and/or suppliers require different approaches to data filtering based on their own existing quality controls and circumstances. As such, National Statistical Offices (NSOs) are recommended to conduct their own empirical research using these approaches before deciding if any data filtering are required and if so which approach is most suitable.

title: Method 1: Attribute-based classification method
text:
Attribute-based classification involves classifying observations in the data by mapping structured variables or attributes available in the alternative data file to the necessary taxonomy classes. Thus each unique product detected is automatically assigned to the mapped class. This method is also commonly called rule-based classification, however will be referred to as attribute-based for consistency.


Why use attribute based classification:
Attribute-based classification is often the first to be investigated by NSOs when they wish to classify unique products. If various attributes in the data (most commonly categorical variables) are stable, then it is convenient to use this method. For instance, scanner retailers may provide National Statistical Offices (NSOs) categorical variables which represent the category the retailer itself applies to a set of products. Alternatively, after scraping a retailer website, the NSO may wish to use breadcrumbs that show which category a specific product on the website belongs to. The NSO may find these type of product attributes (i.e. categories) stable over time and thus may depend on them for classification. This is often tested when NSOs trial different classification methods as part of initial classification. For example if categories stay stable over 13 or 25 months then it may be likely that they stay stable for a while longer and it is simplest to set up a set of rules that look for specific attributes to perform classification.
Attribute-based classification may depend on very granular attributes and may be developed iteratively, such as by manually labelling a sample of the data when developing an initial classification method (using method 0). For instance, after annotating a sample of products, the NSO may find that specific retailer categories (or other attributes) are stable and can map cleanly into the classification categories to which the NSO is looking to classifying data. If the NSO finds that attributes aren't perfect and some attributes (say categories) do not cleanly map to a classification code but need tuning to filter out some products, other methods may be needed (see method 2 for more detail in such a case). 
To adopt attribute (or rule-based) classification however, it is best not to have too many attributes on which rules are based as rules need to be maintained for recurrent classification. If attributes suddenly prove unstable and there are a lot of products and thus rules to review and fix, this may be a non-trivial task to handle during tight production timelines. Hence, NSOs should be cognisant of the risk of failure and not use this method if there are too many rules that need to be maintained.


How to develop and apply attribute-based classification:
Conceptually, there are several ways that NSOs can look to create rules based on attributes:

Iterative sampling approach - NSOs can look to start with a sample of products and manually label them to the category that classification will be done to (see method 0 for more details). Then various structured attributes (such as retailer provided categories) can be determined if they are able to map all or most unique products to categories of interest. As the initial manually labelled sample may be small and not all rules may be found, it is likely that several rounds are needed to make more rules. To do this, the NSO can classify the remaining products from unclassified products, for which rules can be created. This can be continued until all products are classified.
Category-by-category mapping approach - the NSO can either (a) list all categories of interest and then look for attributes in the data that may align with the scope of the category, or (b) look at all attributes and then evaluate each, attribute-by-attribute, creating rules to link them to classes of interest. In the latter case, this is difficult if the dataset has many types of attributes but is quite simple if there are only a couple or ideally one (say retailer specified category). 

In both cases, a clear understanding of what is in-scope and out-of-scope for the categories that the NSO wants must be developed. This taxonomy definition may need to be tuned if gaps are found. It may also be advisable to double check if rules are clear and unambiguous. If there is disagreement whether a retailer category should be assigned to a category of interest, investigate the products in the category. Finally, it is likely that retailer categories will not cleanly map to categories of interest, but a many-to-one relationship (in favour of retailer category) will occur. 
In production (i.e. recurrent classification), this method may be applied on all new products to automatically assign them to a class of interest.


Best practices and quality considerations:
Several approaches of implementation and quality maintenance are recommended:

Develop robust implementation: Implementation of attribute-based methods can be based on spreadsheets in simple cases, however given it is best to do programatically, it is best to store the developed rules and the program as part of a program, such as in a version controlled location. That way there is full transparency what rules were used at which time. For instance, if rules are developed programatically, they can be saved as a distinct .csv or .json file in the same repository as the classification code. Thus the production classification system can import these rules and apply them on newly received products.
Develop reports to detect potential breaks in the rules or new attributes: The relationship between attributes in the dataset and what categories they represent could break over time (in small ways or all at once). Hence, it is necessary to develop checks to sense when this occurs. For instance, if new attributes (for instance categories) are detected, this could be a sign that some old rules are no longer correct. Alternatively, if the amount of products in each category of interest suddenly shifts it may be that attributes may no longer be correctly positioned to map correctly.

Consider an instance where a data supplier provides the prices of a variety of new and refurbished laptops and tablets, with some example observations shown in the table below:

In this case, we may set the following rules to classify data to the "New laptops" class.
Code 1: Example of a rule based on two attributes in the example data of Table 1

There are several options for handling such observations: NSOs may choose to leave these observations as out-of-scope; impute the underlying attribute variable to enable classification; or manually classify such observations in a "mop-up" exercise.

title: Treatment of discounts and refunds
text:
This page contains information on how discounts and refunds should be treated in the data.The statistical agency should examine the treatment of discounts and refunds and assess their impact if possible (see for example Ref. [1]).


Treatment of discounts
In general, prices obtained from scanner data (or web scraped data) should be consistent with the price concept used in the CPI. For example, they should include any taxes and charges that are directly connected to the purchase of the priced product.
In addition to conceptual considerations, the treatment of discounts is very much dependent on the way that discounts are recorded in the data. There can be different types of discounts. For example:

Temporarily reduced prices available to all consumers (for example 20% off). An average transaction price calculated over the reference period would cover both discounted and regular prices.
An additional quantity in the product (for example 20% more weight). Such types of discounts may be linked to changes in the article codes. Linking or grouping techniques may be needed to properly capture these discounts (see Identifying unique products).
Lower prices for damaged or defective products, or products close to their expiry date. It could be argued that such price reductions should not be included in the CPI given these are not products of comparable quality, but it may not always be possible to identify such transactions separately in the data.
Clearance prices for products reaching the end of their product lifecycle - the Dumping filter can help identify these cases when expenditure information is available.
Loyalty cards and loyalty refunds. Very often, information on such schemes cannot be extracted from the scanner data.
Multibuy offers (for example ’Buy 2 get 1 for free'). Such schemes may or may not be captured in the turnover and sales data for a specific article. Depending on the recording of such transactions, the average price may or may not be lower than the price charged for a single article.  

It is very important to discuss these aspects with the data supplier where possible (see section Data requirements specification for scanner data).


Treatment of refunds
Refunds happen when consumers return the product that they have previously purchased. Such transactions are typically treated as negative sales by the retailers. Depending on the data set, returns may or may not be separately identifiable. They can be included in the turnover and sales data of an article code. Turnover and sales could (in theory) become negative, in which case they should best be removed. Refunds may also be shown separately in the data. A further complication is that refunds may be recorded in a period other than the period of purchase. Refunds could play a more important role in some product categories, such as clothing, and may be less common in other product categories, such as food.


Other considerations
Deposits should be excluded from the price used in the calculations. The articles in the scanner data or web scraped data that have a deposit should be identified and the deposit fee should be deducted from the price where applicable.
With web scraped prices, delivery charges or credit card fees may apply. The treatment of such additional costs is discussed in paragraphs 11.78-11.80 of the CPI Manual.
For a review of how discounts and refunds could be treated in scanner data please see Ref. (1).





Reference
(1) ONS (2021). Research into the use of scanner data for constructing UK consumer price statistics. Available at: https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/articles/researchintotheuseofscannerdataforconstructingukconsumerpricestatistics/2021-04-06

title: Outlier filter
text:
Outlier filters aim at excluding or correcting extreme price increases or price decreases, typically compared to the previous period, from the price index calculation



Introduction
Outlier filters aim at excluding or correcting extreme price increases or price decreases, typically compared to the previous period, from the price index calculation.
National Statistical Offices (NSOs) should investigate the reasons for extreme price movement in a given dataset. If the scanner data are thought to provide accurate price information at the product level, outlier filters may not be required since the scanner data is considered an accurate census of transactions. If the data are thought to include noise in price information (from returns or reporting error), or if there is variation in the quality or quantity of the underlying product associated with a price, outlier removal may help exclude pricing errors and help smooth price change due to product variations. Outlier filtering should be more aggressive in unweighted indexes and for offer price data (web scraped) since outlier prices in such cases are not likely to be included in index calculations in a representative manner. 
When products are identified as outliers, it may be necessary to impute these price movements (see section on Treatment of missing prices).
There are a number of different methods available for identifying outliers in the data. The simplest approach is to define "fences" where any data that lie outside these thresholds are removed. Other approaches are also available, although to the best of our knowledge none of these methods are currently used in production. These methods can be applied to price levels, or some measurement of price change (for example, month on month; base period to current period) within a product group in a particular time period. Because there are so many possible combinations it is important to test fully the impact of these methods on the final index values as it is likely to differ between different data sources and/or product groups.
The parameters for these methods to identify outliers should be set very carefully such that the number of outliers remains low and the setting of the thresholds does not lead to any bias of the index results.


User defined fences
This approach creates a range of accepted values by setting a cut off threshold (or "fence"). National Statistical Offices (NSOs) have previously set these ratios to be between ratio 3 and ratio 4 (see the section on current practice). Ratio 3 means that articles whose prices increase by more than 200% or decrease by more than 66% are removed. In order to make sure that decimal errors are detected the ratios should not exceed the value of 10. Of course, the upper and the lower threshold can also not be based on a certain ratio but instead can be chosen separately. For example, Poland has set the upper limit for the outlier filter at factor 3 (200% price increase) and the lower limit at 0.25 (75% price decrease). Moreover, the ratio can be set differently depending on the product group (for example, more volatile product groups may require a higher ratio than more stable categories).

Further research is needed to investigate how to detect the optimal values for this approach. An example of research in this area is from the Office for National Statistics (2022): Outlier detection for rail fares and second-hand cars dynamic price data where the user defined fence with value 3 has since been implemented for used cars and railfares, and subsequent follow-up research for groceries (yet to be implemented) (2023): Outlier detection for grocery scanner data in consumer price statistics


Other approaches
As an alternative to the fixed thresholds, Białek and Beręsewicz (2021) tested removing each month all products with the lowest and the highest one percent of all price changes within each product group. It was shown that this alternative had a bigger impact on the index results than fixed thresholds of ratio 3 or ratio 4.
Another option could be the use of a flexible outlier filter. A flexible outlier filter may take the historic price development of the product group into consideration in order to define whether a price is an outlier or not.
Other potential methods that create a range of acceptable values are the Tukey, kimber and k sigma approaches. These are defined as follows:

Tukey: Tukey’s rule says that the outliers are values that are more than 1.5 times the interquartile range from the quartiles — i.e., either below Q1 − 1.5 IQR, or above Q3 + 1.5 IQR. If Q1 and Q3 are the lower and upper quartiles respectively, then one could define an outlier to be any observation outside the range (in the standard implementation, k here is defined at 1.5 but it is a editable parameter): [Q1 – k(Q3-Q1), Q3 + k(Q3-Q1)]
Kimber: To incorporate the skewness of the distribution and possibly improve outlier detection, Kimber proposed fences using a constant multiple of the lower and the upper semi-interquartile ranges measured from the first and third quartile, respectively. The formula for this is: [LF =Q1 – k(𝑆𝐼𝑄𝑅𝐿), UF= Q3 + k(𝑆𝐼𝑄𝑅𝑈)]
K-Sigma: Given a normal distribution, k-Sigma (usually 3-sigma) follows the idea that nearly all values lie within 3 standard deviations from the mean. Any data that falls outside of this boundary may be determined as an outlier

Finally, there are also other more complex methods to identify outliers that use machine learning. For example, the DBSCAN algorithm is a method that identifies high density areas “clusters” of products. Any products that aren’t identified as a belonging to a cluster are then identified as being outliers. For a wider review of possible methods that can be used for outlier detection, please see previous ONS (2021) research.





References

text:
Requirements for IT systems are dependent on the choice of data source, the implementation plan for each new data source and the availability and knowledge of staff with specialist IT skills. In general, considerations can be split into IT requirements for data collection, transfer and storage, and production systems.

title: Bilateral price index methods
text:
This section presents the basic, commonly known formulas of bilateral price indices. Like the Multilateral price index methods section, it does not include a broader discussion of the legitimacy of using individual indices. For an overview of approaches to select an index method, see the Choosing an index method section.
There are many methods available to calculate a price index. Bilateral price indices use observations from two periods, for instance, they compare the current period with the base one. Unweighted indices use only prices available in the base period and the current period, while weighted indices also use expenditure information for these two periods if available.




Unweighted indices
Three indices are commonly described – the Jevons, Dudot, and Carli. The Jevons can be written as follows:
\[P_{J}^{0, t}=\prod_{i \in G_{0, t}} \left(\frac{p_{i}^{t}}{p_{i}^{0}}\right)^{\frac{1}{N_{0, t}}}\]
where \(G_{0,t}\) is a set of matched products in both months 0 and t, \(p_i^{\tau}\) denotes the price of the i-th product at time \(\tau \in \{0,t\}\) and \(N_{0,t}= \operatorname{card} G_{0,t}\).
The Dutot price index can be written as:
\[P_{D}^{0, t}=\frac{\sum\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} p_{i}^{t}}{\sum\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} p_{i}^{0}}\]
And the Carli price index is an arithmetic mean of price relatives, i.e.
\[P_{C}^{0, t}=\frac{1}{N_{0, t}} \sum\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} \frac{p_{i}^{t}}{p_{i}^{0}}\]
For a homogeneous group of products, a Dutot or a Carruthers-Sellwood-Ward-Dalen (a geometric mean of the Carli and the harmonic mean of price relatives (Lippe, 2007)) can be used. At the same time, the Carli formula overestimates real price change (CPI Manual, 2020), thus the Jevons is recommended by the European Commission when expenditure information is not available in a data set (Eurostat, 2018) and by the 1996 Boskin Commission in the USA, which recommended a shift rom a Carli-like index (Levell, 2015). Eurostat regulations do not allow the use of the Carli index in the construction of the members’ Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP). Furthermore, there has been a general trend of replacing the Carli index with the Jevons or Dudot formulas (Evans, 2012).
A less common but worth noting unweighted price index formula is the Balk-Mehrhoff-Walsh (BMW) index (Eurostat, 2018), which can be expressed as follows:
\[P_{BMW}^{0, t}=\sum\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} \frac{p_{i}^{t}}{p_{i}^{0}} \frac{\sqrt{\frac{p_{i}^{0}}{p_{i}^{t}}}}{\sum\limits_{k \in G_{0, t}} \sqrt{\frac{p_{k}^{0}}{p_{k}^{t}}}}\]


Weighted indices
Since scanner data contain information about expenditures, which can have a big impact on a price index, quantities \(q_i^t\) of sold products can be used to calculate weighted bilateral indices. Two weighted indices which figure prominently in the literature, are the Laspeyres (1871) and Paasche (1874), given respectively by
\[P_{La}^{0, t}=\frac{\sum\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} q_{i}^{0} p_{i}^{t}}{\sum\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} q_{i}^{0} p_{i}^{0}}\]
and 
\[P_{Pa}^{0, t}=\frac{\sum\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} q_{i}^{t} p_{i}^{t}}{\sum\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} q_{i}^{t} p_{i}^{0}}\]
Superlative price indices are also very prominent. Superlative indices can be expected to approximate the Cost of Living Index (COLI), and are ‘exact’ for a flexible aggregator, which is a second-order approximation to an arbitrary production, cost, utility or distance function and they treat prices and quantities equally across periods. The Fisher, Törnqvist, and Walsh price indices are examples of of superlative indices. Superlatives are also commonly accepted as base formulas in the multilateral GEKS method (Diewert and Fox, 2017). 
The Fisher (1922) formula, which can be written as:
\[P_{F}^{0, t}=\sqrt{P_{La}^{0, t} \cdot P_{Pa}^{0, t}}\]
where \(P_{La}^{0, t}\) and \(P_{Pa}^{0, t}\) denote the Laspeyres and Paasche price index respectively. The Törnqvist can be written as
\[P_{T}^{0, t}=\prod\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} \left(\frac{p_{i}^{t}}{p_{i}^{0}}\right)^{\frac{s_{i}^{0}+s_{i}^{t}}{2}}\]
where \(s_i^0\) and \(s_i^t\) denote the expenditure shares of matched products in months 0 and t. Walsh can be written as
\[P_{W}^{0, t}=\frac{\sum\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} \sqrt{q_{i}^{0} q_{i}^{t}} \cdot p_{i}^{t}}{\sum\limits_{i \in G_{0, t}} \sqrt{q_{i}^{0} q_{i}^{t}} \cdot p_{i}^{0}}\]
Some statisticians use the Sato-Vartia index (Sato 1976; Vartia 1976) for scanner data case due to its good axiomatic properties (Lippe 2007; Abe & Prasada Rao 2019). Following Sato (1976), the log-change price index has the following generic form:
\[\ln P_{S V}^{0, t}=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \phi_{i}^{0, t} \ln \left(\frac{p_{i}^{t}}{p_{i}^{0}}\right)\]
where 
\[\phi_{i}^{0, t}=\frac{ \frac{s_{i}^{t}-s_{i}^{0}}{\ln \left(s_{i}^{t}\right)-\ln \left(s_{i}^{0}\right)}}{ \sum\limits_{k \in G_{0, t}} \frac{s_{k}^{t}-s_{k}^{0}}{\ln \left(s_{k}^{t}\right)-\ln \left(s_{k}^{0}\right)}}\]
A wide range of price indices, including an overview of their properties and relationships between them, can be found in the CPI Manual (2020), Consumer Price Index Theory, von der Lippe, P. (2007), and Eurostat (2018). Some less familiar and non-classical formulas of weighted price indices can be found, for example, in the works of Białek (2014) or Białek (2020).


Chaining indices
In the "direct" approach, the resulting price index \(P^{0,t}\) is not influenced by what happens to prices and quantities in the intermediate points in time: 1, 2, ... , t-1.  The idea of chain indices is that a longer interval is partitioned into a subset of smaller intervals on which bilateral indices are calculated and subsequently combined (chained). In other words, a chain index provides a measure of the cumulative effect of successive steps from 0 to 1, 1 to 2, ..., t-1 to t (Lippe, 2007). In general, the chain index takes the following form:
\[P_{ch}^{0, t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t} P^{s-1, s}\]
where the linking formula \(P^{s-1, s}\) is any bilateral price index. For instance, one can consider the chain Fisher price index defined as follows
\[P_{ch-F}^{0, t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t} P_{F}^{s-1, s}\]

title: Treatment of missing prices
text:
This page contains information on how to treat missing prices through product-level imputation methods.



Treatment of missing prices
The focus in this section lies in methods to impute a temporarily missing price possibly caused, for example, by a product not being available at the time of price collection (sold-out, breakdown of supply chains), seasonalities, erratic reporting, or a non-sale (or indeed through the use of outlier detection methods). Of course, it is critical to avoid any bias to the index through imputation.
Following the CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods (2020), various procedures for imputations include:

Overall mean imputation
Target mean imputation
Carry forward
Hedonic (regression) methods

In general, omitting the variety for which the price is missing is not recommended.

Overall mean imputation: Imputing the missing price by the average price change for the prices that are available in the elementary aggregate. This method provides the same result as simply dropping the variety that is missing from both periods from the calculation. It is simple to program and requires no subjective decision-making.
Targeted mean imputation: Imputing the missing price by the price change of an elementary aggregate or an aggregate of similar varieties, that is, varieties expected to have similar short-term price changes (for example, within the same geographic area or type of outlet). A key requirement of this method is an adequate sample size of those items used to calculate the imputation.
Carry forward: Use of the last observed price (i.e., no price change). This method should only be used when the compiler has a high certainty that the price has not changed (for example, for tariffs set annually).
Hedonic (regression) methods: A log-linear regression model is estimated on the pooled data of all periods using Weighted Least Squares with the expenditure shares of the single items in each period serving as weights. When detailed information on the item’s (quantity of) characteristics is available, the Time Dummy Hedonic (TDH) method can be used. An alternative is, in absence of such quality information, the Time-Product Dummy (TPD) method which is based on item fixed-effects. The fitted values of these models (adequately back-transformed) are the imputed missing prices. For a comparison of both methods, see, for example, de Haan, Hendriks, and Scholz (2021).

Only a few studies are conducted that assess the missing pattern in the CPI microdata or compare the performance of the aforementioned imputation methods. Feenstra and Diewert (2000) discuss alternative imputation methods for missing prices in the construction of price indexes. They evaluate the alternatives by their ability to both minimize the erratic movement in the price index and still incorporate all available information.  Bradley (2003) examines and compares diﬀerent imputation methods including an economic approach. Indexes are constructed using these various imputation methods using price and expenditure data from scanner sales of cereal in the New York area. Gomes (2018) investigates empirically the mechanism of missingness (prices in relation to other covariates). Kelly and Mogalanyane (2019) use a multi-year synthetic dataset and find that the overall and targeted mean imputation method most often had the lowest deviation in the imputed price and the overall index.
With regards to new data sources, in scanner data, when a particular item in a particular outlet does not sell in a certain period, it is not possible to determine if this non-sale was the result of no inventories or no consumer demand for the product (because the price was too high). Therefore it is not possible to get a “list” price as one would be able to collect through a standard sampling system. The use of matched-item GEKS price indexes (see Multilateral price index methods) do not explicitly account for new and disappearing items and can suffer from quality change bias or bias due to a change in barcode during a product relaunch. In de Haan and Daalmans (2019) Scanner Data in the CPI: The Imputation CCDI Index Revisited , the authors present a GEKS index that is explicitly quality-adjusted through imputation of the unmatched new and disappearing items’ “missing prices”.

title: Data requirements specification for web scraped data
text:
Outlet identifier
Identification of the online retailer can be provided by the URL that identifies the site. In the case that data is extracted from marketplaces or price comparison websites, it might be useful to collect the URL or other information that characterizes the outlet.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for web scraped data

title: Data requirements specification for web scraped data
text:
Article identifier
To allow a unique identification and track of an article, important characteristics include:

the URL of the article within the site
when available, code of the article such as Global Trade Item Number (GTIN), stock keeping unit (SKU) or the retailer’s own code. Note that for services, this may not apply.
short text with the article description (for example, product name or service description)
additional article’s characteristics (for example, for clothing you may be interested in material or size)
retailers' classification of the article

Note that items (3), (4), and (5) are especially useful for purposes of automatic classification of the articles and stratification into homogeneous products. The use of the items characteristics is also key for the derivation of hedonic indices.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for web scraped data

title: Data requirements specification for web scraped data
text:
Price and Time
The observed product offer of the article displayed in the web site. In some cases, more than one price is displayed by the retailer. The National Statistical Office (NSO) should extract the price that best suits the scope of the CPI. The time or date for which the price is extracted should also be recorded for compilation purposes.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for web scraped data

title: Data requirements specification for web scraped data
text:
Other information
Delivery fees can also be a price determinant characteristic as consumer’s may face different fees according to their residence address. In this case, the collection of such taxes is advisable.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for web scraped data

title: Data requirements specification for web scraped data
text:
Frequency of collection and comparability
The frequency of collection can vary according to the variables characteristics and pricing dynamics of the goods and services being tracked. Information on variables such as product attributes that usually do not change can be scraped on a different schedule (for example, weekly) compared with more frequently changing attributes such as the price.
The frequency of collection of prices will depend on the price dynamics associated with a given sector and retailer. In many cases, a daily collection of prices is enough. However, if significant price changes occur as a function of time of day, collections at higher frequencies could be used. For more details on price dynamics of web retailers see Ref. (1). However, increasing the number of collections has implications for the amount of data storage required and also increases the risk of blocking by the website through the increased burden. In instances where prices are not expected to change much, the collection frequency can be updated accordingly to align to traditional collection (for example, monthly).
Internet prices can also present different results according to different factors such as the internet protocol (IP) addresses and computer brand. These dynamics are more prevalent for services. One should take care that changes in such characteristics are not creating spurious price changes across time.
crumbs: Data requirements specification for web scraped data

title: Data requirements specification for web scraped data
text:
Proxy weights
Web data does not provide information on items and quantities sold for the derivation of elementary weighted indices. However, proxy variables can be adopted for this purpose, and this can require the collection of additional data according to the method adopted. One possibility is to adopt the number of times an item is offered by the site within a given period (most commonly monthly) to derive its weights. In this scenario, it is important to not remove duplicates, that is, products that appear on multiple pages on a website, for example, once in "men's clothing" and once in "ready for summer". Another possibility is to use the retailer’s popularity ranks of most sold items. For more details on the use of proxy weights see the wiki section on expenditure proxies.


Section Example file structures for web scraped and scanner data of this wiki provides a comparison between what a typical file structure may look like for scanner data and web scraped data.

title: Methods for when expenditure data are available
text: This page summarizes potential criteria that could be used by an NSO to decide on an index method for when expenditure data are available.
crumbs: Methods for when expenditure data are available

title: Methods for when expenditure data are available
text:
Axiomatic approach
According to the axiomatic approach, desirable index properties (the so called “tests”) are defined that a multilateral index may, or may not satisfy. The list of tests for multilateral indices can be found in chapter 7 (5) of the latest version of "Consumer Price Index Theory". Interesting considerations concerning tests for price indices in the case of dynamic data sets can be found in Li-Chun Zhang et. al. (2019). 
Common multilateral index formulas (GK, GEKS, CCDI, TPD) meet most of the requirements at the same time, such as transitivity, multi-period identity test, positivity and continuity, proportionality, homogeneity in prices, commensurability, symmetry in the treatment of time periods or symmetry in treatment of products. However, the discussed indexes differ in terms of the total set of tests they meet. For instance: the GEKS, CCDI and TPD indices do not satisfy the basket test, the Geary-Khamis and TPD indices do not satisfy the responsiveness test to imputed prices while the GEKS or CCDI can incorporate the imputed prices of missing products, the homogeneity in quantities does not hold in the case of the Geary-Khamis formula. Please also note that the SPQ index is the only multilateral index that satisfies the identity test, which is a stronger requirement than the lack of the chain drift.
crumbs: Methods for when expenditure data are available

title: Methods for when expenditure data are available
text:
Economic approach
The economic approach to the price index theory assumes that the quantities are functions of prices. This approach assumes that households optimize their purchase by maximizing their utility under a budget constraint or by minimizing the cost of purchases for a given utility level. The multilateral methods involve different assumptions about the functional form of the utility function. For instance, the GEKS index is exact for a "flexible" functional form, i.e.  it expresses the price differences experienced by optimizing consumers without imposing restrictive assumptions about how they can substitute between products. In contrast, the GK is consistent only with linear utility functions, so it may suffer substitution bias if consumer preferences are more complex (ABS). 
Many authors consider and assume the CES (Constant Elasticity of Substitution) utility function. For instance, Diewert and Fox (2017) generated artificial data sets assuming different values of the parameter of the elasticity of substitution (which is constant in the CES model). They found that the CCDI index approximates CES preferences reasonably well. In the same work they showed that the GK indices are upward biased regardless of the selected elasticity parameter while the TPD index has also substantial upward bias for elasticity parameter of 2 or 4 (when the elasticity parameter equals 1, the TPD index is unbiased).
crumbs: Methods for when expenditure data are available

title: Methods for when expenditure data are available
text:
Stochastic approach
The TPD index is based on the assumption that prices can be estimated via an econometric model. Since the weighted least squares (WLS) is a well-known statistical method, the use of the TPD is clearly understandable by users and that index is quite easy for implementation. Please note that the use of the TPD index is justified in situations where the individual products are closely related and thus their prices can be well approximated by the regression model. Note that the econometric model explaining price behavior can be modified with variables related to product characteristics (so-called hedonic models such as the TDH). This is particularly important if the dataset includes numerous new and disappearing products, and the standard multilateral method is based on a bilateral index that includes only matched products (like GEKS). When we want to estimate the prices of missing products, or when we simply want to estimate prices taking into account additional product characteristics, we can use hedonic methods. In particular, the CCDI index can be applied by using bilateral imputation Tornqvist index instead of "classical" matched Tornqvist formula, the TPD method can be replaced by the TDH method, while the standard Geary-Khamis index can be replaced by the explicitly quality adjusted unit value index, where adjustment coefficients are estimated by the econometric model using product characteristics. Some interesting comparison of the TPD and TDH indices can be found in de Haan et al. al. (2021), where the authors decompose the ratio of the two indexes in terms of average regression residuals of the new and disappearing items. The above-mentioned decomposition provides conditions under which the TPD index suffers from the quality-change bias.
crumbs: Methods for when expenditure data are available

title: Methods for when expenditure data are available
text:
Other criteria
With the exception of the SPQ index, by default, the choice of a multilateral index entails the decision to choose the width of the time window and the splicing technique in order to avoid obtaining a revision of already published indexes. Some empirical works suggest that the TPD and GK indices are more sensitive to these choices comparing to other multilateral indices (GEKS, CCDI). On the other hand, the GEKS and CCDI indices seem to be more sensitive to the so called “dump prices” (dumping occurs when a product is sold at reduced prices before removing from the market). In addition, to the aforementioned index selection criterion, which could be called "robustness", some statisticians use additional criteria. Another possible consideration is the time required to calculate the index, such as in the case of the Geary-Khamis (GK) and TPD indices, which take more time compared to the GEKS or CCDI indices (2). Finally, another approach recently proposed takes into account a predetermined probabilistic distribution of prices and / or quantities. Specifically, knowing the theoretical stochastic processes that describe the price evolution of a homogeneous product group, we can determine the expected values ​​for a price change for such a product group in a given time period. The theoretical value of the price index determined in this way can then be compared with the bilateral and/or multilateral indices calculated on the basis of the generated artificial set of data (on the basis of assumed probability distributions). See Białek & Bobel, 2019 for more information.

title: Handbook migration: Confluence → Quarto
text:
Status and coordination notes for migrating the Handbook on utilising new data sources in the production of consumer price statistics from the UN Statistics Confluence wiki (space GWGSD) to this Quarto site, hosted on GitHub Pages under UN-Task-Team-for-Scanner-Data.


The full handbook is converted: all 72 pages from the export’s index.html tree, with the sidebar mirroring the wiki hierarchy, cross-page links rewritten to local targets, and linked attachments (PDF/docx) copied under files/. The whole site passes scripts/verify_site.py with zero defects: every page’s rendered formula and image counts match the Confluence source exactly, every internal link and image resolves, and no page has line-ending corruption. What remains is human review (reading the pages), org repo access, and deployment — see the issue list below.
Batch tooling:
uv run scripts/convert_all.py --plan   # show the page tree, slugs, math/image stats
uv run scripts/convert_all.py --run    # convert everything + rewrite links + sidebar YAML
uv run scripts/verify_site.py          # after quarto render: parity + link check



The site is live at https://un-task-team-for-scanner-data.github.io/cpi-new-data-sources-handbook/
.github/workflows/publish.yml renders the site and publishes it to the gh-pages branch on every push to main (quarto-dev/quarto-actions).


The gh-pages branch must exist before the workflow or quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt will run. Quarto creates the branch only when it can prompt for confirmation, so a non-interactive session must create it first. The error message is circular. It tells you to run the command you just ran.
git checkout --orphan gh-pages
git reset --hard
git commit --allow-empty -m "Initialise gh-pages branch for Quarto publishing"
git push origin gh-pages
git checkout main
quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt --no-browser
Run this from a short local path, for example C:\qp. Windows applies a 260 character path limit. Quarto builds a publish worktree under .quarto/, and the long image filenames in this project pass the limit under a deep directory. Also set git config core.longpaths true.
Pushing gh-pages enabled GitHub Pages automatically. No Pages setting was needed. Quarto writes .nojekyll to the branch, so Jekyll does not process the site.
quarto publish gh-pages writes no _publish.yml. That file records a site ID for the Quarto Pub and Netlify targets. The gh-pages target holds its state in the branch.



Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions must be Read and write permissions. The default is read-only. It caps the workflow token, so the action cannot push to gh-pages.



The site serves from a subpath, not a domain root. site-url in _quarto.yml must match the published URL exactly, or search and the sitemap point at the wrong host while every page still renders correctly.




As agreed by email (Jul–Aug 2026): convert one or two example pages that are heavy in both LaTeX and images, verify they render faithfully, then scale to the full set (~73 pages). Useful facts about the Confluence export discovered during scanning:

Formulas are exported as literal LaTeX text (\( ... \) / \[ ... \] inside <span>s) — not images — so math survives conversion losslessly.
Images live at attachments/<pageid>/<attachmentid>.<ext> and are referenced from span.confluence-embedded-file-wrapper containers.

CRLF doubling: pandoc emits CRLF on Windows; writing its stdout in text mode doubles the CR (\r\r\n), which makes Quarto silently drop whole blocks of a page (images, sections) with no warning. The converter normalizes newlines and writes LF.

.github/workflows/publish.yml renders the site and publishes it to the gh-pages branch on every push to main (quarto-dev/quarto-actions).


The gh-pages branch must exist before the workflow or quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt will run. Quarto creates the branch only when it can prompt for confirmation, so a non-interactive session must create it first. The error message is circular. It tells you to run the command you just ran.
git checkout --orphan gh-pages
git reset --hard
git commit --allow-empty -m "Initialise gh-pages branch for Quarto publishing"
git push origin gh-pages
git checkout main
quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt --no-browser
Run this from a short local path, for example C:\qp. Windows applies a 260 character path limit. Quarto builds a publish worktree under .quarto/, and the long image filenames in this project pass the limit under a deep directory. Also set git config core.longpaths true.
Pushing gh-pages enabled GitHub Pages automatically. No Pages setting was needed. Quarto writes .nojekyll to the branch, so Jekyll does not process the site.
quarto publish gh-pages writes no _publish.yml. That file records a site ID for the Quarto Pub and Netlify targets. The gh-pages target holds its state in the branch.



Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions must be Read and write permissions. The default is read-only. It caps the workflow token, so the action cannot push to gh-pages.



The site serves from a subpath, not a domain root. site-url in _quarto.yml must match the published URL exactly, or search and the sitemap point at the wrong host while every page still renders correctly.

title: Handbook migration: Confluence → Quarto
text:
CRLF doubling: pandoc emits CRLF on Windows; writing its stdout in text mode doubles the CR (\r\r\n), which makes Quarto silently drop whole blocks of a page (images, sections) with no warning. The converter normalizes newlines and writes LF.
Confluence anchor IDs: heading ids like {#...method(WISP)} contain characters invalid in CSS selectors; the converter strips them to [A-Za-z0-9_-].
Layout wrappers: all residual <div>/<span> wrappers are unwrapped so pandoc emits plain markdown; Confluence layout markup carries no meaning in Quarto.
Verify with clean state: always delete .quarto/ before a build you intend to judge (serve.ps1 does this automatically). If the repo lives in a Google-Drive-synced folder, be aware Drive can serve stale file content to build tools; when output looks impossible, re-render from a fresh local copy.

title: Key decision points
text:
The adoption of alternative data sources involves a sequence of related decisions that shape both the technical and organisational direction of implementation.
These decisions are rarely one-off and may need to be revisited as experience grows, systems evolve, and data availability changes. Making these decision points explicit can help NSOs plan their work more coherently and avoid misalignment between strategy, methods, and resources.


What data to use, and for what purpose
One of the first decisions concerns which data sources to use, and what role they are expected to play in CPI production and other official statistical outputs. Alternative data may be used to:

Replace existing survey-based price collection
Supplement existing sources to improve coverage or timeliness
Support research and experimental indices prior to full production use
Support other statistical outputs produced by an NSO

NSOs may also choose to adopt different data sources for different product groups, depending on market structure, data availability, and quality considerations.
When acquiring alternative data sources, NSOs may also wish to consider whether the data could support statistical uses beyond CPI, such as national accounts or purchasing power parities. For example, decisions around the treatment of VAT, the definition of turnover, and the level of aggregation may affect the suitability of the data for other purposes. While CPI specific requirements will often take precedence, early consideration of potential reuse may reduce duplication of data acquisition and processing effort across the organisation. See section Other uses of alternative data sources.
Clarifying the purpose can help determine the level of methodological ambition, the acceptable level of operational risk, and the extent to which existing production processes may need to change.


Sampling from the data versus using the full universe
Alternative data sources often provide far more observations than traditional surveys, leading to a key decision on whether to work with the full universe of observed prices or transactions, or whether to construct samples from the data. Sampling approaches may reduce processing burden, simplify quality assurance, and align more closely with existing CPI practices. By contrast, using the full universe of data may better capture product turnover and changes in consumption patterns, but typically requires more advanced systems and methods.
This decision has direct implications for index method choice, system design, and validation strategies, and should therefore be considered alongside broader implementation plans. Sampling approaches are discussed further in the section Product sampling for price index calculation.


Choice of index method and compilation approach
Index method selection is a central decision point and depends on several interrelated factors, including data availability, product churn, and revision policies. The choice between bilateral and multilateral methods, as well as between static and dynamic compilation approaches, should be informed by both data properties and organisational constraints.
Where alternative data include quantity or expenditure information, NSOs must decide whether and how this information will be used in index compilation. This involves assessing the reliability and conceptual suitability of the data, considering whether proxy measures are appropriate where quantities are unavailable, and determining how frequently weights should be updated.
These decisions strongly influence whether weighted or unweighted index methods are feasible and affect how closely resulting indices reflect consumer behaviour at detailed levels.
Many NSOs adopt a phased approach, beginning with simpler bilateral methods and transitioning to multilateral approaches as experience and system capability increase. Details of these methods are provided in the section on Price index methods.


Integration with existing production systems and user communication
Alternative data sources rarely operate in isolation. NSOs must decide how new data will be integrated with existing CPI production systems, including traditional price surveys, aggregation structures, and dissemination practices. In some cases, parallel systems may be maintained during transition periods; in others, production processes may be redesigned more fundamentally. See section CPI production system requirements for more information.
These decisions affect not only technical implementation but also staffing, maintenance, and long-term sustainability.
Introducing alternative data sources may also affect CPI outputs, even when headline results remain broadly similar. NSOs should therefore consider how methodological changes will be tested and evaluated, how impacts will be analysed, and how developments will be communicated to users. Clear documentation and transparent decision-making are essential to maintaining trust in official statistics during periods of change. These aspects are discussed further in the section on Implementation.
